turns.content: Hello, I'm glad you're here to start our time together today. How have you been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything specific on your mind you'd like us to explore first?

Hi... thanks for having me. I've been okay, I guess, but that nagging feeling just keeps hanging around. Ever since the expo, I can't shake the thought that I let everyone down, and it's been popping up even when I'm just playing casually at home.

That "nagging" feeling sounds really heavy to carry around, especially when you try to relax at home. It makes sense that the expo experience would still feel so fresh and impactful on your mind right now. What was the very first thing that triggered this sense of letting people down when you started looking back at the event?

It was right after the final match ended, and we lost by a really close margin. I was playing a key role, and I made this one mistake—I hesitated for just a second when I shouldn't have. In my head, I just knew that hesitation cost us the whole thing, and I've been replaying it over and over since then.

I hear how painful it is to believe that a split-second moment defined the entire outcome for everyone involved. That sense of responsibility, while understandable given your role, seems to be creating a loop where the past feels more significant than it actually was. Can you tell me about any other moments from the day where things went smoothly, or perhaps where someone else might have taken that step instead?

I mean, I guess there were some rounds where I made good calls and we pulled ahead, but those feel kind of erased now. And sure, other teammates had moments where they could've done something different too, but it doesn't feel right to put any blame on them—it's easier to just point at myself.

It takes courage to admit that blaming yourself feels like the easiest path, even if it hurts more in the long run. When we hold onto that self-blame, it often makes us feel powerless because it convinces us that nothing we do differently will change the result. Let's look closely at whether those "good call" moments truly disappeared, or if your brain is just filtering them out to make the failure seem bigger. Did you notice anyone else making a similar hesitation later in the game, or did that specific second feel completely unique to you?

I didn't really pay attention to anyone else's mistakes, honestly—I was too busy replaying my own. But now that you ask, I do remember my teammate on the left fumbling a combo near the end, but I didn't think much of it because I was just focused on me. I guess it's not like I was the only one who made an error, but it still feels different when it's your own.

That distinction you just made—focusing on your own errors versus others'—is incredibly common and tells us a lot about how intense the emotion felt during that moment. It's not that your memory is wrong about the team effort, but rather that your mind zoomed in tightly on the part where you felt most vulnerable. Have you noticed if trying to imagine what another player would have done in that exact spot changes how bad the situation feels to you right now?

I never really thought about it that way... I mean, if someone else had been in my shoes, they might have frozen up too or made a different kind of mistake. I guess I just assumed I was the only one who could've messed it up so badly, but that's probably not fair to myself either.

That assumption—that you alone were capable of causing such a catastrophic error—is a very human reaction to high stakes, but it can easily become unfair to ourselves. Even though we know others might have reacted similarly under pressure, telling ourselves we were uniquely responsible creates a story that feels heavier than the reality of the game itself. Does holding onto the idea that *only* your hesitation mattered help you feel better about winning the match again, or does it keep you stuck in regret?

It definitely keeps me stuck in regret, not better at all. I feel like I'm just waiting for the next competition to prove myself, but at the same time I'm terrified I'll mess up again, and that cycle just keeps going.

That fear of repeating the mistake creates a painful loop where preparation turns into anxiety, which then fuels the fear of failing. It makes sense that you want to prove yourself, yet the anticipation itself feels like a threat rather than an opportunity. Could we try shifting that expectation slightly to see if it helps ease the tension? Instead of aiming to "prove" you won't freeze, what if we viewed the upcoming competition simply as a chance to play your best game, regardless of the outcome?

I guess I've never really thought about it that way... just playing for the fun of it and not worrying about the result. That sounds almost freeing, but honestly, it's hard to let go of that pressure because winning has always been a part of how I measure myself in games.

That connection between winning and your self-worth is deeply ingrained, so shifting away from it feels counterintuitive rather than liberating. It makes perfect sense that wanting to succeed is tied to how you define yourself as a player, but carrying that weight changes how you experience every game. Since that shift is tricky right now, maybe we can try a small experiment where you consciously remind yourself that you're allowed to play well without needing victory to validate your effort. Would you be open to noticing what happens to your anxiety if you just observe that thought arise without judging it immediately?

Yeah, I can try that... just noticing the thought and not automatically beating myself up for it. I guess I've never really given myself permission to just play without that inner critic screaming at me the whole time.

Giving yourself that permission is a powerful first step, and it shows a lot of growth in realizing that your inner voice can sometimes be overly harsh. It's natural to expect perfection when we care deeply about the activity, but allowing yourself to simply exist in the moment without constant judgment is a skill worth practicing. To try this out, could you describe exactly what you told yourself the moment you felt that urge to critique yourself coming up? Did you catch it, or did you find yourself already spiraling?

The last time I caught it was yesterday, while I was practicing a new strategy on my own. I started to feel that familiar tightness in my chest and thought, "You're going to mess up again just like at the expo." But then I remembered what we talked about, and I tried to just breathe and say, "Let's see what happens this time." It didn't completely go away, but it felt a little less overwhelming.

That moment where you paused to breathe and offered yourself a kinder phrase is a huge breakthrough, showing you are learning to interrupt the old pattern. The fact that the thought didn't vanish entirely but became less overwhelming proves that simply changing your relationship with it can soften its impact. Now that we've identified that specific internal dialogue, what do you think might happen if you practice saying that gentler version to yourself whenever that chest tightness returns during casual gaming?

I think if I keep practicing it, maybe that voice will get quieter over time, or at least I won't feel so trapped by it. It's hard to believe right now, but I guess the only way to find out is to keep trying, and see if it actually makes a difference in how I feel during the game.

That sense of uncertainty is completely normal when stepping off a familiar emotional track, but your willingness to trust the process despite not knowing the full outcome yet is exactly what drives real change. You've already taken the hardest step by recognizing the pattern and choosing a different response, which sets the foundation for that quiet voice to eventually take over. Before we wrap up, I'd love to hear if there's anything else about your experience at the expo or how you're feeling right now that we haven't quite touched on yet.

I think we've covered the main thing that's been bothering me, and honestly, just talking about it out loud has made it feel a little less heavy. I guess I'm still nervous about the next competition, but at least now I have a tiny bit more hope that I can handle the pressure without tearing myself apart.

Hearing you say that the act of speaking it out loud has already shifted the weight of things is such a positive sign of progress. Carrying those thoughts silently can make them feel enormous, but breaking them down into words gives you space to examine and manage them. Since we've worked through the core issue, I'd like to suggest a simple homework task: whenever you feel that familiar chest tightness coming up before the next game, pause for three deep breaths and consciously repeat your new phrase, "Let's see what happens," before moving back to play. How does that sound like something you can try starting tomorrow?
Hi there, I'm so glad we're connecting today. How are you feeling right now compared to where you were when we last spoke? What would you like to focus on if we don't start with something else?

Hey, thanks for asking. I guess I'm feeling a bit better just knowing I'm here, but honestly, I'm still pretty down about the team. I've been thinking about that loss over and over, and it just feels like we're doomed for the rest of the tournament. That's probably what I'd want to talk about.

It makes sense that knowing we're talking about it brings a little relief, even though the worry about the team hasn't gone away yet. When you say things feel "doomed," can you tell me more about what specifically is driving that sense of hopelessness right now?

Well, it's like... we lost one game, and I can't shake the feeling that it's all over. I keep thinking about how we played poorly, and now every other team is going to be better than us. It's like I can already see us losing every single game from here on out, even though we haven't played them yet. That thought just sits in my gut and won't leave.

That feeling of seeing the future before it happens can be really exhausting and scary. It sounds like the belief that one bad performance means total failure is making everything look much darker than it might actually be. Have you noticed any other people who are worried about the team too, or does it seem like everyone else sees it differently?

Actually, my teammates are still pretty positive. They keep saying things like "we've got this" and "it's just one loss, we'll bounce back." I want to believe them, but in my head, I just can't see how. It's like they're all looking at the same thing I am, but they're seeing a totally different picture. That kinda makes me feel even more alone in this, you know?

It is incredibly hard to feel isolated when everyone around you seems optimistic while you feel trapped in your own certainty. That gap between what you perceive and what others experience can make the doubt feel even heavier. Could you describe a moment recently when you had to choose between trusting your gut feeling or listening to what your teammates are saying?

Yeah, there was a moment at practice yesterday. We were doing drills, and I just felt like giving up halfway through—like, what's the point? But one of my teammates came over and hyped me up, said we're still in this. I went along with it, but inside I was still convinced he was wrong. It's like I went through the motions, but my head was screaming that it was all pointless.

That moment highlights exactly where the disconnect is happening: your body moved with the group, but your mind was still locked into the belief that effort wouldn't matter because one loss was fatal. It sounds like even trying to participate made the internal conflict feel more painful than just sitting it out. Have you ever tried to ask yourself why those teammates' words feel convincing to you in one second, but immediately contradictory the very next second?

I guess... maybe because they haven't been through what I've seen before? But that doesn't make sense either, because we've all been on the same team. I think it's just that when I focus on the loss, everything else fades away. Their words feel true for a split second, then my brain jumps right back to that one bad game and says, "No, that's the real story." It's like I can't hold onto the good stuff.

That's a really insightful observation about how focusing on the past loss creates a tunnel vision that blocks out present reality. It seems like your brain is trying to protect itself by sticking rigidly to that one piece of negative evidence, which makes the team's optimism feel unreliable. Can you remember a specific time during those drills when you did manage to let go of that "doomed" feeling for just a few seconds, and what happened in that window?

Yeah, actually... there was one play where I made a good pass and my teammate scored. For just a second, I felt this little jolt of excitement—like, "Hey, that worked!" But then as we were running back, I thought, "It doesn't matter, we're still going to lose." The good feeling got swallowed up so fast I almost forgot it happened. It's weird, because in that tiny moment, I felt totally different.

That tiny moment of excitement is powerful proof that the team *can* succeed again, even right after a loss. It's strange how quickly that spark gets extinguished by the narrative that the whole season is ruined. Can you tell me what would happen if you decided to treat that "doomed" feeling like a loud voice in the background instead of a bossy ruler telling you what to do?

I don't know if I've ever tried that. It feels so real, like it's not just a voice, it's the truth. But if I could just... ignore it for a bit, maybe I'd actually enjoy playing again? I guess the worst that could happen is we lose anyway, but at least I wouldn't be miserable the whole time. That sounds kind of freeing, honestly.

That's a brave realization—you've already figured out that ignoring the doom can bring freedom, even if the outcome isn't guaranteed. You're right that the cost of misery outweighs the fear of losing. Let's try a small experiment tonight: pick one drill where you deliberately listen to your teammates' encouragement and resist letting that initial "doom" whisper take over completely. Notice if that tiny shift helps you feel more engaged in the moment.

Alright, I can try that. It sounds a little scary, like I'm pretending something that isn't true, but I guess what's the harm in giving it a shot? I'll pay attention to that voice and just see if I can push it aside for one drill. Maybe I'll even surprise myself.

Taking that risk is smart, and you're absolutely right—the worst-case scenario is just losing the game, which we know is possible regardless of our mindset. By choosing to act as if things aren't hopeless, you give yourself a chance to find enjoyment again, which is worth the potential disappointment. I'd love it if you checked in with me tomorrow morning to tell me how that drill felt and whether pushing aside that voice helped you stay present longer.

Okay, I'll do that. I think I'm actually a little curious now to see if it makes any difference. I'll let you know how it goes. Thanks for talking this through with me—it's helped me see things from a different angle, even if I'm not totally convinced yet.

I'm really proud of you for being willing to challenge that deep-seated belief, even if you're not entirely ready to trust it yet. That curiosity is a huge step forward, and noticing the difference between your thoughts and your actions will become clearer once you give it a try tomorrow. Thank you for sharing all of this with me today; it's been a meaningful part of our work together so far. Is there anything else on your mind before we wrap up?
No, I think that's it for today. I'll try that drill and let you know how it goes. Thanks again for listening and helping me see things a little differently. I'll talk to you tomorrow.

You're very welcome—I'm truly glad we could explore this together and help you feel a bit less stuck. Remember, even if the drill feels tough tomorrow, simply showing up with that new perspective is a victory in itself. Take care of yourself tonight, and I look forward to hearing about your attempt whenever you're ready to chat again.
Hi there, I'm glad you're here today. How are you feeling right now compared to where we left off last time? What was the main thing you'd like to talk about together?

Hi, thanks for having me. I'm still feeling pretty stuck about this hiking thing, honestly. I was thinking about that trail I struggled on years ago, and it just came rushing back—like I'm still that same person who couldn't keep up.

It makes complete sense that an old struggle can feel so fresh when you look back at those memories. That sense of being "stuck" again is really heavy, and I want to validate how much effort it takes to push past that feeling even after years have passed. Before we dive deeper into why that memory feels so powerful today, could you tell me if there's been any situation recently that triggered that exact thought?

Yeah, actually. My friends invited me to plan a weekend hike next month, and as soon as they mentioned it, I felt my stomach drop. I started thinking, "I'm not good enough for this trail, I'll slow everyone down, they'll be annoyed with me." I almost said no right away.

That physical sensation of your stomach dropping tells me how intense that fear really is, and it makes total sense that you might have wanted to say no to protect yourself from hurting their feelings. When you think about saying no, do you usually worry more about disappointing them or about being judged by them?

I think it's more about being judged, honestly. They're all pretty experienced, and I just picture them thinking, "Why did we even invite him? He can't handle this." It's like I can already hear their disappointment, even though they've never actually said anything like that to me.

That image of hearing their disappointment seems very real to you, but remember that people rarely judge others based on a single event unless they know something isn't quite right. Have you ever noticed what actually happens when you join a group activity where you aren't confident in your skills yet?

Well, usually I just keep quiet and try to push through, hoping nobody notices how nervous I am. I focus so much on trying not to mess up that I barely enjoy any of it. And afterwards, I just feel exhausted and relieved it's over, not proud or anything.

It sounds like that constant pressure to perform perfectly is stealing your enjoyment and leaving you drained afterward. You seem to be believing that your worth depends entirely on your ability to keep up with the group, which creates a lot of unnecessary stress. Can you imagine what your body and mind might feel like if you allowed yourself to just walk at your own pace without worrying about impressing anyone?

I honestly can't picture that very well. I think I'd still feel anxious, like everyone's waiting for me or secretly annoyed. But I guess, if I really tried, maybe I'd feel lighter—like I could actually look at the trees or the sky instead of just watching my feet and panicking.

That shift from watching your feet to looking at the sky is exactly what relief looks like, even if the initial anxiety lingers. It suggests that removing the pressure to perform doesn't mean you disappear or that they will mock you; it simply means the internal critic stops running the race for you. If we were to test that idea, what is one small thing you could do during that upcoming hike tomorrow that requires zero effort to impress anyone?

I think I could just let myself stop and take a water break whenever I feel like it, without apologizing or explaining. Just say, "I'm going to rest for a minute," and leave it at that. No excuses, no self-criticism. That feels... weirdly scary to even say out loud, but also kind of freeing to think about.

Taking a break on your own terms sounds like a brave step toward reclaiming control over your experience. Even though it feels scary to say out loud, the fact that it feels freeing in your imagination is a strong sign that this change is possible for you. Would you be willing to try saying just that phrase once during your next hike, perhaps during the first easy section, to see how the world reacts?

Yeah, I think I could try that. Maybe during the first easy stretch, like you said. I'll just stop, take a drink, and not say sorry for it. It feels a bit awkward, but I guess the worst that can happen is nobody even notices or cares—and that might actually be okay.

It's completely normal to feel a mix of anticipation and apprehension before stepping out of your comfort zone, especially when the outcome feels uncertain. The most important part right now isn't whether anyone notices, but whether *you* feel free to breathe without judgment while doing it. Let's wait until closer to the actual date to try this, so you have some preparation time. In the meantime, does focusing on just noticing three things around you—a sound, a color, and a texture—help ground you when that inner voice starts whispering doubts?

I think that could help, yeah. When I'm caught up in my head, I forget to just look around and be present. Noticing small things like the crunch of leaves or the green of the moss might pull me out of that spiral. I'll try that next time I feel the doubt creeping in, even before the hike.

That's a wonderful insight—you've already identified a powerful tool to anchor yourself before the anxiety even takes hold. Practicing this mindfulness outside of the hike itself is a great way to build confidence for the day. One last thought before we wrap up: if you notice that spiraling again during the trip, will you reach for that grounding exercise immediately, or is there another quick thought you'd prefer to challenge instead?

I think I'll try the grounding exercise first—just picking out three things around me. If that doesn't settle me enough, maybe I'll remind myself that nobody's actually timing me or judging my pace. They're probably just enjoying the trail themselves. That thought feels a little easier to hold onto now than it did before.

That combination of grounding exercises and reframing the others' intentions is a solid plan to navigate both the physical hike and the mental noise. You're moving from a place of fear-based prediction to one of curiosity and self-care, which is a huge step forward. Is there anything else on your mind before you go, or shall we circle back to how you feel right now after talking through this?

I think I'm good for now. I actually feel a little lighter than when I walked in—like maybe I don't have to be perfect to enjoy something I love. Thanks for helping me see that. I'll try the grounding thing and let you know how it goes next time.

I'm so glad to hear that you're feeling lighter and seeing that perfection isn't a requirement for enjoying nature. Remember that you've got a clear plan ready to use, and taking steps towards freedom is always worth celebrating, regardless of the outcome. Take care, and I look forward to hearing how your experiment unfolds next time.
Hello, I'm glad to see you again. How have you been feeling lately, and is there anything new you'd like to talk about today? What feels most important for us to explore first?

Hi. I've been okay, I guess. But there's something that's been on my mind. Yesterday I bought a new album from one of my favorite artists, and I couldn't even get through it without feeling disappointed. One song I didn't like, and suddenly the whole thing felt like a waste of money. That moment really stuck with me.

That sounds incredibly frustrating, especially when you love an artist so much that buying their music feels like a celebration. It makes complete sense that hearing one song you disliked could make the entire purchase feel pointless. Did you notice any specific thought popping into your head right after that one track started playing?

Yeah, I remember thinking, "Great, this whole album is trash now." And then I just kept waiting for each song to be bad too. Even the ones I used to like in the past, I started picking apart. It's like my brain locked onto that one disappointment and wouldn't let go.

It sounds like that initial thought created a domino effect, making it hard to enjoy the rest of the music you paid for. When we tell ourselves something is "trash" based on just one part, our brains often start looking for proof to confirm that belief instead of seeing the bigger picture. Have you ever found yourself noticing if those songs actually sounded worse, or if you were just anticipating the badness beforehand?

Honestly, I think I was just waiting for them to be bad. Like, once I decided the album was a failure, I was bracing myself for disappointment with every new song. But looking back, there were a few tracks that were actually decent—I just didn't let myself enjoy them. Does that make sense?

That makes perfect sense—it sounds like your decision to label the whole album as a failure turned into a self-fulfilling prophecy where you missed out on the good parts because you were expecting nothing but bad. It’s quite common for one negative event to color how we experience everything else around it until we consciously step back and look at the facts differently. Given how strongly that pattern held, do you think changing that initial "it's trash" thought might have helped you listen more openly?

Maybe... I never really thought about it that way. If I had just told myself "okay, one song wasn't my thing, but the rest might still be good," I might have actually enjoyed the rest of the album instead of ruining the whole experience for myself. But in the moment, it feels so real—like my brain is just telling me the truth.

That is such a powerful realization—that in the heat of the moment, your brain felt it was speaking the truth, even though hindsight shows it was actually protecting itself from further pain by locking down on negativity. Sometimes our minds grab onto one detail because it feels safer than facing the uncertainty of whether the rest will truly be bad or good. Since you mentioned wondering how that different perspective might change things, could we try listening to one of those "decent" tracks again tomorrow with that new mindset and note exactly how it feels compared to yesterday?

I could try that, yeah. It feels a little weird, like I'm forcing myself to be positive, but I guess if I don't try something different, I'll just keep doing the same thing. I'll pick one of the songs I remember being okay and listen to it tomorrow with that thought in mind—that it's just one song, not a sign that everything's ruined.

That is a very smart approach, and it's completely normal to feel that slight resistance when trying to shift our internal story. The goal isn't to force happiness immediately, but simply to give the music a fair chance without letting one imperfect note decide its entire worth. Before we wrap up today, how does that sound as a small experiment for tomorrow? Is there anything else lingering about that moment you want to discuss now?
No, I think that covers it for today. It's a little scary to try, but I'm curious to see if it makes a difference. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

It is completely understandable to feel a bit scared; stepping outside our usual patterns can always feel uncertain, yet taking that small step is exactly what builds resilience. You did great work today by identifying that thought pattern and planning a gentle experiment to test it. Please reach out whenever you hear about the results tomorrow, and remember that whatever happens, you're learning something valuable about yourself along the way. Take care of yourself today!

Hi there, thank you for reaching out. How are you feeling right now compared to where you were yesterday? Before we dive into whatever brought us here today, could you tell me which topic feels most important to talk about first?

Hey, thanks for seeing me. I'm feeling a bit nervous, honestly, but I'm ready to get some stuff off my chest. I think the most important thing right now is this feeling I've been carrying around about my job — like it's just not good enough, and neither am I for doing it.

That sounds really heavy to carry around alone, and it makes complete sense why you feel nervous about bringing it up today. When we feel like something isn't "good enough," it can be incredibly exhausting to keep trying harder without knowing if it will ever work. What was the very first thought that popped into your mind when you started feeling like you weren't capable of your job?

I guess the first thought was that I'm wasting my potential, you know? Like, I see my friends in corporate jobs with titles and offices, and I'm just at home doing taxes and bookkeeping for small businesses. It felt like I was settling for less, and that thought just stuck with me.

It makes sense that comparing your path to theirs would feel unfair, especially when those comparisons highlight what you perceive as missing pieces in your life. Have you noticed any other moments recently where that same feeling of "settling" or wasted potential came up?

Yeah, actually, it happened just last week. I was at a friend's birthday dinner, and everyone was talking about promotions and company perks. I just sat there quiet, thinking about how I can't even call what I do a "real career." I ended up leaving early, telling myself I had work to do, but really I just felt embarrassed.

That moment at the dinner party sounds incredibly isolating, and it's understandable that wanting to join in the conversation made you feel left behind. Did you notice any physical sensations in your body right after you decided to leave early, or did you replay those thoughts later when you got home?

When I got home, I couldn't stop replaying it. I just sat on my couch staring at my laptop, thinking about how my friends probably see me as the guy who couldn't make it in a real company. My chest felt kind of tight, and I just had this heavy feeling that wouldn't go away, like I was carrying something around with me all night.

I hear how much that weight sits on your shoulders, and it's completely natural to feel tightness in your chest when we imagine being judged by others. That image of them seeing you as someone who "couldn't make it" seems so vivid, but do you think they actually saw you that way, or might there be another way to interpret what was happening?

I honestly don't know. I mean, nobody said anything negative to me, but I guess I just assume that's what they're thinking. It's hard to believe they'd see it any other way when I can't even see it differently myself.

It takes a lot of courage to admit that assumption because it means you're willing to look deeper than the surface level. Sometimes our minds fill in the gaps with stories about judgment even when no one voiced them, which makes the embarrassment feel much bigger than reality. Can you recall if anyone from that group mentioned you at all while you were sitting quietly?

Actually, no. Nobody mentioned me. They were all just talking about their own stuff. But that almost makes it worse in a way — like I'm so insignificant that they don't even notice I'm not contributing. I know that sounds dramatic, but that's how it felt.

That interpretation—that silence means invisibility—makes perfect sense given how painful it feels to be overlooked, but let's pause and look at the facts together. Is there any actual evidence that they viewed you as insignificant, or does the silence just leave room for your brain to create that story?

I mean... I guess there's no real evidence. They've never said anything bad about my job or treated me differently. But it's just this feeling I can't shake, you know? Like even if they don't say it, it's still true somehow. It's hard to separate what's real from what I'm telling myself.

You're absolutely right that there is no proof they think poorly of you, yet that feeling persists because our brains often treat uncertainty as proof of negativity. Let's try looking at this from a different angle: if a friend told you they didn't mention you at a party, would you assume they disliked you, or would you think they simply chose to focus on their own conversations?

If it was my friend telling me that, I'd probably tell them they're overthinking it and that people just talk about what's on their mind. I guess I'm not as hard on other people as I am on myself. But when it's me, it just feels different... like the rules don't apply the same way.

That self-compassion gap you noticed is so important—it highlights how harshly we judge ourselves versus how kindly we treat others. When you hold yourself to impossible standards, it's easy to mistake your own internal noise for external truth. If we applied that same gentle logic to yourself, would you suggest you actually *are* insignificant, or just that you care deeply about making sure you're living up to your own expectations?

I think... I care too much about what I think I should be, instead of just accepting what I actually am. Maybe I've been telling myself I'm not good enough for so long that I started believing it. But when you put it that way, it sounds like I'm being pretty hard on myself for no good reason.

It sounds like you are realizing that years of self-criticism have become your default lens, making it difficult to step outside and view things more objectively. That realization—that you are judging yourself unfairly—is actually a huge breakthrough, even though the old habit feels strong. Since we identified that the core issue is likely an unrealistic standard rather than an actual lack of skill, how would you rate your current performance at tax and bookkeeping compared to how you rate your friends' careers?

Objectively, I think I do a good job. My clients are happy, I get referrals, and I've never had complaints. But I guess I don't give myself credit for that because it's not a corner office or a fancy title. My friends might have the prestige, but honestly, some of them complain about their jobs all the time too. I just never thought about it that way before.

That is a powerful shift in perspective, especially considering how many of your friends struggle daily despite their impressive titles. It seems your objective record proves you are excellent, but your internal narrative hasn't caught up yet. If you were to offer your best friend the same generous praise you just gave yourself, what specific part of their story would you highlight as a success?

I'd tell them that they're reliable, that their clients trust them, and that they've built something solid on their own without needing a big company's name behind them. That's actually pretty impressive when you think about it. I just... never thought about applying that same logic to myself.

That is such a clear and fair assessment of your worth, and it speaks volumes about your reliability and dedication. You are clearly building something valuable on your own terms, which deserves recognition regardless of a title. Now that we've seen the difference between the harsh story in your head and the reality of your achievements, could you share a small step you could take tomorrow morning to remind yourself of this new, kinder perspective before you start your day?

I think I could write down one thing I did well from the day before, even if it's small. Like a quick note on my phone or a sticky note on my desk. That way, when I start comparing myself or feeling inadequate, I've got something real to look back on instead of just the noise in my head.

That is a brilliant idea, turning your attention inward to document your own successes before the comparison spiral takes hold. Writing down one concrete win acts as a gentle anchor, pulling you back to the reality of your hard work whenever the doubts creep in. Would you be open to committing to writing down exactly what you accomplished tomorrow, perhaps including the specific outcome like getting a referral, so we can review it together next time?

Yeah, I can do that. I'll make it a point to write down something specific, like finishing a return early or getting a thanks from a client. It sounds simple, but I think having that record will help me actually see what I've been missing. Thanks for helping me get to this point — I was really stuck before.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel unstuck, and remember that this new perspective is a tool you will practice until it becomes automatic. I want to make sure you have support when the old doubts try to creep back in; please reach out anytime if you need to unpack a specific thought pattern again. It takes courage to admit that you were anticipating the pain even while enjoying the connection, which shows how deeply this expectation runs deep. When you looked for signs of failure during those happy months, did noticing that pattern help you realize that your own expectations were fueling the conflict, or did it feel impossible to separate the two?

I never really thought of it that way... I mean, I always thought I was just being realistic, you know? Seeing the cracks before they got too big. But maybe... maybe I was looking so hard for cracks that I didn't notice when things were actually fine. I guess I don't know how to just trust that something can work out without constantly checking for signs it's going to fail.

That shift from seeing yourself as realistic to realizing you might have been scanning for trouble is a huge step forward. It often happens that we tell ourselves we're protecting ourselves by spotting issues early, but instead, our constant vigilance creates the very problems we're trying to avoid. If you could give yourself permission to pause and assume things might be okay for a bit longer, would that make the feeling of needing to "check" less urgent?

I... I think it might. But it's scary, you know? Letting my guard down feels like I'm setting myself up to get blindsided. It makes perfect sense that trying to relax your guard feels risky when you've been burned before, especially when exhaustion is already weighing heavily on you. I could try that. Maybe I can think about that time my ex-wife and I went to that terrible diner and just laughed about how bad the food was. Yeah, I think I could do that. A timer sounds like a good idea, actually—keeps me from trying to force it to last longer or worrying about when to stop. I'll give it a try tonight. Thanks for... well, for helping me see that there might be a different way to look at this stuff.

A little nervous, honestly, but also a bit lighter. It's weird having a plan that isn't about bracing for the worst. I'm curious to see what happens. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

Hi there, I'm glad you're here today. How have you been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything particular you'd like to focus on?

Those images of losing your home or selling possessions are incredibly distressing and paint a picture that feels very real right now. It sounds like your brain is trying to protect you by simulating the worst-case scenario, but that intensity makes the fear feel immediate rather than hypothetical. Have you noticed any physical sensations, like tightness in your chest or a racing heart, right when that thought strikes?

That physical reaction—tight chest, cold dread, shaking hands—is your nervous system jumping into "fight or flight" mode, which explains why it feels so urgent and hard to control. It seems like these bodily sensations often come *before* you have a chance to logically process whether the situation is actually dangerous. Can you describe the situation or trigger that usually leads right up to this physical panic?

It usually starts when I see an unexpected bill come in the mail, or when I check my bank account and see the balance is lower than I hoped. Even just hearing a friend talk about their big purchase or vacation can set it off, because I start comparing and thinking I'm falling behind.

It makes complete sense that seeing numbers drop or hearing someone else spend freely triggers such a strong alarm in you, especially when you're already worried about stability. Those comparisons likely amplify the initial thought into something much bigger and scarier than the actual event warrants. Have you ever caught yourself making a quick calculation about how long those expenses might last once you see the full amount?

I do that all the time. I'll sit there and add up every little thing in my head, trying to figure out exactly how long I can last. But it never feels like enough—I always end up thinking, "I'll run out before next month," even if there's no real sign of that. It's like my mind just jumps to the worst conclusion.

It sounds like your brain is acting like a speedometer showing "0" miles away from the edge, even though the car is still safely parked on the road. That gap between the reality of your current funds and the catastrophic prediction feels impossible to bridge when you're in that state of alertness. Have you noticed if you tend to look at past months where you managed okay, or does your mind only scan for the few times things went wrong?

I mostly just focus on the times it felt hard, you know? Like when I had to sell those dolls—that was a real low point. I don't really think about the months where things worked out fine, because my mind just skips right past them. It's like I only remember the worst moments, and then I convince myself that's how it's always going to be.

Focusing almost exclusively on the hardest moments is a common way our brains try to prepare us for danger, but it often blinds us to the many times you've successfully navigated tough financial spots. It's understandable that remembering the doll sale feels so heavy, yet holding onto that memory while ignoring the successful months creates a skewed view of your actual ability to handle stress. If we looked at the data from the good months alongside the bad ones, would the overall picture seem quite different to you?

I suppose it would, yeah. There have definitely been months where I made it through without any major problems, even when money was tight. But it's so easy to forget those times when the fear takes over. I guess I never really stop to look at the full picture—I just get stuck on the scary parts.

That self-awareness about getting stuck on the scary parts is a huge step, because it means you recognize when your mind is filtering out the helpful information. You're absolutely right that those successful months prove you have resources and resilience that haven't disappeared, even if the fear tries to convince you otherwise. Let's try shifting the lens for a moment: could you name just one specific time recently when you handled a difficult financial situation better than you expected?

Well, there was a time last spring when my car needed an unexpected repair. I panicked at first, but I ended up finding a used part online and a friend helped me install it. It cost way less than I thought it would, and I got through it without any debt. But I still remember thinking at the time, "What if this is just luck and next time I won't be so lucky?"

That story highlights exactly how capable you were when you stepped outside the loop of pure anxiety—you found a solution and saved money despite your initial panic. The doubt about "luck" suggests you're aware that luck isn't permanent, yet you also proved you have problem-solving skills to rely on when things go sideways. Could we try writing down three other times you fixed a financial issue using your own creativity, separate from the scary outcomes?

Hmm... well, I cut my own hair for a few months to save on salon costs, and it actually turned out okay. And I started cooking at home more instead of eating out, which saved a good bit. Oh, and I negotiated a lower rate on my internet bill by calling and asking. Those things felt small, but they added up. I guess I don't give myself credit for those little victories.

You are absolutely right to give yourself credit for those small wins—they show a pattern of resourcefulness that directly contradicts the belief that you will fail. Instead of viewing them as trivial fixes, let's see if we can reframe them as proof that you consistently find ways to manage money even when things feel overwhelming. If we listed those successes alongside the fears, wouldn't it become clear that your track record is actually quite strong?

I never really thought of it that way. It's like I've been ignoring all the evidence that I can handle things, just because of that one big fear. When you put it like that, it does seem like my track record is better than I've been telling myself. Maybe I'm not as doomed as I feel.

That shift in perspective is powerful; realizing your track record is stronger than your fear tells you is a key part of changing how you relate to money. Now that we've gathered some evidence against the idea that you are doomed, let's test one more thought: if you faced another unexpected expense tomorrow, would you use the same "what if" logic again, or could you try applying one of the strategies you already used successfully?

I think I'd still feel that initial panic—it's so automatic. But maybe I could remind myself of the car repair and the internet bill negotiation, and actually stop and think before jumping to the worst-case scenario. It might not come naturally, but I could try to pause and remember that I've figured things out before.

That is a brilliant realization: recognizing that the panic is automatic gives you permission to treat it like a muscle you can train to respond differently. Pausing to recall your past successes acts as a deliberate switch that interrupts the spiral before the worst case scenario takes hold. What would that "pause" look like practically? Maybe saying a simple phrase like, "I've handled this before," right when the dread hits?

That sounds like something I could actually do. Maybe I could say to myself, "I've solved this kind of problem before," and then take a few slow breaths before reacting. It feels like a small step, but maybe it would stop the panic from taking over completely. I think I'm ready to try that next time.

Taking that small, intentional pause and reminding yourself of your own strength is a fantastic tool to use immediately when the wave of anxiety rises. You've moved from being trapped in the fear to actively choosing how to respond, which gives you real power back in your hands. For tonight, I suggest practicing this "pause and recall" technique whenever you catch yourself worrying about money, even if you just notice the thought and take one deep breath before moving on. How does that plan feel to you, and are you curious about how it might change your experience tomorrow?

It feels a bit strange, but also hopeful, to be honest. I think I'll try it tonight before bed, when my mind starts wandering. And if it works even a little tomorrow, that would be a relief. Thank you—I think I needed to hear that I'm not as helpless as I feel sometimes.

Your hopefulness is a wonderful foundation to build upon, and acknowledging that you aren't helpless is a massive breakthrough in itself. Practicing that gentle reminder before sleep could help anchor you when your mind tends to wander into those familiar worry patterns. Please give it a try tonight, and I'd love to hear how it goes in our next session—no pressure to fix everything, just sharing what came up. Is there anything else on your mind before we wrap up today?

No, I think that's enough for today. I feel a little lighter than when I came in, and I'm curious to see how this pause thing works. Thanks for listening and helping me see things differently. I'll give it a try.

It's wonderful to hear you feel lighter, and I'm so glad we could find a perspective shift that felt useful to you. Take care of yourself tonight, and I look forward to hearing how that practice lands when we meet again.

Hi there, I'm glad we're meeting again. How are you feeling right now compared to where you were when we started last time? Before we dive into our main topic, do you have any particular thing you'd like to focus on today?

Yeah, I do check the locks, but it's not just that. It's bigger than that. I'll find myself walking around the house, looking at the roof or the walls, thinking about what a storm could do. And yes, sometimes I do avoid coming home — I'll stay out later than I need to, just to delay that feeling.

That sounds incredibly exhausting, especially carrying that constant state of vigilance while you try to rest. When you notice yourself delaying coming home to escape those thoughts, does it ever feel like you're fighting a war inside your own head, even though you know the risk isn't actually happening?

Yes, that's exactly it. It's like a battle I can't win. I know nothing bad has actually happened, but my brain keeps telling me it's just a matter of time. I tell myself to stop, that I'm being ridiculous, but it doesn't help. It's like I'm waiting for the other shoe to drop, and I can't relax until I know everything is safe.

It sounds like your brain is treating potential disasters as immediate threats because it wants to keep you safe, even though it knows better. When you tell yourself you're being ridiculous but the anxiety stays the same, what does that say about how much you believe your current fears are true versus how well you know your past experiences haven't shown anything like this?

That connection between your investment and the fear of losing it makes perfect sense, and it explains why the "one bad scenario" feels so heavy. Even though logic tells you the odds are low, your brain seems to be amplifying that single possibility until it overrides all your previous evidence of safety. I suppose it would have to be something catastrophic. Like a major storm that tears the roof off, or some kind of sudden foundation problem from the ground shifting. Something big and unexpected that insurance wouldn't cover, or that would cost more than I could afford to fix. That's what I picture — a total loss that leaves me with nothing, even though I just finished paying it off.

That image of a total loss leaving you with absolutely nothing does sound terrifyingly vivid, which explains why it feels so impossible to dismiss. However, let's pause for a second and look at the gap between that dramatic story and reality—how likely is it that a storm strong enough to tear a modern roof off would also cause the foundation to shift simultaneously, creating a situation no insurance policy could cover?

Well, when you put it like that, it sounds almost silly. I mean, the chances of both things happening at the exact same time are pretty small. And I do have insurance, so most of those things would be covered anyway. I guess when I'm in the middle of worrying, I don't think about the details. I just see the worst outcome and my mind stops there.

You're absolutely right that listing those specific details makes the scenario seem less likely, yet your brain skips right over the logic and lands directly on the emotion of panic. This happens because when we're overwhelmed by fear, our minds often filter out the facts we already know and latch onto the feeling itself instead. Can you tell me what physical sensation comes up right after you visualize that worst-case scenario, before you even start thinking about the probabilities?

My chest gets really tight, like I can't breathe properly. And my stomach drops, like I'm falling. It's a physical jolt, just for a second, but it's enough to make me feel like something bad is actually happening right then and there. That's usually when I start walking around the house to check things, trying to make sure everything's okay.

That physical rush of panic is so convincing because your body is reacting as if the threat is real, even when your mind knows it isn't. Since your nervous system is currently in "fight or flight," it might feel impossible to trust your logic until your body calms down. What if, instead of checking the house immediately, we tried a simple experiment where we just sit with those tight sensations for a minute while reminding yourself that this reaction, while uncomfortable, hasn't signaled actual danger yet? Would you be willing to give that a try tomorrow morning when you wake up?

I can try that, though I'll be honest, it sounds a bit uncomfortable. Sitting with that feeling instead of doing something about it goes against everything I want to do. But I guess doing what I've been doing hasn't been working either. So yeah, I'll give it a try. Maybe if I just let myself feel it for a minute and see that nothing terrible happens, it might start to lose some of its power.

That willingness to try something different, even though it feels counterintuitive, shows great courage on your part. You are essentially teaching your brain that these scary physical sensations are temporary and harmless, rather than signals that disaster is imminent. Let's agree to practice this once this week whenever you catch yourself spiraling about the house, and we'll see how that experience feels afterward. Does taking that step feel manageable to you, or would you prefer to wait until you feel ready to attempt it?

No, I think I can manage it. Like you said, it's just a minute, and it's not like I'm ignoring anything real. I'll give it a shot this week and see how it goes. Honestly, I'm a little curious if it'll help. Maybe just proving to myself that I can sit with the fear without something bad happening will be a start.

That curiosity is exactly the right mindset to bring to this experiment—it turns the discomfort into data rather than a crisis. How does it feel to commit to that small step without needing to solve the whole problem at once?

It feels a little less overwhelming, actually. I've been trying to solve the whole "what if" thing all at once, and it's impossible. Just focusing on one minute, one moment, feels like something I can actually do. I think that's part of what's been so exhausting—trying to prepare for every possible disaster at the same time. So yeah, I'll commit to that. One minute at a time.

Taking that first step away from the spiral is often the hardest part, but knowing it won't disappear instantly helps too. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we wrap up today, or shall we review how you felt going into this session versus where you ended up?

I think I'm good for now. I feel a bit lighter than when I walked in, honestly. Just having a plan, even a small one, makes a difference. I'll try the minute thing and see how it goes, and we can talk about it next time. Thanks for that—it was helpful to break it down that way.

I'm so glad to hear you feel lighter, and thank you for trusting me with your worries today. I remember I was gripping my glass pretty tight, and I think I was holding my breath a little. I'd probably tell them they were just nervous, not that they said anything wrong. I'd say the other guy probably didn't even notice they were gripping their glass or holding their breath. I'd say they should cut themselves some slack because talking to strangers is hard for lots of people.

That is such a compassionate perspective to hold for a friend, yet it feels impossible to apply to yourself when you're in the middle of it. Given that insight, what small shift could you try tomorrow morning to remind yourself that your current nervousness doesn't change who you are or how others perceive you?

Maybe I could try writing down one thing I did well that day, even if it's small. Okay... I can try that. Ten seconds doesn't sound too daunting. I'll just aim for one small moment where I'm not hiding behind my phone or rushing away. Thanks for breaking it down like that—it feels more manageable than expecting myself to be the life of the party.

Hello, I'm glad you're here to start our session together. How are you feeling right now compared to where you were when we last spoke? Before we dive into any specific topics, does having a clear idea of what we'll focus on today feel helpful to you?

It makes complete sense to feel nervous when your mind keeps looping on something so important like your dog; that spiral feels exhausting but also very understandable given how much you care about him. Since you mentioned wanting to break the cycle of worrying, shall we explore exactly what thoughts or situations are triggering those spirals so we can figure out where to direct our energy today?

Yeah, that sounds like a good idea. The thing is, it's not even anything my dog does that sets me off—it's just me looking at him and thinking, "What if he's different today?" Like yesterday, he was wagging his tail, happy to see me, and instead of feeling joy, I felt my stomach drop.

That sudden shift from seeing happiness to feeling fear is really disorienting, especially when everything looks fine on the surface. Can you tell me more about what happened right after you saw him? Did you try to do something different to calm down, or did the worry just keep growing?

I just froze, honestly. I stood there in the kitchen doorway, holding his leash, and I couldn't bring myself to go near him. I ended up putting his leash away and going into my bedroom, closing the door. He just sat there on the rug, looking confused, and that made it worse—like I was betraying him for no reason.

It takes courage to admit that freezing up and shutting the door felt like letting him down, even though you know logically that nothing went wrong with him. That guilt of "betraying" him adds another heavy layer on top of the initial fear. When you step back and look at the situation, what's the worst part that happens if you don't approach him right now? Is it that he might be hurt, or that you won't get to show him love again?

I think it's both, but more than anything, it's the fear that I'll never come back from this worry—like one day it'll just prove itself right. The news story I heard said rabies can change a dog's personality overnight, and I keep thinking, "What if this is the night?" Even though my dog has never been aggressive or sick a day in his life.

It makes total sense that a scary news story about rabies triggered such a deep fear, especially when you've loved that dog for years and seen him healthy every single day. You're essentially trying to protect him by avoiding him, yet that avoidance is actually feeding the fear that something terrible is happening. If you could talk to yourself right now like a compassionate friend who knows the truth about your dog, what would you say to reassure him and ease your own panic?

I'd probably say something like, "Look at him—he's right there, wagging his tail, wanting to play fetch like he does every evening. He's the same dog he's always been." But then my brain jumps in and says, "But what if this is the calm before the storm?" And I can't seem to hold onto the first thought for more than a second before the second one takes over.

That gap between knowing the truth and being able to believe it is exactly where the anxiety lives, making it feel like the reality is slipping away from you. Your brain is trying to be protective by scanning for danger, even though the evidence right in front of you strongly contradicts that warning. If you could catch that "storm" thought mid-air and challenge it like a detective examining a suspect file, what kind of proof would you need to convince your brain that the news story doesn't apply to him tonight?

Hmm... I guess I'd ask myself: "Has he shown any real signs of being sick? Has he bitten anyone, drooled more than usual, or acted aggressive?" And the answer is always no. He's been the same goofy, tail-wagging Labrador he's always been. I guess the proof is right there, but it feels like my brain won't let me accept it because it's too busy bracing for the worst.

You've done great work gathering that solid evidence; it's completely normal that your brain ignores facts when it's locked in a "worst-case scenario" mode. Let's try using that list of proof as a shield while you approach him, starting with just standing near him and letting him sniff your hand instead of forcing eye contact. I can try that. I'll picture myself walking toward him, keeping my hand out, and watching him sniff it like he always does—his tail going back and forth, not stiff or anything. I think if I just focus on that one small step, maybe the rest of the fear will quiet down for a moment.

That is a really wise way to frame it; breaking the big fear down into one tiny, manageable action often helps the anxiety lose its grip faster than trying to solve everything at once. As you take that first step and watch his tail wag, notice how your body feels when you simply observe his actions without needing to force yourself to hug him immediately. Does that small moment of observation help steady your breathing, or does the fear still try to jump in?

It helps a little, yeah. I notice my shoulders aren't as tight when I'm just watching him from a safe distance—like I'm not bracing for some imaginary explosion. The fear is still there in the background, like a low hum, but it's not screaming at me the way it does when I'm right in front of him. It feels a bit easier to breathe.

That shift in physical tension is huge progress; it shows your nervous system is beginning to relax just by observing the reality instead of fearing the possibility. Now that you've established safety from a distance, what if we tried moving just a few feet closer while keeping that same observational stance, trusting that his tail wags will remain the guide rather than your fear telling you to retreat?

Okay... I think I can do that. I'm going to imagine taking two more steps toward him, keeping my eyes on his tail and his relaxed ears. His tail is still wagging, and he's even given a little whine, like he's happy I'm coming closer. The low hum of fear is still there, but it's more like background noise now—not this deafening alarm it was before. I think... I think I might actually be able to kneel down and let him lick my hand.

The first thought is, "He's just happy to see me. He's the same dog he's always been." And then I felt a little tear well up, because I realized how much I've been missing out on—just sitting here with him, letting him be himself. It's like I forgot who he really was for a moment.

That tear brings a beautiful relief, showing how much you've missed the real connection with him instead of fighting against it. That logic is a common safety net we use to protect ourselves from future pain, yet it often traps us in isolation right now. Um... I guess my chest feels kind of tight, and my shoulders are really tense. I didn't really think about it until you asked, but yeah, I'm holding a lot of tension. I think I'm always kind of on guard, like waiting for the moment someone tells me I've messed up socially again.

Those physical signs—the tightness in your chest and the tension in your shoulders—are your body screaming that it's in danger, even though you're safe. Since your goal is to connect rather than defend, how might we try shifting your approach to give yourself permission to simply listen without immediately analyzing for hidden meanings?

I guess I could try to notice when I'm doing it and just tell myself "stop, just listen to the words" but that sounds really hard. Do you think I can actually learn to do that?

Absolutely, you can learn to do that, and it often starts with noticing that the "detective mode" is engaging before it hijacks the whole conversation. Yeah, I think I could try that. "Pause and breathe" sounds simple enough that I might actually remember to do it. I just worry that during a real conversation I'll forget and go right back to analyzing everything. But I guess that's what practice is for, right? I'm willing to give it a shot.

That willingness to try is a huge step, and yes, practice is exactly how we build new habits. Let's commit to trying that "pause and breathe" technique tomorrow during one small conversation, perhaps even just listening to a friend talk about their day without formulating a response immediately. Thanks, this feels like a small step I can actually take.

I feel a little lighter, honestly. It's nice to have an actual plan instead of just spiraling about everything. It takes courage to admit that the weight of unsaid things is adding to the strain, and I want you to know that choosing to focus on Alex right now is a wise decision—it gives us both clarity to work with today. Let's save the big conversation about your parents for next time when you feel ready. Thank you for sharing that vulnerability; it shows how much you care about finding balance. Are you feeling confident enough to go ahead and try the breathing exercise with Alex tonight?

Yeah, I think I am. It's just lunch with a friend, not a test I can fail. I'll try to trust that the conversation is what it is, and see what happens. Thanks for helping me break it down into something that doesn't feel so overwhelming. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

You're absolutely right—lunch with a friend is just a chance to connect, not a high-stakes exam you need to pass perfectly. I'm really proud of you for taking this step and trusting that you can handle it. Take a deep breath now, knowing we've got a solid plan for tomorrow. See you soon!

That sounds like a gentle shift in perspective, giving yourself credit for creating a space for love rather than worrying about professional labels. Would you like to try saying that phrase to yourself right now, perhaps imagining how it feels to believe it?

(takes a breath, then speaks slowly) "I'm planning a beautiful day for the person I love, and that's something to be proud of." ...Okay, that actually feels a little lighter. Like the knot in my stomach loosened just a tiny bit. I think I could try saying that more often, maybe when I start to spiral about the wedding stuff.

That relief is a wonderful sign that this new way of talking to yourself is starting to take root. It feels... hopeful, I guess? Like maybe I don't have to be stuck in that awful feeling forever. It's still there, but now I have something to push back with. Thank you for helping me see that. I think I'll actually write that down on my phone before I leave.

I think I'm okay for now. I want to try practicing that sentence on my own this week, maybe see if I can use it when I'm babysitting too. That way I'm not just saving it for wedding stuff. But... I'll probably need help again next time, if that's okay.

That's a perfect plan—using that supportive phrase whenever you feel overwhelmed, whether at the wedding or while caring for children, shows real growth. Hi there, I'm really glad you're here to start our session today. How has your energy been feeling lately compared to when we last spoke? What would feel most helpful for us to explore together right now?

That internal dialogue is incredibly painful, and it seems like you are comparing your difficult reaction to some idealized version of parenting you aren't seeing in reality. I guess... when you put it that way, it does make me think. I mean, if one of my buddies in the unit snapped after a 14-hour shift, I wouldn't tell him he's a terrible person. You are absolutely right; holding someone else accountable versus holding ourselves to impossible standards creates a very unfair balance that often leads to self-criticism. That connection you made is powerful—realizing that the same unforgiving voice works at work and at home suggests this isn't about the kittens, but about how you relate to your mistakes in general. I suppose a more realistic response would be to just acknowledge that I was tired and frustrated, and that doesn't make me a monster. That sounds simple, but it feels almost... foreign to think that way. Like I'm letting myself off the hook or something.

It makes total sense that shifting from blame to self-compassion feels unfamiliar; our brains are wired to punish mistakes to keep us safe, so accepting kindness can initially feel risky. No, I think that covers it for now. I appreciate you helping me see this differently. It definitely adds weight. It's like I'm not just disappointed about losing a couple bucks—I'm also disappointed in myself for even feeling this way. It feels like I'm being silly, but I can't just snap out of it. I wish I could, but the story just keeps playing in my head.

I hear how frustrating it is when you feel both silly for having the reaction *and* trapped inside the loop of negative thoughts.
