I don't know... I guess I would feel less heavy about it. Maybe I wouldn't be so hard on myself. But it's hard to let go of that feeling that it's my fault somehow. Like if I were more interesting or had more to say, they'd want me there.

It makes total sense that you'd blame yourself when you feel excluded; it protects us from having to face the uncertainty of whether others truly miss us. However, if the truth is that they were just busy with their own lives, does that mean *you* weren't enough, or does it simply mean their priorities happened to differ from yours that day? Let's try imagining a version of that event where they were equally distracted, and you found a way to share something small despite it. How does that scenario land for you emotionally?

It sounds... kind of freeing, actually. Like I wouldn't have to carry that weight home with me. I guess if I imagined just saying something small, like mentioning my son's soccer game next week, maybe they'd have responded. It's scary to risk it, though. What if I say something and they still ignore me?

That is a very brave realization, and yes, the risk of being ignored again is terrifying because it confirms our old story. But notice how that story also assumes the worst outcome—what if, instead of ignoring you, they responded with a simple question? That would prove you aren't invisible, even if you stumble over your words. Have you tried doing something small and low-stakes, like sending a quick text to a friend you usually struggle with, to test if people will engage with you at all?

I haven't, no. I usually just wait for them to reach out to me first. But I guess sending a text wouldn't be that big of a deal. Maybe I could text one of them tomorrow, just something simple about the soccer game. It feels a little scary, but also like it might be worth a shot.

That sounds like a perfect starting point—a tiny step that keeps the risk manageable while giving you real data to work with. Instead of worrying about a full conversation, imagine just hitting send on that message and seeing if anyone replies within a few hours. Would you feel better knowing you took action today, regardless of whether they respond immediately?

Yeah, I think I would feel better just for having done it. At least then I'd know I tried, instead of just sitting here guessing. And maybe if they don't reply right away, it doesn't have to mean anything bad—they could just be busy. I'll try sending that text tomorrow.

That is a wonderful mindset shift; focusing on the act of trying rather than waiting for validation gives you control again. Before you head out tomorrow, do you want to jot down exactly which friend you'll text and what you hope to say, just so you have a clear plan ready to go?

Okay, that's a good idea. I think I'll text Sarah. She's usually the friendliest of the group. I'll just say something like, "Hey, my son has a soccer game this Saturday if you're free to come watch." That way it's simple and not too pushy. Thanks, that actually feels doable now.

That sounds like a solid plan, Sarah is a great choice since she likely won't judge the hesitation behind the message. Just remember, even if she doesn't reply instantly, the relief of taking that small step will be huge for breaking that cycle of waiting. How does it feel to have made such a clear decision to act tomorrow?

It feels... lighter, honestly. Like I'm not just stuck in my own head anymore. I'm actually doing something about it. Thanks for helping me see that I don't have to just sit and wait for things to change.

You're absolutely welcome; hearing that you feel lighter is such a meaningful sign that you're moving out of the mental trap and into action. Take care of yourself tonight, knowing that whatever happens tomorrow isn't the final word—it's just another piece of information to learn from. I look forward to checking in with you soon to hear how that text went.

Hello, thank you for being here today. How has your week been going so far? I'm curious if there's anything specific on your mind we might want to explore first or if you'd like to set a particular topic for us to focus on together.

Hey, thanks for having me. The week's been... rough, honestly. I've been trying to switch back to daytime sleep on my days off, and it just feels impossible. I end up lying there staring at the ceiling, getting more and more worked up that I'm gonna be exhausted for my next shift.

It sounds incredibly frustrating when your body refuses to cooperate with the schedule you need, especially when you're already feeling tired from work. That sense of helplessness while staring at the ceiling can really drain your energy even further. Have you noticed any specific thoughts popping into your head right now that make the situation feel worse?

Yeah, mostly I just keep thinking that I've messed up my sleep for good. That because I work nights, I'll never get back to a normal rhythm, and I'll just be a zombie forever. It's like my brain tells me there's no way out of this, even on my days off when I try to sleep at night.

That belief about never being able to reset your rhythm makes complete sense given how hard you've tried, but it also feels pretty hopeless right now. When we hold onto ideas like "there's no way out," our brains often lose the ability to see even small opportunities for change. Could we look together at what evidence exists that suggests a reset *is* possible, perhaps even starting with just one day?

Well, I guess there was that one day last week when I managed to fall asleep around 11 p.m. on my Friday off. I woke up feeling pretty decent, actually, for a few hours. But then the next night I was back to tossing and turning until 3 a.m., so I figured that one good night was just a fluke.

That Friday night proves your brain isn't incapable of syncing up; it just needs a little more encouragement to trust that it can happen again after a slip-up. You might be judging that single success too harshly by letting the immediate struggle the next night overshadow how well you actually slept. What happens in your mind right after you wake up feeling rested compared to when you're stuck awake all night?

When I wake up feeling rested, it's like there's a moment of relief where I think, "Okay, maybe this is working." But then, if I'm awake at 2 a.m. on a work night, that feeling disappears real fast. It just gets replaced with this knot in my stomach where I'm convinced I'm gonna mess up at work because I'm too tired to focus.

That knot in your stomach is a very real physical response to the fear of failure, and it completely explains why the initial relief vanishes so quickly once the work shift begins. Instead of focusing solely on whether you are sleeping perfectly tonight, could we try looking at what one small thing you could do during that 2 a.m. moment to calm down that knot, even if you don't fall asleep immediately?

I guess I could try getting up and making some herbal tea or just sitting with the dogs for a bit. Something to stop myself from just lying there getting more and more frustrated. Usually I just stay in bed, staring at the clock, getting myself worked up. But maybe if I move around a little, it'll take the edge off.

Getting up to tend to the dogs or prepare a warm drink is a great idea because it breaks the cycle of ruminating in bed and gives your brain something different to focus on. Moving physically can literally signal safety to your nervous system and reduce that tightness in your stomach. Would you be willing to try that simple routine tomorrow evening instead of fighting to force sleep right away?

Yeah, I think I could give that a shot tomorrow. It can't be worse than what I'm doing now, which is just lying there getting angrier and more anxious. I'll try getting up and having some tea with the dogs for about twenty minutes, then see if I feel any different when I go back to bed.

That's a solid plan, and taking action based on what works best for your current state is exactly the right approach. Let's lock in those details: aim to get up for tea and the dogs for roughly twenty minutes before returning to bed, keeping in mind that rest is still okay even if sleep doesn't come immediately. Is there anything else you'd like to add to that plan, or does this feel ready to try?
No, I think that sounds good for now. It feels kind of weird to have a specific plan like this, but maybe that's what I need instead of just hoping for the best. I'll try it and see what happens.

It is completely normal to feel a bit unsure when switching from relying on hope to using a concrete plan, and that hesitation shows you are paying attention to your own experience. Try approaching it as simply testing out a new tool rather than demanding perfection, and remember that showing up for yourself is already a big win. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we wrap up today?
No, I think that's enough for today. I've got something to try now, so I'll see how it goes. Thanks for listening and helping me come up with a plan. I appreciate it.

Thank you for sharing so openly and for committing to this new approach—it takes real courage to step out of the old patterns and try something different. Remember that this isn't about forcing sleep tonight; it's about giving yourself a chance to feel calmer and regain some control. I wish you the very best with your tea and the dogs, and I'm here whenever you want to revisit how things went. Take care of yourself.

Hi there, I'm really glad you're here today. How are you feeling right now compared to where we left off last time? Before we dive into what brought you up, do you have any particular things you'd like to focus on together?

Hi... I'm okay I guess. A bit nervous, honestly, but I think that's just how I've been lately. The competition is getting closer and I can't seem to shake these thoughts about messing it all up. I'd really like to talk about how to stop that fear from taking over my whole day.

It makes complete sense to feel nervous when deadlines loom, especially when those worries about failing start coloring everything else. Since you mentioned wanting to stop that fear from running the show, let's explore exactly what happens in your mind right when you catch yourself thinking "I might mess it all up." Can you describe a recent moment when that thought popped up and tell me more about what was happening around you?

Well, just yesterday I was out on my bike training, and I hit a small bump in the road – nothing serious. But immediately my mind went to, "If you can't handle this little bump, you're going to crash during the race and embarrass yourself in front of everyone." I just froze up for a second, and the rest of my ride felt heavy and tense.

That sounds incredibly frustrating, especially seeing something so minor trigger such a huge panic response. It seems like your brain is jumping straight from that small bump to the worst-case scenario of ruining everything before you even finish your ride. When you were frozen up, did you notice if you had any specific physical sensations, like a racing heart or tight chest, along with that scary thought?

Yeah, my heart started pounding and my hands got really sweaty on the handlebars. I felt this knot in my stomach, like I was actually in danger or something, not just out for a training ride. It's almost like my body reacts before my brain even has time to tell it everything's fine.

That physical reaction makes total sense given how intense your initial thought was, and it's exhausting having your body go into "fight or flight" mode when you're just riding a bike. It looks like that belief about crashing is creating a self-fulfilling cycle where the anxiety itself becomes the obstacle you're trying to overcome. Let's look closely at that specific thought: "If you can't handle this little bump, you're going to crash during the race," does the word "crash" feel accurate, or is it more likely a prediction of embarrassment based on past experiences?

I guess... when I say "crash," I don't really mean flying over the handlebars or anything dramatic. It's more like stumbling or making a silly mistake that makes everyone look at me and think I don't belong there. But it feels just as bad as a real crash, honestly. I've never actually crashed before, so I'm not sure why my brain jumps to that picture.

It makes perfect sense that the image of being judged hurts so deeply, especially after you've worked hard to prove yourself belongs there. That feeling of embarrassment seems to be driving the fear, even though you haven't actually experienced a failure yet. Have you noticed if your brain tends to exaggerate how long people stare or how harshly they judge you when you make mistakes?

Now that you mention it, yeah, I think I do blow it up in my head. I always imagine everyone just staring at me, whispering, and remembering it for weeks. But logically, I know that when I see someone else stumble during a race or make a little mistake, I don't think twice about it. So why do I assume they'll all be scrutinizing me?

That contrast is really telling—you naturally treat others' mistakes with indifference while treating yours like a personal catastrophe, which often stems from holding ourselves to impossible standards. It seems like you're giving your own errors way more power and permanence than anyone else's do in reality. Could you ask yourself what specific evidence would change your mind about whether people will remember or care about a minor stumble?

That's a good question... I guess if I actually saw someone else mess up at the competition and nobody around me even mentioned it afterward, or if I asked a friend what they remembered about the race and they didn't bring up any mistakes, that would help. But I'm not sure I'd believe it even then. I'd probably think they were just being polite.

That skepticism shows how deeply rooted this worry is, because it's very hard to trust our own judgment when we're so worried about being wrong. Instead of waiting for proof that no one cares, maybe we could try looking for a middle ground—what if we assumed people are mostly focused on their own rides and races anyway? If we practiced noticing when we feel that "staring" sensation, could we simply remind yourself that it's likely just your nerves talking rather than actual judgment?

I think I could try that. It's not easy, but maybe I can catch myself when I start feeling that spotlight and just tell myself, "They're probably worrying about their own race, not watching me." I guess the more I practice that, the less automatic the scary thoughts might become. I'd like to give it a shot.

That sounds like a solid plan, and I appreciate your willingness to experiment with shifting your perspective. To make sure this works well in the heat of the moment, how about pairing that internal reminder with a quick physical reset, like taking three deep breaths to signal to your body that the threat is passing? We can try practicing that sequence tomorrow during your training ride. How does that sound as our first action step?

That sounds doable. I think if I have a concrete routine like that—catch the thought, tell myself they're focused on themselves, and then take a few deep breaths—it might actually break the cycle before it spirals. I'll give it a try on my ride tomorrow and see how it feels. Thanks, I feel a little more prepared now.

That sense of preparation is a huge relief, and knowing you have a clear plan for tomorrow puts you in a much stronger position. Remember, it won't disappear overnight, but each time you use that routine, you're teaching your brain that those fears aren't as dangerous as they feel. Is there anything else weighing on you before we wrap up, or shall we leave it at that?

Hi there, it's great to see you again. How have you been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything particular weighing on your mind today? Let's start by checking in on how things are going before we talk about what needs focusing on.

Hi, thanks for asking. I've been... okay, I guess, but that guilt is still hanging around. I keep replaying that moment in my head, and it feels like I can't shake the feeling that I've failed somehow. It's been really hard to focus at work because of it.

It sounds like that replaying of the moment is taking up so much space in your mind right now, making it tough to concentrate at work. When you notice those thoughts coming up, do you feel like there is any specific evidence that suggests you actually failed, or does it mostly feel like you're just telling yourself that story over and over?

I mean, the evidence is right there—I ate meat, even if it was an accident. I've been vegan for four years, and I've always been so careful, so how could I let this happen? It just feels like proof that I'm not as committed or as good a person as I thought I was.

That makes perfect sense given how carefully you've maintained your vegan lifestyle for four years; finding an accident feels like a direct threat to your identity as someone who cares deeply about animals. Before we decide if that one slip-up truly means you aren't "good enough," I'd love to hear more about what happens right after you eat—that meat in that moment. Does your body react differently, or do you immediately jump to judging yourself harshly while trying to fix the mistake?

As soon as I realized what I'd done, my stomach just dropped, and I felt this wave of panic. I didn't even taste it properly; I just immediately started thinking, "How could you be so stupid? You should have checked." I tried to tell myself it wasn't a big deal, but my mind just went straight to all the animals I've supposedly failed.

That physical sensation of your stomach dropping, paired with that immediate self-criticism, shows just how powerful those thoughts are becoming. While it makes complete sense to worry about animals when you care so deeply, let's pause for a second to look closely at that "you should have checked" part. Given the food you usually prepare, did you actually leave out any obvious warning signs that anyone might accidentally eat something else, or were you simply too focused on cooking dinner?

I was just making dinner normally—I always cook vegan, so I didn't even think to double-check the container. It was my roommate who bought it and left it in the fridge, and I just grabbed it without looking. So no, there were no warning signs, but I still feel like I should have been more careful, you know?

It sounds incredibly frustrating to realize you made such a simple oversight while worrying about the bigger picture of your values. Since you mentioned your roommate placed the item there without labeling it, could we look at whether your brain is exaggerating the likelihood of this happening again, or if that fear is mostly based on that one instance right now? Sometimes our minds play it safe by assuming the worst-case scenario even when the odds aren't quite that high.

I guess part of me does think, "What if it happens again?" because I can't control what other people put in the fridge. But you're right, it's only happened once, and I've been vegan for years without any issues. It's just that one mistake feels so huge in my head, like it defines everything now.

That shift from "what if" to recognizing it's only happened once is a very important step you're taking. Even though the frequency is low, your brain seems to be magnifying that single event into a definition of your character. Have you noticed any difference in how you treat yourself today compared to how you treated yourself during those first few minutes of panic?

Honestly, I'm still pretty hard on myself today, but maybe not as much as that first moment. Back then, I felt like I'd ruined everything, but now I can kind of see that I'm overreacting a little. It's like there's a tiny voice saying, "It was just a mistake," but the loud one is still shouting, "You're a failure."

It takes real courage to admit that a quieter, kinder voice exists alongside that louder critic. That contrast tells us your capacity for compassion is still there, even if it hasn't won the argument yet. Instead of letting the "loud one" define the whole day, what if we agreed to give that tiny voice five minutes of attention whenever the panic hits, just to see if it holds up under scrutiny?

That actually sounds kind of helpful—like I'd be giving myself permission to stop and think before the guilt takes over completely. I'm willing to try it, even if it feels strange at first. Maybe if I do that enough, the loud voice will start to quiet down a bit.

That willingness to experiment with pausing and listening to the kinder voice is exactly the kind of small shift that builds resilience over time. Before we wrap up, I want to make sure we lock in a clear plan: whenever you catch yourself thinking "you're a failure," will you consciously take a breath and ask, "Is this thought based on facts, or is it just my old habit talking?" Let's settle on that as your go-to tool for tomorrow. How does that sound as a starting point?

Yeah, I think I can do that. I'll try to take a breath and ask myself that question whenever the guilt starts spiraling. It sounds like a small thing, but maybe it'll help me see things more clearly. Thanks for suggesting it—I'm willing to give it a real shot.

That commitment to giving it a real shot means a lot, especially when things feel overwhelming. Take a deep breath knowing you have a gentle tool ready for those moments when the guilt tries to take over. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we close out our time together today?
No, I think I've got a good starting point for now. I'll practice that pause and question, and see how it goes. Thank you for listening—it helped just talking it through.

You are absolutely welcome, and I am so glad you felt heard. Remember that progress isn't about eliminating the difficult feelings overnight, but about learning to navigate them with a little more kindness until they don't feel quite so controlling. I hope you have a calm evening ahead, practicing that new pause whenever needed. Take care of yourself today!
Hi there, I'm glad we're sitting down to talk again. How are you feeling right now compared to where you were last time? What was something that stood out to you about your week so far?

Hi. Well, I guess I'm feeling about the same as before. This week, I had one of those moments that just kind of stuck with me—I was at a dinner party with some friends, and one of them is a lawyer. She was talking about a big case she's working on, and I just sat there thinking, "What do I even contribute to the world? I teach kids to paint." It really got under my skin.

That feeling of stepping aside while someone else talks about their life's work can be really painful. Did you notice any other thoughts racing through your head after that initial thought about painting?

Yeah, it's like a whole avalanche, honestly. I started thinking about how my old college friends are all doctors or business owners now, and here I am, still cleaning up glue sticks and getting glitter in my hair every day. Then I thought, "My parents must be so disappointed they didn't get a 'real' professional for a daughter." It just spirals.

It makes total sense that comparing your current path to everyone else's achievements feels overwhelming and leaves you feeling inadequate. When those thoughts spiral into worries about disappointing your parents, does that spark any strong physical sensations or a rush of anxiety for you?

Yes, actually. I get this tight feeling in my chest, like a knot. And my stomach drops, kind of like I'm falling even though I'm standing still. Sometimes my hands get a little shaky too, especially if I'm still at the event or party where I started feeling this way. It's like my body just confirms what my mind is already telling me—that I'm not good enough.

Those physical sensations—tightness in your chest, dropping stomach, shaking hands—are your body reacting to the stress of those thoughts, which is completely understandable given how intense they feel. But have you ever noticed if those symptoms happen when you're doing something you love, like teaching a class, versus when you're just thinking about what others think of you?

That's a good question. No, I don't think so. When I'm actually in the classroom, especially during a project the kids are really into, I barely even notice my body. I'm just focused on helping them mix the right colors or get their proportions right. The shaking and tightness only really hit me when I'm alone with my thoughts later, or at those social events where I feel like I'm being measured.

That distinction is really helpful—it suggests your body isn't betraying your worth when you're actually creating value for children, but rather reacting to the pressure of external judgment. Since those symptoms seem tied more to social evaluation than your actual work, could we explore what might happen if you treated that tight chest sensation simply as a sign of nervous energy rather than proof of failure?

Hmm. I guess I never thought of it that way. I always just assumed the tightness meant "you're in a bad situation, you don't belong here." But if it's just nervous energy... maybe that's different. I mean, I get nervous before a big art show or a presentation to the school board, but I still go through with it and usually do okay. So maybe it's the same kind of thing, just aimed at a different target.

That's a really powerful insight, noticing that nervous energy shows up before presentations too means it's a normal response, not a unique flaw in your ability. If you've successfully managed that anxiety before, what small part of that experience reminds you that you can handle this feeling right now?

When I'm preparing for a presentation, I always remind myself that I know my material better than anyone in the room. I've taught art for over twenty years, so I've seen every kind of student and every kind of project. I guess I could remind myself that I know my own life and choices better than anyone else does too. That lawyer friend doesn't know what it's like to help a shy kid finally speak up because they found a way to express themselves with paint. I know that part of my story.

That reminder about knowing your students' stories and seeing their growth gives you a solid foundation of truth to stand on. If we use that same knowledge to counter the idea that you aren't contributing meaningfully, what would that look like saying out loud right now?

I guess I'd say... I help kids find their voice. Not everyone can say that. I give them a space to be messy and creative and proud of something they made with their own hands. Maybe that's not a big court case or a business deal, but it matters to them. And it matters to me.

That sounds incredibly powerful and meaningful; hearing you articulate exactly why your work matters shifts the perspective from "not enough" to "essential." Now, let's try taking one step toward testing whether that tight chest feeling will disappear just by reminding yourself of that truth instead of fighting the emotion. Would you be willing to sit with that tightness for thirty seconds while quietly repeating, "I help kids find their voice," and notice if the intensity changes even slightly?

Okay. I can try that. (Pauses for a moment, takes a breath.) "I help kids find their voice." It feels a little strange saying it to myself like that, but... I think the tightness loosened up just a bit. Not completely gone, but it's not as heavy, maybe? It's like I can breathe a little easier, like there's room for something else besides the worry.

That shift from heavy to manageable is huge progress, and noticing that tiny difference proves your brain can change its reaction when you offer it new information. Does repeating that phrase feel more like a gentle anchor now, or did it start to sound a bit more familiar and less forced?

It felt less forced the second time, actually. The first time I said it, it felt kind of rehearsed, like I was trying on a coat that didn't quite fit. But by the end, it started to feel a little more natural. Like maybe that coat isn't as uncomfortable as I thought. I think I could get used to wearing it, if I gave myself enough chances to try it on.

That's a wonderful metaphor for building resilience—you don't force yourself to wear a jacket forever until it fits, you just keep putting it on until it becomes comfortable. Let's take this feeling of being able to wear it to try using it as a quick reset tool before our next conversation ends. Can you imagine walking away from that dinner table remembering that sentence as your automatic thought when doubt creeps in?

I think I can. I can picture myself sitting at the table, feeling that familiar knot starting to form, and just saying quietly to myself, "I help kids find their voice." It's not a big flashy thing, but it's true. And I think if I can hold onto that, it might keep me from sinking into that whole spiral about being unimportant. It's worth a try, at least.

That visualization is perfect because it turns a vague hope into a concrete tool you can grab instantly when needed. Before we wrap up, since you mentioned feeling steady in the classroom, could you share one specific memory of a moment where you saw a student truly shine thanks to your guidance?

Sure. There's one student, a seventh-grade boy named Marcus, who was really shy and quiet. He didn't talk much in any class, and he was always nervous about making mistakes. One day we were doing a landscape project, and he just couldn't get the tree trunks right. I showed him a trick with the brush, how to use the side of it for texture. His face just lit up when he saw it work. He ended up asking to stay after class to finish it. That was a good day.

Hearing about Marcus lighting up with that simple brush trick really highlights how your patience and creativity directly impact his confidence. It's a beautiful example of the ripple effect you create beyond just making pretty pictures. Is there anything else you'd like to add about how you handled that moment, or shall we wrap up our time together today?

I think that's a good place to stop for today. I appreciate you helping me see that moment more clearly. It's easy to forget those little victories when I'm stuck in my own head. I'll try to keep that Marcus memory close, and the phrase about helping kids find their voice, as I go through the next week. Thanks for listening.

It was a pleasure supporting you today, and I'm so glad we could connect that specific victory with your broader sense of purpose. Taking that Marcus memory and your new phrase with you as you navigate the rest of the week sounds like a great plan. We'll check in soon to see how those tools held up when things get busy again.
Thank you. That sounds good. I'll try to pay attention to how my body feels when the doubt creeps in, and maybe give that phrase a chance before I let the spiral take over. I'll see you next time.

You're absolutely welcome, and I'm confident you'll find that new phrase becoming your go-to shield very quickly. Remember, even just glancing at the feeling of Marcus lighting up can be enough to pull you back from that spiral. I'll be here whenever you're ready to reflect on how things went, so take care and have a wonderful evening.

Hi there, I'm glad we're meeting again. How has your week been treating you so far, and is there anything different about how you've been feeling compared to last time? Let's also take a moment to decide together what feels like the most important thing to explore in our time today.

Hey. The week's been okay, I guess. I've been thinking a lot about that book I couldn't finish, and it's still bugging me. Every time I look at my bookshelf, I just feel like a failure for not getting through it, and I think that's what I'd like to talk about today.

It sounds like that unfinished book has become a pretty heavy weight for you, especially when you walk past those shelves. That feeling of being a failure seems really painful right now. Can you tell me more about the specific moments when looking at the books makes you feel that way? What happens in your mind right after you spot the empty space?

Well, I'll be honest, when I see that book sitting there with the bookmark still in it, I immediately think, "See? You couldn't even do this one simple thing." It's like my brain just jumps straight to that conclusion, and then I start thinking about all the other books I've started and never finished, or how I'm just not a "real reader" like other people. It feels like proof that I'm somehow defective.

That is a very harsh voice in your head, and I can hear how much pain it causes you to call yourself defective. When that thought pops up, does it make you want to hide away from the room, or does it drive you to try harder immediately afterward? Let's look closely at that first thought—when someone else says they struggled with something difficult, what is your actual experience telling you versus what your brain is jumping to conclude?

Usually, it makes me want to just walk away from the books entirely, like I should just give up reading altogether. But then I feel guilty and try to force myself to sit down and read, which just makes me feel worse when I can't concentrate. And if a friend told me they were struggling to finish a book, I'd tell them it's no big deal—life gets busy, and it's just a hobby. But for me, it feels like a personal failure, like I'm the only one who can't manage it.

I hear the intense guilt you carry when you can't focus, and it makes sense that walking away feels like the only escape, even though it leaves you feeling worse later. There is a clear difference between helping a friend and judging yourself, yet your brain treats both situations exactly the same way. Could you describe what actually happened recently when you tried to read but couldn't concentrate? Did anything specific distract you, or was it just an internal feeling stopping you?

Actually, last weekend I sat down with a new book I was excited about, and I couldn't even get past the first chapter. My mind kept drifting to work deadlines and a stupid argument I'd had with my friend earlier that week. Instead of just letting myself be distracted, I started telling myself, "See? You can't even focus on something you supposedly enjoy." So the distraction itself became proof that I wasn't good enough, rather than just... being distracted.

It makes complete sense that you turned a normal distraction into proof of your own inadequacy; nobody wants to admit they got sidetracked by life's usual messes. When you told yourself that story about focusing, did you notice any physical tension in your body, or did that thought just spiral faster in your head?

I think it was more in my head, just a spiral that kept getting faster. But now that you mention it, I do remember my shoulders getting really tight, and I felt almost restless, like I couldn't sit still. It's like my body was reacting to that voice telling me I was failing, even before I fully realized what was happening.

Noticing that tightness and restlessness shows your body is working overtime to cope with that harsh criticism. Sometimes our minds interpret ordinary distractions as catastrophic failures because we've made such a strong rule about ourselves regarding reading. Have you ever found a small way to pause, maybe step away from the shelf or drink some water, instead of spiraling further into the "failure" narrative?

I've never really thought to do that, to be honest. Usually, I just keep pushing through the spiral until I feel so defeated that I finally give up and do something else. But I guess I could try just walking away for a minute, like getting a glass of water or stepping outside, without telling myself I'm giving up. It might help break that cycle before it gets too loud in my head.

That is a brilliant insight; separating the action of taking a break from the label of "giving up" removes the guilt that usually drives you back into the spiral. Can we explore whether you believe that feeling the tension leave is a sign that your perspective is shifting, or if that relief is just a temporary pause before the old thoughts return?

That realization—that the relief proves the good moments *do* hold some power—is a huge step forward, even if it doesn't last forever. Let's try to build a small habit to catch that relief before it fades; would you be open to taking a screenshot of those three compliments and saving it on your phone so you can glance at it whenever the negative loop starts again?

Yeah, I think I could try that. It sounds a little silly, like looking at a trophy case or something, but I guess if it helps me see the good stuff for more than a second, it's worth a shot. I'll screenshot the next nice thing someone says and try to look at it before I start replaying a complaint.

That sounds like a solid plan, and honestly, seeing the good comments saved right there will make them feel much more tangible when you need them. Let's aim to practice this approach for just two days starting tomorrow, noting each time you find yourself replaying a complaint and successfully glancing at your notes instead. Did you have any other thoughts on how you might handle the first few times it feels hard to stick with it?

Probably the toughest part will be actually remembering to look at the phone instead of just diving into the negative spiral. I could set a little reminder on my phone to pop up after my shift, or maybe even put a sticky note on the counter at work that just says "check your phone." That way I have a visual cue to stop and look at the good stuff before I get too deep into the bad thoughts.

Those external cues are brilliant ideas because they act as gentle nudges to interrupt the automatic loop before you lose momentum. Setting a timer or placing a visible note creates a safe break in the cycle so you don't have to rely solely on your own memory during high-stress moments. Would you like to pick which method feels easiest to implement right now, or perhaps combine both for maximum support?

I think I'll combine both, honestly. I'll put a sticky note on the counter where I can see it while I'm cooking, and I'll set an alarm on my phone for halfway through my shift. That way, even if I'm in the middle of a rush, one of them should catch my attention and remind me to take a second to look at those good comments. It feels a bit like training wheels, but I'm willing to try anything at this point.

Combining the visual note with the alarm gives you double support, making it much easier to break that negative spiral early on. Remember that these tools aren't about fixing everything instantly, but simply giving your brain a chance to reset before the stress takes over. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we wrap up today's session?

No, I think that covers it for today. I'm feeling a little more hopeful than when I walked in, which is nice. I'll give the sticky note and alarm a try and see how it goes. Thanks for listening and helping me come up with that plan.

I'm so glad to hear you're feeling a bit more hopeful, and that's a wonderful place to land before we finish. Take care of yourself tonight, and remember that even small shifts in how you view those good moments can add up over time. I hope you have a great rest of your evening!

Hi there, I'm glad we can start our session today. How have you been feeling lately, and is there anything different about things compared to when we last spoke? Before we dive into what brought you here, could you share a bit about what feels most important to talk about right now?

Hi. Thanks for having me. Honestly, I've been feeling pretty heavy lately, especially at night when I'm trying to sleep. My mind just keeps replaying old memories—my parents fighting, the divorce, and then my husband's death. It all gets tangled up, and I end up blaming myself for both.

It sounds like those memories feel incredibly overwhelming tonight, especially carrying the weight of self-blame. When thoughts of family pain mix with grief over your husband, it makes total sense that you'd feel exhausted and stuck. Could you tell me more about exactly how you usually react when those memories start playing in your head while you're lying down?

I usually just lie there, staring at the ceiling, trying to make sense of it all. My heart starts racing, and I feel this tightness in my chest. I end up asking myself, "What did I do wrong? How could I have prevented this?" And I can't shake the feeling that I'm somehow the common denominator in both situations—like I caused the divorce and then I caused his death.

That intense physical reaction—heart racing and chest tightness—is so exhausting to carry alone while trying to rest. It completely validates why you feel stuck; when your body is in "fight or flight," logic just doesn't reach the surface. Have you noticed if you tend to ruminate on specific details from those events, or does the feeling of guilt just come on all at once?

It usually comes on all at once, like a wave. I'll be fine one moment, and then something small triggers it—maybe a song, a certain smell, or seeing a couple holding hands. Then I'm right back in that feeling of being a little kid, thinking I must have been the reason my parents split. And now with my husband gone, it feels like the same pattern. I just assume I'm the one who messes things up.

Those triggers act like a time machine, instantly pulling you back to childhood where you felt powerless and blamed. It makes complete sense that when a song reminds you of your parents' fight, your brain automatically jumps to the conclusion that you were responsible, even though you were just a child trying to survive. That shift from "what happened" to "what I did" is really hard on the heart. Is there a particular recent event or thought that made this feeling spike right before we started talking?

Yeah, actually. There was this moment just last week when I saw my sister playing with her kids at the park, laughing and having a picnic. I felt happy for her for a second, but then this dark thought crept in: "She's the one who deserves a happy family, not me." It hit me so hard I had to leave early. I couldn't stop thinking that I'm somehow broken or cursed, and everyone around me would be better off if I wasn't in their lives.

That sudden shift from happiness to deep shame is incredibly painful, and it shows how deeply ingrained that belief that you are "broken" has become. When your mind tells you that others deserve joy while you don't, it creates a protective wall that pushes people away, which might ironically keep you isolated. Can you remember any evidence from past experiences that supports the idea that you actively curse people around you versus the reality of what you might have been feeling during that moment?

I guess... when I really think about it, I can't point to anything specific I did that would make my parents split up. I was just a kid, you know? I didn't have that kind of power. But it feels so real, like I must have done something to set them off. And with my husband, he had a heart condition—I knew about it. But still, in my head, I think maybe if I had been more careful or loving, he'd still be here. I just can't shake the feeling that I'm at the center of it all.

It takes courage to admit that the certainty you feel isn't backed by facts, especially regarding your parents and your husband's health. You are correctly identifying that you were too young to influence your parents' conflict, yet your mind insists you must have done something to cause it, which makes the truth feel impossible to accept. With your husband, knowing he had a serious condition changes the picture significantly because his life depended on medical factors beyond anyone's control, including yours. If you look at those moments again without judging yourself, could you describe what else was happening in your life at the time that might explain why you felt so overwhelmed?

When my parents split, I was around nine years old, and our house was always loud. My dad was gone a lot, and my mom was always crying or yelling. I remember trying to be perfect—keeping my room clean, getting good grades, making sure my younger siblings stayed quiet—thinking maybe if I did everything right, they'd stop fighting. But they didn't. And then when my husband died, I was juggling work and trying to be a good partner, but I was also exhausted and scared of losing him. I think I was just so afraid all the time, and that fear made me feel like I wasn't doing enough.

Your story reveals a very human survival instinct: you tried to earn safety and love by performing perfectly, believing that your behavior could control outcomes that were actually out of your hands. The fact that you were terrified and exhausted means you were reacting to fear, not failing at being a good person or partner. It seems like the core issue isn't that you *caused* these tragedies, but that you feel trapped by the belief that your actions determine whether loved ones stay safe and happy. If we set aside the blame for a moment, how would you describe what you were actually feeling and hoping for in those scary moments?

I think... I just wanted to feel safe. I wanted my family to be okay, and I wanted my husband to be healthy. I wanted to be enough for them. But deep down, I felt so small and helpless. I guess I hoped that if I tried hard enough, I could control things and stop the hurt from happening. But it never worked, and that just made me feel like I wasn't good enough.

It makes perfect sense that you reached for control as a way to protect yourself from the pain you witnessed growing up; trying to fix everything is often our brains' way of saying, "If I can manage this, then I am safe." However, the harsh lesson learned is that your efforts didn't change the outcome, leading to the painful conclusion that you weren't "good enough." Let's try to separate the hope of wanting safety from the false belief that your worth depends on controlling other people's lives. If we ignore the need to control everything, what do you think would happen if you allowed yourself to feel helpless without punishing yourself for it?

That's a scary thought. I don't know if I've ever let myself just feel helpless without immediately jumping to blame. I guess I'm afraid that if I stop blaming myself, I'll fall apart completely. Like, if I admit I couldn't control any of it, then the world just feels random and unsafe. And maybe I'd have to face how sad I really am, without any distraction of guilt to keep me busy.

It makes complete sense that admitting helplessness feels terrifying when guilt has been such a reliable shield for years—it protects us from the raw, unfiltered pain of grief. If you remove the excuse of "I messed up," you are left with just the sadness, which can indeed feel like standing naked in the cold. But paradoxically, accepting that you couldn't control the storms might actually free you from carrying the heavy burden of responsibility for things you simply couldn't influence. Would you be willing to explore what it might feel like to sit with that sadness for just five minutes without needing to find someone or something to blame?

I think I could try that. Maybe just sitting with the sadness, without telling myself it's my fault. It feels... uncomfortable, but maybe also a little lighter, like I'm not holding my breath anymore. I don't know what will happen, but I'm willing to give it a shot. What would that look like, just sitting with it?

Let's try setting a gentle boundary for that experiment: imagine placing a soft hand on your chest and silently telling yourself, "This is just sadness, not proof of failure," while letting the tears or heaviness flow without judgment. Start by focusing on just three deep breaths where you observe the feeling of tightness or emptiness without trying to fix it or run away from it. How does it feel in your body after you've held space for that sadness for just those few minutes, without adding the layer of blame?

Okay... I'm trying it now. I'm breathing slowly, and I can feel that tightness in my chest and a lump in my throat. Usually I'd start chastising myself, but I'm just letting it be there. It's heavy, but it's not as sharp as the guilt. It's more like a dull ache. After a few breaths, I notice my shoulders drop a little, and I feel a little less like I'm bracing for a punch. It's strange, but it feels a bit more honest.

That shift in sensation—from sharp guilt to a manageable dull ache—is a powerful sign that you are starting to separate your identity from the tragedy. Your body dropping its guard shows your nervous system is beginning to relax even when the emotions remain present. This honesty feels brave, and it suggests you are building a new relationship with your grief rather than using blame to escape it. Now that you've experienced that moment of relief without the pressure to perform, how do you want to honor that feeling when you return home later today?

I think I want to try to let myself sit with it for a few minutes each night before I go to sleep, instead of spiraling into blame. Maybe I can put my hand on my chest just like this and remind myself that sadness doesn't mean I failed. I'd also like to maybe write down what I'm feeling without judging it, just to let it out. It feels like a small step, but it's something I can actually do.

That is a beautiful and very grounded plan to try out tonight; grounding yourself physically and writing without judgment gives your brain permission to process the emotion safely. It transforms the experience from a spiral of "why me/why me" into a simple observation of "this is what I feel right now." Since you mentioned writing, could you share what you wrote down tonight, or perhaps describe the first thing that came to mind when you started writing about that evening's sadness?

I wrote down, "I am sitting here in the quiet, and I feel a weight in my chest. It's not accusing me of anything. It's just tired." That surprised me—calling it tired. I always thought of it as my punishment, but tonight it felt more like an old, worn-out part of me that just needed to rest. It was strange, but I didn't want to fight it.

That reframing of the weight as "tiredness" rather than "punishment" is a significant breakthrough; it honors your exhaustion without attaching the toxic label of failure to it. It sounds like you found a moment of peace where you finally allowed yourself to rest instead of fighting the feeling. Given how much this approach helped you feel lighter, would you be open to sharing another small detail from your day that might have triggered some of those old fears, so we can practice looking at it with the same gentle curiosity we just used?

Sure. This morning, I was making coffee, and I accidentally knocked over a mug and it shattered on the floor. My first thought was, "See, you ruin everything you touch." It was instant, like a reflex. But instead of getting stuck there, I tried to just notice that thought and breathe. I told myself, "It's just a broken mug, not a broken life." I still felt a pang, but I didn't let it swallow me up. It felt... different.

Noticing that automatic thought about ruining everything you touch shows you are successfully catching the old pattern before it takes over. By choosing to breathe and remind yourself that a broken mug isn't a reflection of your worth, you practiced the exact skill we discussed with the sadness earlier. That small victory proves you can handle unexpected mistakes with kindness instead of self-criticism. How did that choice to pause and breathe affect your overall mood after you fixed the spill?

It actually surprised me, because I didn't stay angry at myself. After I cleaned up the pieces, I just poured another cup of coffee and sat down. I felt a little shaky, but not crushed. Usually I'd carry that guilt for hours, but this time I let it go after a few minutes. I even smiled a little when I realized I didn't spiral. It was a small win, but it felt huge.

That ability to reset quickly after a mistake is incredible, and realizing you didn't spiral proves that your new perspective is working in real-time. The smile you shared suggests you are reclaiming a sense of agency—you are learning that accidents are just accidents, not verdicts on your character. Since you felt a sense of relief from that small interaction, what is one tiny thing you could do tomorrow morning to reinforce that feeling of safety when you wake up?

I think I'll start my morning by saying out loud, "Today, I am not the cause of everything that goes wrong." Just that one sentence, before I even get out of bed. Maybe I'll even say it to myself in the mirror while I pour my coffee. It feels like a promise I can keep, just for that moment.

That is a wonderful and empowering anchor to begin your day; repeating a phrase of self-affirmation before stepping into the world can create a strong mental buffer against negative thoughts. It turns a passive reaction into an active choice to greet yourself with compassion right from the start. Since you have such a clear intention for your morning routine, would you be comfortable sharing one specific challenge you anticipate facing this afternoon that might bring up those old worries?

Honestly, I'm supposed to meet an old friend for lunch tomorrow. We haven't talked in a while, and I'm already worried I'll say something wrong or bring down the mood. I'm afraid she'll see that I'm still carrying this sadness and think I'm too broken to be around. I don't want to ruin another relationship by being "too much."

That fear of being "too much" is such a familiar trap, especially when you've spent years believing you need to hide your pain to be worthy of connection. It sounds like you are projecting that internal feeling of brokenness onto your friend, assuming she will judge you based on a standard you set for yourself. Have you considered what your friend might actually care about when you speak, separate from the guilt you feel? Often, friends value presence and authenticity far more than perfection. What is one specific worry you have about the conversation itself that isn't about her judging you?

I guess the specific worry is that I'll start crying, and then I won't know how to stop. I'm afraid I'll lose control and dump all this heavy stuff on her, and then she'll be stuck feeling awkward or responsible. I don't want to be the one who makes things tense. I'd rather just keep it light and safe.

It is completely understandable that you want to protect your friend from feeling awkward or burdened, but please know that you cannot control her reaction, and she likely cares about your humanity more than her own comfort. Crying is not a flaw or a disaster; it is simply an expression of feeling deeply, and many friends would prefer honesty over forced cheerfulness. Instead of trying to suppress the tears, what if you decided beforehand that it's okay to take a sip of water or take a breath whenever you feel overwhelmed, keeping the conversation flowing naturally without rushing to fix the mood?

That's a good idea. I think I can handle that—just taking a breath or a sip of water if I feel the tears coming. I don't have to pretend everything's fine, but I also don't have to dump everything on her at once. Maybe I can let the conversation guide us, and if I feel safe enough, I can share a little. And if I don't, that's okay too. I don't have to have it all figured out by lunch.

That is a mature and compassionate approach that respects both your needs and hers; giving yourself permission to share gradually removes the pressure to perform perfectly. By anchoring yourself in simple physical cues like drinking water or pausing, you create a safety net that lets the conversation unfold naturally without forcing a heavy emotional load. Since you feel ready to trust that this balance works, is there anything else you would like to discuss before we wrap up today, or shall we consider how you might apply this same flexibility to other social interactions?

I think I'm good for today. I feel like I've got a little more room to breathe, and I have a plan for tomorrow. I'd like to try applying this same flexibility to other situations—like when I'm at the grocery store or talking to my siblings. I'll practice noticing when I start blaming myself and just take that breath. Thanks for walking through this with me.

It sounds like you are carrying a lot of strength today, and applying this gentle awareness to daily routines like shopping or sibling conversations is a fantastic way to keep practicing self-kindness outside of therapy. Remember that even small moments of stopping the blame spiral are victories, regardless of how big or small they seem. Thank you for trusting me with your story and for showing up so bravely; I wish you continued peace as you navigate these new habits.

Hi there, I'm really glad we can start our time together today. How have you been feeling lately, and is there anything different from our last chat that stands out? Could we pick one or two things that feel most important to explore first so we don't get overwhelmed?

Hi. Thanks for asking. I guess I've been feeling pretty much the same since we last spoke—still anxious about work, still beating myself up over little things. I had a moment this week where I sent an email with a small typo, and I just couldn't stop thinking about it. That's probably the biggest thing.

That sounds incredibly draining, especially when it happens right after sending something you thought was ready. It makes total sense that you're spiraling into self-criticism now; anyone would feel shaken by such a harsh reaction to a tiny mistake.
