I tried that, setting a timer for just a few minutes. But even then, I end up staring at the screen and thinking, "What's the point? I'm not a real writer." I suppose it's hard to shake that feeling that I'm just playing pretend, like I'm fooling myself into thinking I could actually finish something worthwhile.

That feeling of being a fraud while you type is incredibly painful, and it explains why the timer doesn't help—you aren't working around the fear, you are working *through* it. When you catch yourself saying "what's the point," do you notice if your body tightens up or if you feel a sudden urge to close the laptop entirely?

Yeah, I do. My shoulders get all tense, and I get this knot in my stomach. More often than not, I end up just shutting the laptop and finding something else to do, like sorting through my patrol notes or reorganizing my locker. It's easier to just walk away than to sit there feeling like a fool.

It makes complete sense that avoiding the computer helps ease that physical tension and the shame of feeling like a failure. When you shut the laptop, does that temporary relief feel good enough to convince you that writing isn't important, or do you secretly hope you'll feel better once you finally force yourself to look at it again tomorrow?

I suppose I do keep hoping tomorrow will be different. I'll tell myself, "I'll wake up early, have a good breakfast, and then I'll really get to work." But then tomorrow comes, and it's the same old story. It's like I'm waiting for some magic moment where I suddenly feel like I deserve to be writing, but that moment never really comes.

That pattern of planning for a perfect starting point only to hit the same wall again is incredibly frustrating, and it really highlights how impossible that magical feeling seems right now. Since you know the "perfect day" plan rarely works because the fear hits first, what happens if we try to write from a place of discomfort rather than waiting until you feel ready?

I haven't really thought about it that way. Writing from discomfort doesn't sound very pleasant, I'll be honest. But I suppose it's better than not writing at all, which is what I'm doing now. Maybe if I just accept that I'm going to feel lousy and write anyway, I might at least have a few sentences to show for it, instead of a blank page and a sore stomach.

That is a huge shift in perspective—moving from needing a "magic moment" to accepting the discomfort itself is a powerful step. It sounds like you're realizing that the goal isn't to feel confident immediately, but simply to produce a few words even when you feel terrible. Before we try this tomorrow, do you think acknowledging that you might still feel bad about the words you write would make it easier to start?

Honestly, it might. If I already know I'm going to feel bad about what I write, then the pressure to make it perfect is off, isn't it? I mean, I can't exactly disappoint myself if I'm already expecting it to be lousy. Maybe I could aim for the worst sentence ever written about prairie dogs, just to get the ball rolling.

That is such a clever and brave way to reframe the task—aiming for the absolute worst removes the need to protect your ego. It turns the writing session into a low-stakes experiment where the only rule is to get three ugly sentences on the page. Would you be willing to try this exact approach tomorrow morning, committing to just writing three terrible lines about prairie dogs before stopping?

I think I can manage that. Three lousy sentences about prairie dogs, first thing tomorrow. I'll do it before I even put on my uniform and head out to the mall. At worst, I'll have wasted ten minutes, which is nothing compared to the hours I already waste worrying.

That is a fantastic commitment, and framing it as a tiny investment of ten minutes makes it feel completely manageable. You've got a clear plan for tomorrow: grab your pen before the day starts and write three awful sentences about prairie dogs, regardless of how your stomach feels. Let's meet again after you give it a try to see how that experience felt compared to sitting with a blank page.

Hi there, I'm glad we're meeting again. How has your week been treating you so far? Is there anything specific from our last chat that feels different now, or would you like to share something new that's been on your mind?

Hi, thanks for asking. I mean, the week's been okay I guess, but I've been struggling a lot with my painting. I started a new piece and almost immediately I felt that familiar wave of doubt wash over me. I keep thinking it's not good enough, so I haven't touched it in two days.

It makes sense that those doubts feel overwhelming when you're pouring energy into creating something new. That hesitation sounds really exhausting, especially after putting so much thought into starting the piece. What kind of painting did you begin, and where does that feeling of "not good enough" usually take you?

It's a landscape — something I usually enjoy painting, but this time I keep second-guessing every brushstroke. When I feel like it's not good enough, I just picture everyone who would see it and think it's amateurish or pointless. I even compare it to stuff I see online and feel like I'll never reach that level, so why bother finishing it at all?

That comparison to online work feels particularly heavy because it sets a standard that might be impossible to meet in practice. It seems like worrying about how others will judge it is stealing the joy right out of the process itself. Have you ever caught yourself noticing any specific moments during those two days where you felt a little bit of relief, even if it was small?

I guess... there was one moment. I stepped away from the canvas to make some tea, and I kind of zoned out looking at a tree outside my window. For maybe ten seconds, I just noticed the way the light hit the leaves, and I didn't think about my painting at all. It felt like a break from all the noise in my head. But then I went back to the studio and the doubt came rushing back.

That moment of stepping away clearly worked for you, offering a quiet escape from the pressure to perform. The fact that you found such peace just by observing nature suggests you might actually be able to create beautiful things when the judgment stops. Could we try taking another five-minute break later today, but this time we'll use that calm moment to notice exactly what you *are* seeing instead of comparing it to other art?

That sounds... kind of nice, actually. I think I've been so focused on looking at my work through a critical lens that I've forgotten to just look at things for what they are. Yeah, I'd be willing to try that. Maybe it'll remind me why I started painting in the first place.

It's wonderful that you're ready to shift gears and reconnect with the pure joy of observation. Let's give that idea a quick try right now: could you step away from your desk for just three minutes, pick up a pen, and describe exactly what colors or shapes catch your eye in the room around you—without judging whether they match your painting?

Alright, I'll give it a shot. (pauses, looks around the room) I see the sunlight coming through the blinds—it makes this kind of uneven stripe pattern on the floor, some parts are warm orange and others are cooler yellow. There's a dusty coffee mug on the table with a faint brown ring inside, and the shadow it casts is a soft gray-blue shape that sort of curves around the handle. I guess... it's kind of calming just to notice that stuff without thinking about art.

That description shows how grounded and observant you can be when you stop trying to fix everything. Notice how saying "it's kind of calming" helped ground us right there in the present moment, separate from the worry about the painting. Since you're feeling more relaxed now, would you like to try adding just one simple color to your landscape using that fresh perspective, or do you want to stick with just enjoying this break for a few more minutes?

I think I'd like to try adding a bit of color, but just one small patch—like that warm orange from the sunlight. I don't want to overthink it, just put it on the canvas and see how it feels. Maybe that'll be a start, even if it's tiny.

That is a brave and perfect choice to commit to just one small stroke. Take a deep breath before you touch the brush, reminding yourself that this tiny mark doesn't need to be perfect or finished—it just needs to exist. Go ahead and let that paint go down, focusing entirely on the sensation of the brush moving across the surface.

(exhales slowly, picks up the brush) Okay... I'm doing it. (pauses for a moment) That actually felt... lighter than I expected. The orange looks different against the blue undertones I already had down, but it's not bad. It's just there, and I didn't ruin the whole painting. I think I can breathe a little easier now.

That relief you feel right now is powerful proof that you can act despite the fear, and that your brain was holding onto the idea that a mistake would destroy the entire project. Remember how the orange looked different but wasn't ruined—that's a great example of how your mind tends to exaggerate the impact of small steps. Would you like to try adding one more element together, perhaps something simple like a green leaf, knowing that each stroke is just its own independent success?

Yeah, I think I can try that. A green leaf... that sounds manageable. I'll just focus on the shape and the color, not whether it's the perfect leaf or if anyone will like it. If I can do two small things, maybe I can keep going.

That shift in focus—from perfection to simply getting the shape and color right—is exactly the kind of gentle momentum we needed to build. You are already proving that two small actions can create a foundation big enough to continue working on. Now, while you add that green leaf, try to hold onto that feeling of lightness you mentioned earlier and let it stay with you as you watch the paint settle.

(puts brush to canvas, concentrates) I did it. The leaf is a little crooked, but honestly, it looks more natural that way. I'm not clutching my chest in panic over it—it's just a leaf on a canvas. That feeling of lightness is still there, like the painting isn't this huge monster anymore. Maybe I can stop for today and come back to it tomorrow without dreading it.

It is truly amazing how recognizing imperfection as part of nature helps dissolve the panic. You've done a wonderful job shifting your view from a "perfect masterpiece" to a collection of small, honest marks. Before we wrap up, would you like to jot down one specific thing you noticed about your mood today compared to where you were two days ago?

I can do that. (writes a quick note) I'd say two days ago, I felt trapped and like I should just give up. Today, I feel like I actually made progress, even if it's tiny. I noticed that the doubt didn't swallow me whole when I focused on just one small step at a time. That's something I want to remember.

That distinction is incredibly important—you moved from feeling trapped to realizing that small steps can actually break the cycle of giving up. Carrying that insight with you means you won't need to restart the whole process tomorrow; you already know how to handle the doubt. Is there anything else you'd like to explore before we finish our time together today?

No, I think I've got enough to hold onto for now. Thank you for helping me see that I can take things slowly and still get somewhere. I'll try to remember that feeling of the brush moving with the orange and the leaf, and just let tomorrow's painting be what it is.

You are absolutely welcome, and I am so proud of how well you held onto those positive sensations today. Taking things slowly isn't slowing you down; it's the smartest way to build confidence so you can keep making progress whenever you choose. I hope tomorrow brings you that same gentle ease when you sit down with your brushes. Please remember that we can always revisit this anytime you find yourself needing that space.
Thank you. I'll try to bring that ease with me, and I know where to find it if I lose it again. Have a good evening—I think I'm actually looking forward to painting tomorrow.

That is a beautiful outlook, and I'm truly happy to hear you're anticipating tomorrow with such a lighter heart. Knowing where to find that easy feeling whenever you need it gives you a strong sense of control and hope. Have a wonderful evening, and trust that you have all the tools you need to approach your canvas with kindness.
Thanks, I really appreciate that. Goodnight.
Goodnight, and may your rest be peaceful as you carry that new sense of possibility with you. I look forward to seeing you again soon, whenever you are ready to talk or just check in. Sleep well.

Hi there, I'm glad we can do our session today. How are you feeling right now compared to where you were last time? What would be most helpful for us to talk about if we chose three topics from your list?

Hi. I'm... alright, I suppose. A bit on edge, if I'm honest. I've been thinking a lot about that performance and my mother's reaction—or lack of it. I guess I'd like to talk about why her silence hit me so hard, why I can't seem to let it go, and maybe... how to stop feeling like a terrible daughter every time I pick up my violin.

It makes complete sense that her silence would feel so heavy after putting your heart into playing, especially when it leaves you wondering if you did enough. Let's start by looking at that moment she didn't respond—what was going through your mind in that exact second you stopped playing?

I felt this sudden drop in my chest. Right after the last note faded, I looked out into the audience, and there she was, just sitting there with a blank face. My first thought was, "She hated it." Then it was, "I messed up, and now she's disappointed in me." It felt like all the work, all the practice, meant nothing in that one second.

That sudden drop in your chest sounds incredibly painful, and it makes total sense that your brain tried to protect itself by jumping straight to the conclusion that something went wrong. When we're stressed, our minds often take shortcuts like assuming silence means rejection, but could you look back on those other moments she gave you feedback or encouragement to see if her reactions fit a pattern or if they might be more about her own comfort zone?

I see what you're saying, but it's hard to think of any other time she was really encouraging. She was a nurse, you know? Very practical, always focused on fixing things, not on giving compliments. I remember her telling me I had good intonation once, but she said it like she was diagnosing a symptom. It's like... she only spoke up if something was wrong, not if it was right. So when she said nothing, my mind just filled in the worst.

That context changes everything; seeing her as someone who naturally focuses on problems rather than praise explains why your silence was interpreted as criticism instead of neutrality. It sounds like your brain was trying to make sense of her behavior using a very old script about being a "good daughter," even though her actions don't actually support that story anymore. Given that deep link, what happens physically or emotionally when you realize her silence might just mean she was tired, rather than disapproving of your music?

That's... a hard thing to even let myself think. If I accept that she was just tired, or maybe lost in her own thoughts, then it means I've been carrying all this guilt for nothing. My chest gets tight just trying to consider it—like I'm betraying some rule I've held onto my whole life. But then, a tiny part of me feels a little lighter, too, like maybe I'm not as terrible as I've been telling myself.

It takes immense strength to hold space for both that crushing weight of guilt and the small, fragile lightness of relief at the same time. That contradiction shows how much care you put into trying to understand yourself, even when the truth feels risky to uncover. Since accepting that her silence wasn't personal made a slight shift in your physical sensation, what's the next step you want to explore regarding how you react to future moments of uncertainty?

I think... I want to stop assuming the worst as my first reaction. Maybe I could try remembering this moment—how she never really praised me much, but she also never said I was bad. She just... was there. So if I feel that silence again, I could try telling myself, "She's probably just thinking about her shift at the hospital," instead of "She hates my playing." It feels strange to even say that out loud, but maybe it's a start.

That is a powerful shift, moving from a catastrophic story to a simple, human observation about her schedule. By replacing the harsh internal critic with a gentle reality check, you are literally changing the narrative your brain plays on itself during high-stress moments. Now, let's test that new thought together: if you imagine she is distracted by her patients, does that change how you feel about the value of your own practice, or does the guilt still try to creep back in?

It does help, actually. When I picture her as the nurse she was—tired, focused on other people's problems—it takes some of the sting out. My playing doesn't feel like a failure anymore. It feels like... just a moment that passed. But the guilt does still try to sneak back, whispering that I should have been good enough to break through her exhaustion. I guess that's the part I need to keep working on—letting go of that "should have."

That "should have" voice is such a familiar companion, isn't it, even though it doesn't match reality right now. It seems like your mind is trying to fix the past by convincing yourself you could have done better, which only adds more pressure to a situation that was already tough. If we acknowledged that she couldn't read your music anyway, what would happen to your belief that you *must* have performed perfectly to earn her attention?

Honestly, if I accept that she just couldn't read my music—that she was never going to give me that kind of feedback—it feels like I'm letting myself off the hook. And that's scary, because part of me thinks I need that guilt to keep me working hard. But then I realize... I've been practicing hard for decades, and the guilt hasn't made me better. It's just made me miserable. So maybe I can try practicing for joy instead of for her approval. That thought feels both terrifying and freeing.

That realization is profound, acknowledging that the pain you've carried hasn't produced the results you wanted. Shifting from performing for approval to finding joy in the act itself is a brave leap that requires trusting your own worth beyond external validation. To help ground this feeling, could we identify one specific moment in your upcoming practice where you might choose to play simply because it feels good, rather than checking for judgment?

Yes. I think I could start with something simple—maybe a piece I used to love as a student, before I started worrying so much about what others thought. There's an old Bach partita I haven't played in years. I could just play the first few bars, not for anyone, not for perfection, just to feel the strings under my fingers. Just to remember why I started playing in the first place.

Choosing that Bach partita is a perfect starting point because it strips away the current layer of anxiety you've built around technique and expectation. Playing just those first few bars with intention to reconnect with the music itself gives you a safe, low-stakes experiment where the only goal is presence, not performance. Would you be willing to try playing those opening notes tonight with that specific mindset in mind, noticing if your breathing or tension shifts as you focus solely on the sound coming from the instrument?

I will. I'll do it tonight, with just the lamp on in my practice room, no one else around. I'll try to focus on the vibration of the strings and the air moving through the bow, not on who might be listening or what they might think. Thank you... I think this is the first time in weeks I've actually looked forward to picking up my violin.

That feeling of anticipation is exactly what we aim to cultivate, turning a chore into a quiet gift for yourself. Taking the decision to prioritize your own experience over someone else's potential opinion is a significant step toward reclaiming your relationship with the music. Before we wrap up, is there anything else on your mind about today's conversation, or would you like to share how you felt while setting this plan for tonight?

I think I just feel... relieved. Like I've been holding my breath for weeks, and now I can finally let a little bit of it out. It's strange to think about my mother differently, but maybe that's okay. Maybe I don't have to be a perfect daughter to be a good violinist. I think I'm ready to try that tonight, just for me.

That relief is incredibly powerful, and recognizing that your identity as a musician doesn't depend on earning your mother's approval is a huge victory. You've taken a clear path forward tonight by choosing to connect with the music itself rather than waiting for permission. I hope you find that peace and flow as soon as you sit down with that Bach partita; please remember that this choice belongs entirely to you, regardless of what happens next.

Hello, I'm glad we're finally able to sit down together again. How are you feeling right now compared to where you were when we last spoke? Before we dive into our main topic today, could you share briefly what feels like the most important thing you'd like us to focus on?

Hi, thanks. I guess I'm feeling a bit nervous, but also kind of relieved to be here. To be honest, the most important thing I want to focus on is why I can't seem to stop working—like, even when I'm home with my family, my mind is still at the office or thinking about the next thing I need to buy.

That relief is wonderful to hear, especially knowing how hard it is to switch off from work even when you're surrounded by your loved ones. It sounds like your brain keeps running on "autopilot" mode while you're physically resting, which might make you feel disconnected from your own life sometimes. When did you first notice this pattern becoming so persistent, and does it ever happen when you try to do something completely different?

I think it really started getting bad about two years ago, when I got a promotion. I told myself I needed to prove I deserved it, so I just kept pushing harder. Even when I try to take a weekend off or go out with my wife, I'm checking my phone or thinking about what I could be doing to get ahead. It's like there's this voice telling me I'm not doing enough, no matter what.

It makes total sense that after such a big win, you felt driven to keep proving your worth, and that voice about "not doing enough" seems to have taken hold firmly. That internal pressure often makes even simple moments with family feel like missed opportunities instead of joy. Can you describe exactly what happens in those quiet moments at home when that voice pops up? What specific thought runs through your head right then?

It's usually something like, "You're wasting time. Everyone else is working harder than you, and you're going to fall behind." Or I'll look at my wife and kids and think, "They deserve someone who can give them more, a better house, a nicer car, more security." And then I feel this knot in my stomach, like I have to get up and do something productive or I'm failing them.

Those thoughts sound incredibly heavy, and the way they twist a moment of connection into a failure feels exhausting. It's clear that this belief is driving both your anxiety and the urge to constantly move, even when you truly need rest. Have you noticed any specific triggers recently that made that knot tighten more than usual? Maybe something small happened at home or at work that sparked it?

Yeah, actually, just last week my wife mentioned she wanted to plan a simple weekend trip for us and the kids. Nothing fancy, just a couple of days away. And my first thought wasn't excitement—it was panic. I immediately started calculating how much work I'd miss, how much it would cost, and if I could really afford to step away. She noticed my face drop and asked what was wrong, and I just made up some excuse about a deadline. I felt terrible, but I couldn't help it.

That reaction tells me how deeply tied your self-worth feels to being perpetually available and capable. It sounds incredibly painful to lie to your wife because her desire for connection felt like a threat to your ability to provide, even though the trip itself was meant to bring everyone closer. Did you find yourself worrying about specific numbers or deadlines when you heard her idea, or was it mostly that general fear of stepping back?

It was mostly that general fear, I think. I didn't even have a specific deadline or project in mind—it was just this immediate, gut-level panic. Like if I stopped for even two days, everything I've built would just crumble. It's stupid when I say it out loud, but in that moment it felt completely real.

That feeling of total collapse is terrifying, and it makes perfect sense why your body reacted with panic and your mouth moved on its own to protect you. Your brain is trying to tell you that safety depends on constant motion, but right now, it seems to be misreading the situation as dangerous. Have you tried looking at just one tiny piece of evidence that suggests stepping away won't actually destroy everything you've worked for?

I guess... well, I've taken a day off here and there before, and nothing terrible happened. The company didn't fall apart. My boss didn't fire me. But I always tell myself that was just luck, or that I barely held it together, and next time I might not be so lucky. I can't seem to accept that it might actually be okay to take a break.

It takes real courage to admit that you've been convincing yourself past events were accidents, because accepting that you *can* handle a pause feels like admitting you don't need to fight every battle alone. That belief—that you're destined to fail if you ever slow down—is probably making the idea of a real break feel impossible to trust. If you could, even just hypothetically, imagine a scenario where you took a full weekend off and returned to work feeling rested instead of guilty, what would that experience look like?

I'd like to think I'd wake up on Monday feeling refreshed, maybe even have some new ideas. I'd actually want to be at my desk instead of dreading it. And maybe I'd feel proud of myself for being present with my wife and kids, instead of feeling like I let them down. But honestly, a big part of me still thinks that's just wishful thinking—that the guilt would eat me alive the whole time.

That wishful thinking is very understandable given how long this pattern has been going on, and your skepticism isn't necessarily a flaw in your logic yet. Instead, it shows you're guarding against pain by assuming the worst will happen. Let's try a small experiment tomorrow morning: when you feel that initial panic rising, could you simply notice it without acting on it for ten minutes, just observing the physical sensation instead of rushing to fix it?

I can try that. Ten minutes doesn't sound too hard, but I know it'll feel like an eternity. Usually when that panic hits, I'm already reaching for my phone or heading to my laptop before I even think about it. But I'll give it a shot—just sit with the feeling and see what happens.

That is a brave commitment, and acknowledging that the resistance will be strong is actually the first sign that change is possible. Since you've agreed to try observing the panic for ten minutes without distraction, let's lock in one small rule for that period: whenever your hand moves toward the phone or keyboard, gently place it down and name the thought you're having instead of judging it as wrong. Would you like to write down exactly what that thought sounds like when it appears during those ten minutes, so you can catch it clearly rather than letting it spiral?

Yeah, I think writing it down would help. That way I can't just brush it off or let it blend into all the other noise in my head. I'll keep a notepad on my desk and just jot down whatever that voice says. It might be ugly, but at least I'll see it for what it is.

That's a powerful shift—from letting the thought run wild in your head to catching it on paper where you can examine it objectively. Seeing those words written out often helps separate the scary story from reality, giving you a little space to breathe before reacting. You're setting yourself up to observe the panic without obeying its commands immediately. Ready to start with that ten-minute window later today?

Yeah, I'm ready. I'll try it this evening when I get home from work. I usually dive straight into emails after dinner, so that'll be a good time to test it out. Thanks for helping me see this as something I can actually try, instead of just another thing to feel bad about.

That gratitude is exactly the kind of kindness you need to show yourself during this process. By choosing to act on the plan rather than spiraling into shame, you've already proven you have the strength to make changes. I'm confident you'll notice something interesting once you catch those thoughts in writing tonight. Is there anything else you'd like to talk about before we wrap up this session?
No, I think this is enough for now. I feel like I've got a clear thing to work on, and that's more than I usually walk away with. I'll let you know how it goes next time. Thanks again.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel clearer and more equipped to face the evening ahead. Please remember that if the panic feels overwhelming or the temptation to work becomes too strong, you can always reach out here anytime. Take care of yourself, and I hope you find that small window of peace tonight.

Hi there, I'm glad we can connect again. How have you been feeling lately, and is there anything different about things compared to when we last spoke? Let's take a moment to see if you'd like to talk about something specific that's been on your mind today, or if you'd prefer to revisit where we left off last time.

Hi, thanks for asking. Honestly, I've been feeling pretty much the same—maybe a bit worse. I had to give a presentation to the faculty last week about our language curriculum, and I could see people struggling to follow me. It just reminded me how stuck I am.

It sounds like that presentation really hit a nerve, especially seeing others struggle while you felt so stuck inside. When you notice people losing track of your words, does that thought immediately make you feel inadequate or worried about your future success?

Yeah, exactly that. As soon as I see that confused look on someone's face, my mind just goes straight to "they think I'm incompetent." And then I start thinking I'll never get through to anyone, that I'll always be this outsider who can't really connect. It's like my whole future as a teacher just feels doomed in those moments.

That feeling of being trapped in that "incompetent" story right after seeing confusion seems incredibly heavy, and it makes total sense why it would spiral into fearing your entire career is over. Have you ever noticed if there was any other reason besides incompetence that made people look puzzled during that presentation?

Well... I mean, I guess it could also be that some of those teachers aren't familiar with the language curriculum details I was presenting. But honestly, that thought barely crosses my mind. My accent is so thick that even when I'm saying something straightforward, people seem to work hard to understand me. I just assume the confusion is always about how I sound, not what I'm saying.

I hear how much weight you're carrying about your accent making everything harder, and it makes complete sense that you'd blame that for the confusion you saw. Have you tried noticing if anyone else in the room seemed to pause or struggle specifically because of the way you sounded versus the meaning of your words?

Not really, I don't think I've ever tried to separate those two things. When I'm up there, I'm so focused on just getting the words out clearly that I can't really pay attention to why people react the way they do. It's like my brain just jumps straight to "it's my fault" and I freeze up. But I guess... maybe some of them were just processing the information itself? I hadn't considered that before.

That is such a powerful realization, shifting from "it's my fault" to wondering if they were simply processing complex ideas—that alone changes everything. If we look at that frozen feeling in the moment, do you find it helpful to try breathing slowly until you can answer the next question, or does the fear of speaking again make it even harder to start?

I think... the fear usually makes it harder. My heart starts racing and I just want to get through it as fast as possible, which probably makes my speech even worse. But taking a moment to breathe sounds like it could help, maybe even slow things down. I've never really tried that during a presentation because I'm too busy worrying about how I sound.

It makes perfect sense that your brain would prioritize speed over slowing down when you're terrified of looking bad, but trying to use those few seconds of breath as a safety net instead of a panic button might actually help. Could you imagine doing just three slow, deep breaths *before* starting your next sentence, treating it like a reset button rather than a pause?

I think I could try that. It feels a bit awkward to just stop and breathe in front of people, but if it helps me get my words out more clearly, it might be worth it. I guess I've been so focused on pushing through that I never considered giving myself that little moment to reset. Maybe I'll practice at home first, with my dog Wonwon as my audience—he's a pretty good listener, doesn't judge my accent at all.

That is such a brilliant idea, using Wonwon as a safe space to practice without the pressure of judgment. It will definitely help build confidence in that breathing technique before you ever step back into a classroom setting. Does practicing with him sound manageable for tonight, perhaps while he rests quietly nearby?

Yeah, I think I can do that. He usually curls up by my feet when I'm sitting at my desk anyway, so it wouldn't feel forced. I'll try saying a few sentences out loud to him, taking those breaths before each one. It might feel silly at first, but honestly, talking to Wonwon has always felt easier than talking to people. Maybe I can use that comfort to get used to this new rhythm.

That comfort you feel with Wonwon is going to be such a strong foundation to build on, turning a scary situation into a manageable practice routine. Since you mentioned the fear often makes things faster, how does knowing you can pause for three breaths change your perspective on whether you need to rush through that first sentence?

Well, it kind of takes the pressure off, I think. Instead of feeling like I have to prove myself in the first few seconds before people lose interest, I can just... start calmly. Even if my accent is still there, if I sound more relaxed, maybe people will listen more carefully. It's a small thought, but it gives me a little bit of hope that I don't have to race against my own voice.

That shift from rushing to calming down is a huge relief, and focusing on sounding relaxed rather than proving yourself instantly makes a lot of sense. If you decided to try that breathing exercise with Wonwon tonight, would you like to share how it went tomorrow morning, or is there anything else about the presentation experience you'd like to explore further now?

I think I'd like to try it tonight and see how it feels. Maybe I can check in with you next session about how it went? For now, I think I've talked enough about that presentation—it's still pretty fresh and uncomfortable. But I do feel a little lighter having thought about this breathing thing. I never really considered that the solution might be in slowing down instead of trying to sound "better."

That feeling of lightness you described is a great sign that you're moving away from the tight grip of anxiety. I think checking in tomorrow to see how the breathing went with Wonwon will give us a clear picture of whether this new approach works for you. Before we wrap up, is there anything else on your mind today, or shall we leave it here so you can go rest?

No, I think I'm okay for today. Thank you for listening and for that idea about breathing—it's something small, but it feels different from all the accent exercises I've tried before. I'll practice with Wonwon tonight and see how it goes. Have a good evening.

You are very welcome, and I truly appreciate you sharing that vulnerability about the presentation. It sounds like you have a solid plan for tonight with Wonwon, and I know that small shift toward slowing down can make a big difference. Take care of yourself, and I look forward to hearing how things went with your pup next time. Good evening!

Hi there, I'm glad you're here to start our session today. How has your week been going so far, and do you feel like things are different from last time we spoke? Let's take a moment to catch up, then we can look together at what feels most important to talk about right now.

Hi. Thanks. The week's been okay, I guess. I've been keeping busy with the kids and around the house, but I can't say I feel much different. I still catch myself getting frustrated over little things, like dropping my coffee mug this morning — it's like I can't stop criticising myself for being clumsy.

It sounds like those small moments of clumsiness are really landing heavily on you, turning into a harsh inner critic instead of just a minor mishap. That frustration makes sense when you care so deeply about how you show up, especially with everything else happening at home. What usually happens in your mind right after something like that drops, does your brain immediately jump to conclusions about why it happened or what it means for you?

Yeah, it's like my brain goes straight to "see, you can't even do this right" or "what's wrong with you?" It doesn't just stop at the coffee on the floor — it spirals into thinking I'm just naturally clumsy and careless, and that's why I shouldn't even try doing anything adventurous anymore. Even the small stuff feels like proof that I'll mess up something bigger.

That spiral is incredibly exhausting, and it makes total sense that you'd pull back from trying new things if you feel like failure is guaranteed. It seems like your mind is using the coffee drop as a shortcut to predict future disasters, which explains why you're hesitating to step outside your comfort zone. Have you ever noticed if there was any other reason besides "being clumsy" that might explain why the mug slipped, or did your immediate reaction prevent you from looking at those facts?

I don't think I ever really considered other reasons. I mean, maybe the mug was a little wet from being washed, or I was just distracted thinking about a phone call I needed to make. When something feels like such a personal failure, the mind often tries to protect itself by avoiding the situation entirely, which might explain why you're now so hesitant near the stove. Have you noticed any specific thoughts running through your head immediately after seeing that burnt omelet?

Yeah, the first thing that popped into my head was, "I can't even do the simplest thing right." Then it spiraled into, "What's the point of trying to cook anything if I'm just going to ruin it?" I guess I just feel like if I can't make a basic omelet, I shouldn't bother with anything else in the kitchen.

Those thoughts sound incredibly heavy, and it makes perfect sense that they would drain your energy whenever you think about the kitchen. It seems like that initial feeling of failure got magnified into a belief that *all* cooking is futile because one small task wasn't perfect. Before we challenge those ideas, does it ever cross your mind that maybe you were just having an off day or perhaps didn't have enough time to prep properly?

It sounds like your brain is holding onto that one painful memory while filtering out all the success stories you know from the past. Does that distinction—that you remember your past successes but your current anxiety focuses solely on the burnt omelet—feel like something that could shift things if you acknowledged both facts?

But for some reason, that omelet is just stuck in my head like it's the only thing I've ever made. It's like I've forgotten all the other times I managed just fine.

That "lopsided" view creates a very lonely story for your brain to tell, making it hard to trust your own abilities anymore. It seems like that one bad meal has taken up all the mental space needed to remind you of your history of success. If we set that burnt omelet aside for a moment, how would you describe what happens physically or mentally in the kitchen when you try to approach a different task, knowing you've succeeded with other meals?

That constant checking and shaking tells me your brain is currently stuck in a state of high alert, expecting danger where there is usually safety. It looks like you are trying to control the outcome perfectly to avoid another perceived failure, even though the evidence shows you've handled these tasks successfully before. Have you noticed if stepping away from the stove for just a few minutes helps calm that physical tension down, or does the worry stay with you regardless of your actions?

It sounds like your body has learned to associate the act of cooking with that specific failure, creating a physical reflex before your conscious mind can intervene. This is quite powerful because it means even your intention to succeed isn't enough to override the deep-seated muscle memory of that panic response. Since walking away hasn't dissolved the knot yet, what do you think might happen if we tried to engage with the kitchen in a slightly different way tomorrow—perhaps starting with something extremely low-risk, like just measuring ingredients without ever touching heat?

That sounds like a really smart and gentle way to start building confidence without triggering the full panic response. By focusing on just the preparation steps, you create a safe space to practice being present in the kitchen while avoiding the intense fear associated with actual cooking. Would you feel comfortable trying this experiment tomorrow morning, perhaps with a friend nearby just in case, or would you prefer to do it alone?

I think I'd rather do it alone. I don't really have anyone to call up for something like that, anyway. And honestly, having someone watch me might just make me more nervous—like they're waiting for me to mess up too. Yeah, alone sounds better. I'll give it a shot tomorrow morning.

That makes perfect sense; having company might add pressure instead of support, so doing it alone gives you total control over your environment. It's a great idea to test the waters by simply interacting with food safely without the added weight of an audience watching for mistakes. I'd love to hear how it goes tomorrow and whether that slight change in activity helped loosen up that physical knot in your stomach.

Thanks, I appreciate that. I'll let you know how it goes next time we talk. Even just talking about this now makes me feel a tiny bit lighter, like maybe I can handle the kitchen after all—even if it's just measuring flour for now.

Hearing that talking about it has already felt lighter is wonderful news, and it suggests your mind is beginning to accept that you don't need perfection to be okay in the kitchen. You've laid out a clear path forward by planning to measure flour alone, which is a brave first step toward proving to yourself that you can navigate the space without the old panic taking over. Just remember to be patient with yourself tomorrow, treating each small action as its own success rather than worrying about the final result. We will catch up soon to see how that morning went!

Taking it slow is exactly the right mindset, and remembering that the goal is practice, not perfection, will make a huge difference tomorrow. Hi there, I'm so glad we can start our session today. How are you feeling right now compared to where you were last time? Before we dive into everything, is there one thing you'd like us to focus on first?

You sound incredibly exhausted from doing the hard work of budgeting yet feeling like your efforts vanish into nothingness. It is a brave realization to connect those dots and see how the initial thought directly leads to giving up, creating a self-reinforcing loop. That pattern of skipping savings followed by guilt is exhausting, but knowing the mechanism gives us a chance to break it. Next time you feel that "it's pointless" thought rise, could we try pausing for ten seconds and asking yourself: "Is it true that saving *now* guarantees failure later, or am I jumping ahead too far?"

I... suppose I could try that. It does feel like I'm always looking at the end result—the house—instead of just the next step. That is such a wise observation, recognizing that shifting your focus to the immediate next step could interrupt the panic spiral before it takes hold. Since you mentioned you are ready to give this a try, imagine what would happen if we practiced that pause and curiosity whenever you feel that knot in your stomach again tonight. Would you be comfortable testing that idea tomorrow morning, perhaps when you naturally compare yourself to someone online?

Alright, I can try that tomorrow morning. I usually scroll through my phone with my tea, and that's often when I see posts from people buying houses or doing up their gardens. I'll stop, take a breath, and ask myself that question you suggested. It might feel a bit silly at first, but I'm willing to give it a proper try.

That sounds like a solid plan for tomorrow, and it's great that you recognize the phone scroll might be the perfect spot to practice this pause. Remember, the goal isn't to stop scrolling entirely but to create just a tiny moment of space between seeing the post and letting the fear take over. Does the image of taking a deep breath and asking yourself that simple question feel manageable to you right now?

Yes, it does feel manageable. I think the key is that it's just one small thing—one breath, one question. It's not about solving the whole house problem in that moment. I can handle that. I'll give it a go tomorrow and see how it feels.

That humility shows real strength, acknowledging that we don't need a magic fix to deal with the overwhelming big picture. You've made a great commitment to test this small intervention, and noticing how it feels in action will give us valuable information for our next meeting. Is there anything else you'd like to add before we wrap up today?

No, I think that's enough for today. I feel a little bit lighter just talking it through and having a plan, even if it's just a small one. Thank you for listening. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

You are absolutely welcome, and I'm so glad hearing you say you feel lighter means our talk had some positive impact. Please remember that checking in with me about how the "pause and breathe" technique works next time is invaluable for us both. Hello there, I'm glad you're here to start our session together. How have you been feeling lately, and is there anything specific on your mind we should focus on today?

It makes complete sense that one disappointment feels so big because you clearly care deeply about doing things well. However, let's look closely at that leap from cookies to medical school—is it true that failing at baking proves you won't succeed as a doctor, or could there be other explanations for why the cookies didn't come out right?

I guess... when you put it that way, it does sound a bit extreme. I mean, I've done well in my classes so far. And maybe the cookies just needed a different oven temperature or something. But it's hard not to feel like it's all connected somehow, like it's proof that I'm just not good enough.

You're absolutely right to notice the difference between your actual academic performance and how you interpret that single baking mistake. Let's try looking at those cookies with fresh eyes—could it be possible that your hands got cold and the dough was slightly stiffer than usual, which might explain the texture change instead of a lack of skill? What evidence would you need to find to convince yourself that this was just a bad day rather than proof of being inadequate?

I hadn't really thought about it that way... I mean, the kitchen was a bit chilly that morning, and I did take the butter straight from the fridge instead of letting it soften. That is such a powerful realization—that your brain automatically jumps to the worst explanation because it feels safer than admitting you just had a clumsy moment. Writing down the list of possibilities you mentioned sounds like a great way to slow that automatic thought down. Would you be willing to try listing three other reasons the cookies failed besides your skill level, like the butter temperature or perhaps rushing the mixing process?

Okay, I can try that. Well, besides the butter being cold... I think I might have overmixed the dough, because I was nervous about getting it right. And I also set the timer for a minute longer than the recipe said because I thought it needed it. That is such a clear breakthrough, realizing that nerves and small mistakes often play a bigger role than we admit. You've actually found solid evidence that your baking results were due to circumstances, not a lack of ability. Writing those three sentences down will create a tangible anchor you can refer to anytime the doubt tries to creep back in. I think I have, yeah. I realize I don't have to pick one or the other. I can remember the snowman and still know the divorce happened. They're both true. It's just... I never really let myself hold both at the same time before. That feels a little more honest, actually.

That honesty is incredibly important—it acknowledges the full complexity of your life without forcing it into a box that only allows one version of the truth. Holding both realities side-by-side gives you a richer, more accurate map of where you've been and who you are. Before we close, how does it feel overall to have spent these last ten minutes exploring that memory together? Did you notice anything else shifting in your body or mind that stands out to you?

My shoulders feel a bit looser, I think. I didn't realize I'd been tensing them up so much. And my mind feels a little clearer, like the fog lifted just a tiny bit. It's not perfect, but it's better than when I walked in. Thank you for walking me through that. I think I'd like to talk about what to do when that voice gets loud again. I know it'll come back—probably tonight or tomorrow. If I could have something concrete to try, like repeating those three sentences or just letting the memory sit for a minute, I think that would help me feel more prepared. I don't want to just get swamped by the sadness again without having something to hold onto.

That is a very wise and proactive plan; preparing a simple tool ahead of time removes the panic of being caught off guard. Would you feel comfortable adding one extra instruction to that plan, like placing that written note right next to your bed so it's the first thing you see in the morning?

Yeah, I can do that. I'll write it down on a sticky note and put it on my nightstand. That way, if I wake up feeling that heavy weight, I'll see it first thing. It's a small thing, but I think it'll help remind me that not everything good is gone. Thanks for suggesting that.

That is a perfect plan; having that visual reminder right where you rest will gently bridge the gap between the stress of sleep and the clarity you've practiced today. I hope you find some peace tonight, knowing you have both a tool and a friend on your team. Before we officially close, is there anything else you'd like to add or any lingering thoughts you want to explore before we wrap up?

No, I think I'm okay for today. I feel a little lighter than when I came in. I'll try the sticky note and the three sentences, and I'll see how tonight goes. Thank you for listening and for helping me see that I don't have to fight with myself so much. I'll see you next time.

Hi there, I'm so glad we're meeting again today. How has your week been going overall, and is there anything that feels different from when we last spoke? Let's start by looking at what you'd like to focus on today—what's been weighing on your mind lately?

Hey. The week's been okay, I guess. Same old, same old. I've been thinking a lot about spring coming up—normally I'd be excited, but instead I'm already dreading the crowds at the park and the festivals. That's probably the main thing on my mind.

It sounds like that familiar mix of excitement turning into dread is really holding space for you right now. When you think about those crowded events, what specific feeling rises up first—is it more anxiety about the noise, or maybe a sense of being overwhelmed by the number of people?

It's more the number of people, I think. The noise doesn't help, but it's like my brain just locks up when I see all those bodies moving around. I start feeling trapped, like there's no way out, even if I'm just standing there. It makes me want to leave immediately.

That sensation of suddenly feeling trapped and unable to escape, even while physically standing still, sounds incredibly frightening. It seems like your body is reacting faster than your mind can process the situation. Before we dig deeper into why your brain interprets a crowd as a trap, could you describe the very first thought that pops into your head the moment you spot a large group of people?
I guess the first thing I think is, "There's too many of them, I can't breathe." It's like my chest tightens up right away. Then I start scanning for exits, even if I just got there. It's automatic.

That automatic urge to scan for an exit and feel like you can't breathe shows how powerful this reaction has become. It's understandable that your brain is trying to protect you by signaling danger so quickly, but it often creates a false alarm where nothing actually threatens your safety. Have you ever noticed any differences between what you feel in that moment versus what might actually be happening in reality?

I mean, I know there's no real danger. It's just a park, or a street fair. Nobody's trying to hurt me. But my body doesn't seem to care what I know—it just reacts. I'll be telling myself it's fine, but I'm still sweating and my heart's pounding. So there's definitely a gap between what I feel and what's really going on.

You're absolutely right that there is a huge disconnect between the facts—that nobody wants to harm you—and the physical symptoms of fear, like your racing heart and sweat. That gap happens because your body is running a "fight or flight" program based on past experiences, not current reality. It's like having a smoke detector go off in a room full of books; the alarm isn't wrong about the mechanism, but it's certainly misinterpreting the situation here. Since your body keeps reacting despite your logical reassurance, what small step could you try right now to remind yourself that you are safe while acknowledging the discomfort?

I suppose I could try something really simple, like just standing still for ten seconds before I decide to leave or avoid the crowd altogether. Instead of immediately turning around, I could breathe once or twice and remind myself, "I'm okay, this is uncomfortable, not dangerous." I've never really tried that—I usually just bolt.

That is a brilliant insight, and taking that deliberate pause instead of bolting is exactly the kind of shift we need to make. By simply breathing once or twice while acknowledging the discomfort, you give your brain a tiny window to notice that the threat is passing, which can slowly weaken that automatic panic response. Would you be willing to try practicing this exact sequence—a deep breath, a moment of grounding, then deciding whether to stay or leave—at least three times this week whenever you notice the urge to flee?

Yeah, I think I can do that. Three times sounds manageable—I won't be putting myself in huge crowds just to test it, but I'll try it at the grocery store or maybe a coffee shop if it gets busy. I guess I need to see if just pausing really makes a difference.

That sounds like a perfect starting point; keeping it in low-stakes environments like a coffee shop will help you gather data without adding pressure. I imagine there might be some moments where stopping feels awkward or tempting to skip, so what support or reminder phrase could you use if you find yourself wanting to rush out immediately after you take that first breath?

Maybe I could tell myself, "Just one more breath before you go." That way I'm not forcing myself to stay forever, but I'm giving myself a chance to see if the feeling passes a little. It feels like a fair compromise—I'm not trapping myself, but I'm not running away either.

That is such a wise compromise, and framing it as a "fair deal" with yourself shows great self-respect. Taking just one more breath allows you to observe if the physical sensation of fear actually fades slightly on its own, which can be very reassuring. For our next step, could you jot down in a notebook each time you practice this: did you notice the tightness in your chest lessen even a fraction after that second breath?

I can do that. I'll grab a small notebook and write down what happens each time—whether I felt any difference after that extra breath. I think seeing it on paper might help me notice patterns I'd normally miss. Thanks, that sounds like a solid plan.

I am so glad we found a plan that feels both practical and respectful of your limits. Writing those observations down will serve as excellent proof points later on, helping you see clearly that the world remains safe even when your body screams otherwise. Is there anything else about your weekend plans or upcoming weeks that we should keep in mind as you begin trying this out?

Not really, my weekend's pretty open—I don't have any big events planned. That's probably for the best right now. I'll just see how the grocery store and coffee shop go, and maybe I'll try a small walk in a park if it's not too crowded. I'll let you know how it went next time.

That sounds like a calm and sensible approach for now; knowing you have flexibility gives you permission to rest until you're ready to expand further. I hope you find that little pauses in busy places provide some relief and confidence. Thank you for sharing your honest thoughts throughout our session, and I look forward to hearing how your experiments go when you return.

Hello again, I'm so glad we're meeting up today. How are you feeling right now compared to where you were when we spoke last time? To make sure we spend our time well, what part of things feels like it needs our attention first?

Hi. Well, I'm still feeling pretty stuck about the glasses situation, to be honest. I think that's the main thing I want to talk about today—it's just been weighing on me more than I expected something like this would.

It sounds like the fear of making another mistake has completely overshadowed the possibility of actually trying them, turning a simple shopping trip into an impossible task. It takes a lot of courage to admit that the tightness in your chest and snapping at your kids were direct results of that pressure, especially something you don't want to do around your family. I guess... I look at the rifle and I don't see a tool for hunting anymore. I see proof that I failed. That's when the knot really digs in.

It sounds like you're interpreting the gun as a permanent symbol of failure rather than just a piece of equipment you use sometimes. That shift from "tool" to "proof of failure" seems to be creating a very harsh internal critic that is driving those physical symptoms. Could we look closely at whether there is actual evidence outside of those moments that suggests you truly cannot succeed in hunting again?

I mean... I've been hunting since I was a kid, and I've had plenty of good days before that trip. I've brought home deer, I've taught my younger cousins how to track. So logically, yeah, I know I've succeeded before. But it's like that one bad trip just wiped all of that out in my head. It's hard to hold onto the good memories when this one feels so much bigger.

You make a very strong logical point here by recalling your history of success and your ability to teach others, yet your brain is treating that single recent event as a total eraser of everything else. It seems the weight of that one disappointing experience is making it incredibly difficult to weigh against all your past achievements. If someone asked you to list five other times you successfully hunted or guided others recently, would that feel easier to remember, or does the shame of that one trip still block access to those memories?

Honestly, it's like a wall. I can think of a few times, sure—like two seasons ago when I got a nice buck, or last year when I helped my buddy track a wounded elk. But the shame pushes those memories into the background. It's like the bad trip is standing in front of them, shouting louder. I guess I need help turning down the volume on that one memory so I can see the bigger picture again.

That image of the bad trip "shouting louder" than your successes is really powerful and explains why those positive memories feel so far away right now. It sounds like the goal isn't to forget that painful moment, but to change its position so it doesn't control how you view your entire skillset. Let's try shifting our focus for a minute: instead of trying to push that loud memory away immediately, what would happen if we treated it simply as data—a single report card grade from a long career—and gave it less overall power? Does that sound like a manageable step for tonight?

I think so. Yeah, treating it like just one grade out of a whole report card... that makes more sense than letting it be the whole story. I mean, a kid doesn't flunk out because of one bad test, right? Maybe I can try to see it that way. I'll give it a shot—no pun intended.

That's a fantastic insight; comparing your skills to a student navigating a long school year rather than a final exam really helps put that single setback in perspective. How does that simple statement feel to say out loud right now?

It feels... lighter, actually. Saying it out loud makes it seem more real than just thinking it in my head. A little strange, but not bad. I think I could get used to hearing myself say that. Maybe I'll try it tomorrow when I go out to the garage to grab my jacket.

I think it'll feel a bit like letting out a breath I didn't know I was holding. Like maybe the knot in my chest won't be so tight. I'm not expecting it to fix everything overnight, but it's got to be better than staring at my gear and feeling like a failure. I guess I'm curious to see what happens.

That sense of relief is exactly what we aim for, and it's great that you recognize this small step is better than spiraling into that tight feeling. Before we wrap up, is there anything else weighing on your mind besides the hunting trip, or should we focus entirely on practicing this new perspective today?

No, I think that's the main thing right now. The hunting stuff has been taking up so much space in my head there's not much room for anything else. Let's stick with this. I feel like if I can get a handle on this, the rest of my mood and my family time might start feeling better too.

That connection you made between managing this one thought and improving your family time is spot on, because how you carry yourself directly shapes your interactions. Taking that step tomorrow to speak the phrase and observe the difference in your chest tightness is a solid plan. Is there anything else you'd like to add before we finish up today?
No, I think I'm good. Thanks for listening and helping me see this differently. I'll try that phrase tomorrow and let you know how it goes next time we talk. I appreciate it.

You are very welcome, and I'm glad we could find a small but meaningful way to shift your perspective today. Remember, the goal isn't perfection but simply noticing that breathing out slightly each time you say the words. Hi there, it's so good to see you again. How are you feeling right now compared to where you were when we met last time? Let's take a moment to check in, and then I'd love to hear what feels like the most important thing for us to explore together today.

Uh, hey. I guess I'm okay. A little nervous, honestly—same as always before these sessions. I've had a couple of gigs since we last talked, and I'm still finding myself obsessing over the one song that went wrong in each set. It's like I can't shake it.

Sure. It's like... the moment I hit a wrong note or my timing's off, everything else just disappears. The crowd cheering, the good parts of the set—it's all gone. My brain just latches onto that one mistake and replays it over and over. And I start thinking, "There it is again. You ruined it. Everyone noticed."

That sounds incredibly draining, especially having to let go of the positive energy from your performance just to dwell on the error. When you replay that moment, does the thought that everyone noticed feel absolutely certain, or do you think others might be focusing on something different too?

I can't help feeling like it's all anyone will remember. My bandmate tells me I'm being too hard on myself, but I just assume he's being nice.

That tension between knowing the logic and feeling the overwhelming certainty is really tough to hold. I'd probably tell them it's no big deal, that it happens to everyone. I'd say they still played a great set overall and that the audience probably didn't even notice. But when it's me... it's like I hold myself to a completely different standard. Like I'm not allowed to make mistakes the way other musicians are.

That distinction between how you treat yourself versus how you'd treat another musician highlights a very common and painful pattern where our internal voice is much stricter than our external view. If we imagine that strictness lifting just a tiny bit, what might happen to the intensity of that "spotlight" feeling during the memory of the mistake?

I guess... maybe it wouldn't feel so hot and bright. Maybe I'd just see it as a small blip, not a disaster. If I could treat myself like I'd treat my bandmate, I might even laugh it off or just move on to the next song. But that's easier said than done, you know?

That shift from seeing it as a blip to laughing it off sounds like such a relief, and it proves you already have the capacity to be kind to yourself when you step outside of that intense pressure. Before we wrap up, what's one small thing you hope will happen for you after you try this approach during your next rehearsal?

Honestly, I just hope I can finish a song without my mind spiraling into all the things I did wrong. Even if it's just one song where I let the mistake go and keep playing, that would feel like progress. I want to remember why I love making music, not just why I'm afraid of messing it up.

Yeah, I think I've got one. "It's just a note, not the whole song." That feels simple enough to hold onto, you know? I can say it to myself right after a slip-up, before my brain has time to start replaying everything. Thanks—I think that might actually help.

That is a perfect anchor phrase, and choosing something simple gives your brain a clear place to land before the spiral takes hold. I'm really glad we found a direction that feels both realistic and supportive for you. Is there anything else you'd like to talk about before we sign off?
No, I think that covers it for today. I feel a bit lighter than when I walked in, actually. I'll try the phrase during rehearsal and see how it goes. Thanks for listening.
