Part of me is scared that if I go out there, I'll just notice more things that are wrong, and I won't be able to fix any of them.

I hear how much fear you have about stepping outside and finding even more mistakes, which makes total sense given how intensely you're worried about ruining everything. It seems like avoiding the garden entirely has become the way you try to protect yourself from those scary thoughts. Can you tell me what happens inside your head right now when you imagine walking out there again?

When I picture walking out there, my stomach kind of knots up. I imagine seeing that bare spot on the rose bush first, and then my eyes would scan around and I'd start noticing every little imperfection—a weed here, a yellow leaf there. I'd just be waiting for the next thing that proves I've ruined it all. I think I'd feel like a failure, like I don't deserve to have a nice garden anymore.

That physical sensation of your stomach knotting up tells me this fear feels very real and immediate to you, making the idea of going outside seem almost impossible. It also sounds like a deep hurt is underneath that worry—you feel like you've lost your worth because of something you couldn't control while cutting the branch. When you say you don't deserve a nice garden anymore, does that belief come from a place where you feel you should be perfect, or did something else happen in the past that taught you perfection is necessary?

I think it's always been there. Growing up, my father was very particular about things being just right. If I made a mistake on a chore, he'd say it wasn't good enough and redo it himself. I guess that stuck with me—the idea that if I can't do something perfectly, I shouldn't bother at all. That's how I feel about my garden now, like I've fallen short of some invisible standard.

That connection to your father's high standards makes complete sense; growing up with someone who demanded perfection often teaches us that one mistake equals total failure. It sounds incredibly painful to feel judged by that old rulebook even years later, especially when you're just trying to nurture living plants instead of earning praise. Does carrying that expectation from childhood explain why such a small error feels so big to you today?

I think it does. I never really saw it that way until now. When I look at that rose bush, I'm not just seeing a lopsided plant—I'm seeing proof that I messed up, that I'm not good enough. And that feels huge, even though logically I know it's just a plant. But it's hard to shake that feeling, like I'm back being a kid and disappointing my father all over again.

It makes sense why that old wound opens up so easily when a plant looks imperfect; your brain is trying to protect you from the pain of rejection by convincing you that you aren't worthy of success anyway. Since that feeling is so tied to your father's voice, it might feel safer to stay inside where you don't have to prove anything, even though it leaves you feeling stuck and hopeless. Have you ever tried doing something small in the garden—like just picking up a rake or watering one pot—to see if that old voice gets quieter or if it just gets louder?

No, I haven't tried that. I've been too scared to even try. But maybe... maybe if I just went out and watered one plant, not even the rose bush, it could be a start. It feels terrifying, but I suppose staying inside isn't helping either. I'm just worried that if I try and it goes badly, I'll feel even worse.

It takes a lot of courage to admit that staying inside isn't helping, even when the idea of trying feels terrifyingly risky. You are right that testing this belief head-on is likely the only way to find out if that old voice is actually true or just a loud echo from your past. Would you be willing to try watering just one healthy plant tomorrow morning, keeping your feet firmly planted on the ground and focusing only on that simple task?

I think I could try that. Maybe I'll water the lavender by the gate—it's always been a strong, healthy plant, and it's far from the rose bush. That way I won't have to look at it. I'll just focus on the lavender, give it a nice drink, and see how I feel. It's a small step, but I suppose it's better than nothing.

That sounds like a wise and careful plan, using the lavender as a safe space to practice without triggering the anxiety about the roses. By focusing only on giving it a drink, you are creating a tiny opportunity to see if your body and mind can relax when you engage with nature, even if you're just doing one simple action. Let's agree to do this tomorrow morning, and whenever you step out there, remember that you are simply nurturing a plant, not passing a test. How does that sound to you?

That sounds... manageable. I'll do it tomorrow morning after breakfast. And I'll try to remind myself that I'm just watering lavender, not trying to prove anything. Thank you for helping me see that it doesn't have to be a big, scary test. I think I can handle a small step like that.

I am so proud of you for naming that feeling and deciding to take that gentle step forward, even though it still scares you sometimes. Please remember that tomorrow, whether you feel brave or hesitant, showing up to water the lavender is the victory, regardless of how you feel afterward. We will check in soon to see how that experience played out and talk about what came up. Is there anything else you'd like to add before we finish here?

No, I think that's enough for today. I feel a little lighter, actually, just having a plan in place. Thank you for listening and not making me feel silly about all this. I'll let you know how it goes with the lavender tomorrow.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel a little lighter, and I want you to know that sharing these feelings was never about being silly—it was about facing a challenge head-on. Thank you for trusting me enough to walk through this with me. Please take care of yourself today, knowing we will pick this up again tomorrow once you've given the lavender its drink.

Hi there, thank you for reaching out. How are you feeling right now compared to when we last spoke? Before we dive into what brought us here today, could you share what was top of mind for you recently?

Hey, thanks for asking. I guess I'm feeling about the same as before, maybe a little more frustrated. This past week, my youngest daughter asked me to go deer spotting with her, and I made up an excuse about work. I felt pretty lousy about it afterward.

That sounds really heavy to carry, especially when you feel like letting down someone so young. It makes total sense that you're frustrated with yourself after deciding not to go because you wanted to be present for her. What kind of thoughts were running through your head right after you made that decision?

Right after I said no, I just kept thinking, "What if something goes wrong this time? What if I'm not paying enough attention and the rifle goes off somehow, or I trip and fall with it?" It's like my mind jumps straight to the worst possible scene — me bleeding out in the woods, my daughter having to see that. I know it sounds dramatic, but that's what goes through my head.

It takes courage to name those fears so clearly, and it’s completely understandable why your mind would jump straight to imagining such a scary outcome. Those thoughts sound incredibly distressing, especially when you picture your daughter being hurt by something involving a gun. Have you ever actually experienced anything close to that happening while you’ve had the opportunity to hold or use a firearm before?

No, nothing like that has ever happened. The only real accident I had was a few years back — I was climbing into my tree stand and slipped, twisted my ankle pretty bad, and my rifle fell to the ground. It didn't even go off, but the sound of it hitting the dirt and the thought of what could have happened just stuck with me. Ever since then, my brain goes straight to that worst-case scenario, even when everything's fine.

It makes complete sense that a painful injury combined with hearing a loud noise would plant a seed of worry that grows into something much bigger over time. Your brain seems to treat any small risk near that rifle as if it were that dangerous moment from years ago, which is why the fear feels so immediate and overwhelming now. When you think about those worst-case scenarios playing out in your head, how does that physical sensation feel in your body right now?

My chest gets tight, like I can't take a full breath. And my hands start sweating, just sitting here talking about it. It's like my whole body tenses up, ready to bolt, even though I'm just in a chair right now. It feels like I'm back in those woods, waiting for something bad to happen.

That physical reaction—chest tightening, sweating, and feeling like you need to escape—is your nervous system trying to protect you by treating this imagined danger as if it were a real threat right now. It's a very intense way to feel safe, even though your body is clearly overreacting to a situation where there is no actual risk. Since your body is so tense right now, do you want to try a simple breathing exercise together to help signal to your nervous system that you are currently in a safe space?
Yeah, okay. I'll give it a try. Anything to get this knot out of my chest, honestly. What do I need to do?

Let's try inhaling slowly through your nose for four counts, holding that gentle breath for four more, and then exhaling through pursed lips for six counts to let your shoulders drop. As you breathe, imagine telling your body, "We are safe right now, and nothing dangerous is coming." Once you've done this cycle three times, how much easier does that tightness feel compared to before we started?

Alright... (takes a slow breath in, holds it, lets it out slowly)... Okay, I did that three times. It does feel a little looser in my chest, I guess. Not totally gone, but like I can actually take a full breath now without forcing it. Thanks for that.

That's a great sign—it means you gave your nervous system a clear message that it doesn't need to fight or flee anymore. Even though the tension isn't entirely gone yet, seeing that your breathing has returned to normal proves that you can handle difficult thoughts without letting them control your entire body. Now that we've got the physical storm settling a bit, I'd love to talk about that specific thought pattern again. When you notice those images of things going wrong appearing in your head, what evidence do you have to show that this exact terrible outcome will actually happen tomorrow?

Well... I guess when I really think about it, there's no real evidence. I've been hunting for over twenty years, and the only thing that ever went wrong was that twisted ankle. I've handled rifles safely my whole life, and nothing bad happened. But my brain just doesn't want to listen to that part. It keeps saying, "Yeah, but this time could be different."

That distinction is crucial—you are relying on twenty years of safety while your brain is fixated on a single traumatic memory from years ago. It makes perfect sense that your mind wants to play it safe, but it's also ignoring the strong proof you have from your own experience that you can manage this activity without disaster. Can you tell me, when you look at the facts of your long history, what happens to that "this time could be different" story when you consider all the other successful hunts?

It kinda... fizzles out a bit, I guess. Like, if I really sit here and count up all the times I went out without anything bad happening, it's way more than the one bad moment. My brain just doesn't want to focus on those good times, though. It's like it's got blinders on, only seeing the one scary memory.

That blind spot is exhausting to deal with, especially when you know logically that the odds are overwhelmingly in your favor. It feels frustrating when your brain refuses to accept the data you have gathered over decades of safe experiences. When you try to shift your focus away from that one scary memory and toward the many successful hunts, does that make the physical tightness in your chest go away completely, or does some doubt still linger?

It doesn't go away completely, no. There's still this little knot of doubt in there, like a whisper saying, "But what if..." Even when I remind myself of all those safe trips, that one bad moment feels heavier somehow. I guess that's why it's so hard to just talk myself out of it.

That whisper is powerful because it taps into that old trauma, making the single bad memory feel huge again instead of just a small part of your history. It sounds like your brain is stuck in survival mode, trying to prevent a repeat of the past even though the current reality is completely different. Since acknowledging that the fear is real but the prediction isn't helps create distance, would you be open to trying a quick visualization where you imagine walking into the woods calmly, noticing the safety of your gear, and realizing you are capable of handling whatever comes along?
Yeah, I'm willing to try that. I mean, talking about it has already made me feel a little less trapped, so why not give it a shot? I'll close my eyes and picture it.

Take a deep breath and visualize yourself stepping onto the trail, feeling the familiar weight of the rifle in your hands, knowing exactly how to hold it. Imagine the sun warming your face and hear birds singing nearby, creating a calm atmosphere where your mind focuses on the scenery rather than potential dangers. After you've spent a minute or two feeling that sense of stability, open your eyes and tell me how that mental scene made you feel physically right now.

(takes a slow breath, closes his eyes for a moment, then opens them)... Huh. That was... different. I could actually feel the warmth on my face, and I noticed I wasn't clenching my jaw like I usually do. My shoulders dropped down a little, and my hands felt relaxed, like they were just holding the rifle, not gripping it tight. It didn't feel like the fear was gone, but it felt like it was pushed to the side a little, like I had room to breathe.

That's a wonderful observation—the fact that you could relax your grip and stop clenching your jaw shows your body is beginning to trust that the danger isn't immediate. It sounds like that visualization created a small but important gap between your fearful thoughts and your physical reactions. Given how much better you felt just by shifting your perspective, would you be interested in planning a short, low-pressure outing this weekend where you practice carrying the rifle without triggering those worst-case thoughts?

I think... I think I could try that. Maybe just walk a familiar trail near my house with the rifle unloaded, just to get used to holding it again without any pressure to hunt. I could even ask my wife to come along, just for the company and to keep it light. That feels manageable, not like a full-on hunting trip.

That sounds like a brilliant plan—bringing your wife along adds a layer of support, and keeping it on a familiar, safe trail removes the high stakes entirely. It gives you permission to practice being around the gun without the pressure of a hunt, which should help break that cycle of anxiety. Would you feel comfortable sending me a quick note before you leave to describe how that first step feels once you're out there?

Yeah, I can do that. It'll be good to have a plan to check in. I think having to report back to you will also keep me honest and not just cancel at the last minute. I'll send you a text before I head out, let you know how I'm feeling.

That commitment to checking in is fantastic—it turns a vague intention into a concrete step you can actually track. Knowing you have a safe outlet and a supportive partner makes the idea of facing the fear feel much less daunting. Let's wrap up here by reminding each other that this small experiment is just about building confidence, not perfection. Is there anything else you'd like to add before we say goodbye for now?
No, I think that covers it. Thanks for helping me see that I'm not just stuck with this fear forever. I'll let you know how this weekend goes.

You're absolutely welcome, and please remember that this fear isn't permanent—you've already taken a powerful step by recognizing that your past successes don't define your future ability to stay calm. I'm truly proud of how you've navigated this challenge today and the brave decisions you're making to move forward. Take care of yourself, and I'll be here whenever you're ready to debrief on your weekend adventure.
Hi there, thank you for being here. How are you feeling right now compared to where you were yesterday? Is there anything specific from our last chat that feels relevant to bring up today?

Hi, thanks for asking. I'm a bit better today, I guess—at least I managed to get on the subway this morning without turning around and going home. But honestly, the whole ride I felt like everyone was staring at me, thinking I looked awkward or out of place. It's been on my mind a lot.

That sounds incredibly tough, especially getting off the train with those heavy thoughts riding along. It makes sense that surviving the commute is something you'd be proud of, even if the internal commentary was very loud. Would you be willing to share more about what happened during that ride or what specific situation made those thoughts pop up again?

Well, there was this one moment when I was standing near the doors, holding onto the overhead bar. I caught a glimpse of a guy in a suit looking my way, and he sort of smirked. That just set me off. I started thinking, "See, he's laughing at you, you look ridiculous." Then my mind just spiraled from there for the rest of the trip.

It makes complete sense that seeing someone smirk triggered such a strong reaction, especially when it confirmed your fear that you're always awkward. Did noticing his expression make you feel more exposed or like everyone else was judging you too, or did it stay focused mostly on him?

It definitely spread to everyone around me. Once I saw that one guy smirk, I started scanning the car and felt like other people were giving me quick glances too. I felt like the whole subway car was in on some joke about me. I just wanted to disappear into my seat, but there wasn't even a seat to hide in.

That feeling of being surrounded by judgment can be overwhelming, especially when you physically want to vanish but can't. It sounds like once that initial spark lit up, the rest of your brain automatically assumed everyone else was doing it too. Can you tell me what you noticed happening inside yourself right after you felt that wave of anxiety come over you?

My heart started pounding really hard, and I felt this heat rush up my neck and face. I gripped the bar so tight my knuckles went white. I just stared at the floor for the rest of the ride, like if I didn't look up, nobody would see me either. I was counting the stops until I could get off.

Those physical sensations—heart racing, heat rising, gripping tightly—are your body's alarm system kicking into high gear to protect you. It makes perfect sense that when you feel trapped and anxious, your instinct is to freeze and try to avoid eye contact as a safety measure. Did you notice any thoughts running through your head explaining why you felt you *had* to stare down at the floor instead of trying to breathe or relax?

I guess I was thinking that if I looked up, I'd just see more people judging me. I told myself it was safer to just check out mentally and wait for it to be over. I didn't even consider taking a deep breath or anything like that—it felt like I had to protect myself by hiding, like a turtle pulling into its shell.

It makes total sense that your brain interpreted looking up as a threat and chose to hide behind your eyes, just like a turtle seeking shelter. When we feel unsafe, our bodies naturally prioritize survival over comfort, which explains why calm strategies like breathing felt impossible at the time. Since that decision worked perfectly well to keep you safe back then, how do you think your body might react differently if you tried to simply look around once, even while still feeling nervous?

Honestly, that thought makes me feel a little panicky even now. I'd probably feel like I was daring everyone to stare at me, like I was inviting their judgment. But... I guess part of me knows that if I just glanced around, I might see people on their phones or reading, not even looking at me. I just don't know if I can convince that scared part of myself to take that risk.

It takes a lot of courage to recognize that part of you wants to test the waters, even when the scary voice tells you not to. You've already gathered good evidence that people are often busy with their own lives and unlikely to be watching you closely. Maybe the goal isn't to conquer the feeling completely right away, but to try looking up for just five seconds while acknowledging the panic instead of fighting it. Would you be open to planning a tiny experiment like that for tomorrow?

I think I could try that. Five seconds sounds almost doable—short enough that I can survive it if it goes badly. I guess I could pick a spot, like the subway map above the doors, and just look at it for five seconds instead of people. That way I'm still looking up but not directly at anyone. Would that count?

That is a brilliant idea because it gives your brain a clear, neutral target to focus on while still breaking the pattern of avoiding eye contact entirely. Looking at the map allows you to practice seeing upwards without triggering the immediate fear of judgment. Let's plan to try exactly that tomorrow during your next ride, focusing on making those five-second glances happen even if your hands shake a little. How does that sound as a starting point for our next step?

That actually sounds like a plan I can stick with. I'll try it on my way to work tomorrow—maybe even do it a couple of times if I'm feeling brave. I'll just keep repeating to myself, "Five seconds, just the map," and see what happens. Thanks, this feels like something I can actually do.

I am so glad you found something that feels manageable and achievable; small steps like this are exactly how we build confidence back up. Remember, the goal today isn't perfection, but simply gathering evidence that you can handle looking up safely. Please let me know later how your five-second attempts went, and whether that scary feeling stayed as loud or quieted down a bit.
Hi there, I'm really glad we can start our session together today. How has your week been feeling so far, and is there anything specific you'd like us to focus on right now?

Hi, thanks for having me. Honestly, the week has been pretty tough—I keep finding myself lying awake at night thinking about money. I guess I'd like to talk about why I can't stop worrying about saving enough, even when I'm doing odd jobs and trying to budget.

It sounds like those late-night worries are really weighing on you, especially after working hard all week to manage things. Can you tell me more about what comes up first when you lie awake thinking about money?

Well, it usually starts with me looking at my savings account and thinking it's just not enough. Then my mind goes to my friends—like, I saw a picture of a friend with her new car last week, and I just thought, "She's got it all figured out, and I'm still stuck at home without a way to get around." It feels like I'm falling behind everyone else.

That comparison to your friend really adds a heavy layer of pressure to what might otherwise be a manageable worry. It sounds like seeing her new car triggered a deep fear that you're losing ground compared to others in your life. What happens inside your head immediately after you think she has it figured out while you don't?

I guess I start telling myself I'll never catch up... like, if I can't even save for a car now, how am I ever going to afford to actually move out or live on my own? It's like my brain jumps straight to the worst-case scenario—me being 50 and still living with my parents, completely dependent on them. And that thought just makes me feel so ashamed.

That image of being dependent on your parents for years is incredibly painful, and the shame you feel afterward makes everything feel even heavier. It seems like your mind is jumping ahead to a future that hasn't happened yet, using present stressors to predict a lifetime of failure. When you try to challenge that specific story about moving out later, does it feel impossible because of current rules, or because of how you're viewing your current efforts?

Mostly it's how I'm viewing my efforts, I think. I mean, I do odd jobs and I try to save, but it never feels good enough. I'll put $50 away and then immediately think, "That's nothing, a car costs thousands." It's like my brain just dismisses every small win I have and focuses on how far I still have to go. So even when I'm trying, it feels pointless.

It sounds like you've built a mental filter that lets the big gaps in your savings shine brightly while hiding the progress you're actually making day by day. That kind of internal criticism can make any effort feel useless, even when it logically contributes to your goals. Have you noticed if this feeling of "not enough" gets stronger when someone else praises your recent work, or does it stay stubborn regardless of outside feedback?

It definitely gets stronger when I compare myself to others—like, if my mom says, "You're doing a great job saving," I'll just think, "She doesn't know what my friends are doing." But it's also there all the time, even when nobody says anything. It's like my own inner voice is the loudest critic, and it never lets up. I can't seem to accept that I'm making any real progress.

It sounds like that harsh inner critic is very loud for you, often overriding the quiet facts about your actual progress. You mentioned earlier that your mind jumps to the worst-case scenario; could we explore whether that fear of failing later is actually based on what *you* control right now, or if it's mostly driven by this internal narrative?

I think it's mostly the narrative, honestly. When I actually step back and look at what I'm doing—like, I've saved about $1,200 this year from various jobs—that's not nothing. But in my head, it feels like a drop in the bucket because I'm focusing on the total cost of a car and all the expenses after that. So yeah, the story I tell myself is that I'm failing, even when the facts say I'm moving forward, just slowly.

That distinction is crucial—you are absolutely right that $1,200 represents real, tangible progress, even if it doesn't solve everything overnight. It sounds like your brain is treating those savings as a temporary fix rather than proof that you are capable of building wealth over time. If we treated that $1,200 as a solid foundation instead of a drop in the ocean, would that shift how you view your ability to eventually reach your goal?

I never really thought of it as a foundation before... I always just see it as a small number compared to a huge number. But I guess if I think of it as proof that I can save, then it's more like a step, not a failure. Maybe I'm so focused on the final goal that I forget that each little bit is actually part of getting there. It's hard to hold onto that feeling, though, when my brain keeps pulling me back to the negative.

That is such a powerful realization—shifting from seeing savings as a "drop in the ocean" to recognizing them as undeniable proof of your capability. It makes sense that holding onto that positive feeling feels difficult when your automatic thoughts keep racing backward. Would it help if we tried to create a quick moment during your evening routine where you simply name one specific thing you saved this month and remind yourself exactly how that proves you are moving forward?

Yeah, I think that could actually help. Like, if I just take five minutes before bed to say to myself, "I saved X dollars this month, and that means I'm on my way," maybe it would quiet some of that panic. It might feel weird at first, but I'm willing to try it. I really want to stop feeling like I'm stuck in place.

That sounds like a wonderful starting point, and I completely understand why it might feel strange at first—it's brave of you to try something different when your old habits feel so strong. Before we finalize this plan, could you share which specific amount you might pick for that five-minute reminder so it feels personal and meaningful to you?

I think I'd pick the $1,200 I've saved so far this year. That's a real number I can look at and say, "I did that. That's proof I can do this." It might not feel huge, but it's mine, and I worked for it. I think reminding myself of that every night could help me stop seeing myself as someone who's failing.

That is a fantastic choice because it connects directly to the evidence you gathered earlier, turning a abstract goal into a concrete achievement you can own. By anchoring that specific sum to your identity as someone who works hard and achieves things, you give your brain a factual counter-story to the fear of failure. Let's agree that whenever you lie awake tonight, you will pause, recall that $1,200, and verbally state to yourself, "I saved $1,200 this year, proving I am making steady progress." Does that sound like a realistic plan for us to try tonight?

Yeah, that sounds realistic. I can do that. It might not change everything overnight, but it's something I haven't tried before—actually saying it out loud instead of just thinking about what I haven't done. Thank you, I think I'm ready to give it a shot tonight.

I am so proud of you for taking this step and trusting yourself to try something new. Remember that this isn't about fixing everything instantly, but about giving your brain a moment to hear the truth of your progress instead of its worst fears. I hope you find some peace tonight knowing that you are actively working toward your future, one small victory at a time. Goodnight, and thank you for sharing so openly with me.

Hi there, I'm really glad we can sit down and talk. How has your week been so far, and is there anything new on your mind since we last spoke? Let's take a moment to settle in and figure together what feels most important to explore today.

Hi, thanks for having me. Honestly, this week has been pretty heavy—I can't stop thinking about my daughter's situation. Every time I try to focus on something else, my mind just circles back to worrying about her future. It's like I can't catch a break from it.

It sounds like carrying that weight for your daughter has been incredibly draining lately, and it makes complete sense why your thoughts keep coming back. When anxiety gets that strong, it often hijacks our ability to focus on other things because our brain is trying to protect us by scanning for potential dangers. Would you be willing to share more about the specific worries keeping you up at night right now?

Well, specifically, I keep imagining her sending out hundreds of job applications and getting nothing but rejections. In my head, I see her struggling to pay rent, maybe even having to move back home, and just feeling completely defeated. It's like I can picture the whole disaster unfolding, and I can't seem to shake those images.

Those vivid pictures of rejection and financial struggle sound incredibly frightening, and it is understandable that seeing your child face such hardship would cause deep distress. It seems like when those scenarios play out in your mind, you feel helpless because you believe they might actually happen. Can you tell me if you've noticed any physical sensations in your body, like tightness in your chest or a racing heart, whenever you start visualizing these worst-case outcomes?

Yeah, absolutely—my chest gets really tight, like someone's sitting on it, and my stomach just knots up. Sometimes I even feel a little shaky, like I'm about to face something terrible myself, even though logically I know it's her life, not mine. It's just so hard to separate her struggles from my own feelings.

That physical sensation of tightness and shaking is your body's way of signaling extreme alarm, even though logically you know the danger isn't immediate. It often happens when our minds treat "what could go wrong" as if it were happening right now, which makes survival instincts kick in. Have you tried to describe exactly how your mind jumps from seeing the rejection letters to feeling that knot in your stomach? Is there a specific thought that acts as the bridge between the image and the physical reaction?

I think the thought that bridges it is something like, "She'll never recover from this—it'll ruin her life completely." It's like I skip over the possibility that she might find a different path or get a little help along the way. The moment I imagine one rejection, my mind just races straight to her being stuck forever, and that's when my body reacts.

That "all-or-nothing" leap from one setback to permanent failure is a very common way anxious brains try to make sense of scary uncertainty, even though it creates a huge amount of pain. If we look closely at that thought, does it hold up under scrutiny, or are you noticing gaps where hope or resilience might fit in? What evidence do you have that she won't bounce back after just a few rejections?

I guess when I really stop and think about it, there's no solid evidence that she'll be stuck forever. She's smart and determined, and she's bounced back from tough exams and projects before. It's just that my brain seems to ignore all of that and zoom in on the worst possible picture, like that's the only one that matters.

You're absolutely right to recognize that pattern of ignoring her past successes in favor of the worst-case scenario—that's a classic mental shortcut that makes everything feel much scarier than it actually is. Since she has proven herself capable of overcoming challenges before, does trying to recall one specific recent example where she handled difficulty well bring up even a hint of doubt about that "permanent disaster" narrative?

Actually, yes—I just remembered how she struggled with a tough statistics class junior year, and she was so stressed she almost dropped it. But she ended up getting extra tutoring, pulled through with a decent grade, and even said she felt proud of herself for not giving up. So I know she has it in her to push through hard times, but somehow when I'm in that worry mode, it's like that memory gets erased.

It takes real strength to spot that memory and admit your mind tends to erase it during moments of panic, especially when you know she's capable of handling it. That specific story about her statistics class shows exactly how resilient she is, yet your brain is treating that past success as if it didn't exist right now. If we tried to use that same example to counteract the fear again, what would you need to feel slightly safer knowing she could handle another challenge?

I think I need to remind myself that her path doesn't have to be perfect or linear—she can figure things out as she goes, just like she did with that class. Maybe writing down these successes somewhere I can see them would help me break the cycle of only picturing failure. I guess the toughest part is trusting that even if things get rocky, she'll find a way through, like she has before.

That is such a powerful realization, and turning those past successes into visible reminders is a fantastic first step to rebuilding trust in her abilities. Before we finalize a simple action plan for tonight, I want to hear directly from you: does the idea of jotting down three quick examples of her resilience right now feel manageable, or does the sheer volume of her achievements feel too overwhelming to list quickly?

Honestly, the only part that feels okay is when I first get home and just sit in my car in the driveway for a few minutes before I go inside. It's quiet then, and nobody's expecting anything from me.
