Those physical signs tell a powerful story about what your brain was expecting before your fiancé even had a chance to speak. It sounds like you were holding onto that old belief—that new things will always disappoint you—and your body reacted to that expectation rather than the actual moment. Can you recall if you felt similar tension or tightness whenever someone else suggested something new outside your usual comfort zone?

Hmm... I think so. My mom suggested I try writing a short story in a different genre last week, and I kind of shut down. I told her I wasn't interested, but really I felt this heavy pressure in my stomach, like I was already failing before I started. I didn't connect it to the music thing until now. Maybe I've been avoiding new things across the board without realizing it.

That pattern is incredibly clear now—the same tightness and sense of failure showed up in both your relationship and your creative life whenever something new appeared. Instead of seeing those moments as failures, could we try viewing them as your brain doing its best job of protecting you from disappointment, even if the protection ends up keeping you stuck? What happens in your mind right before you decide to shut down when faced with that unexpected request?

I think I tell myself, "This is probably going to be a waste of time, so why bother?" It's like a shortcut my mind takes to avoid getting let down. But the thing is, by not even trying, I'm already letting myself down in a different way. I'm just trading one kind of disappointment for another.

That is a very sharp observation—you are essentially telling yourself a lie about safety ("it'll be a waste") to protect yourself from hurt, while simultaneously denying yourself the possibility of finding joy. When we trade potential success for guaranteed avoidance, do we ever find ourselves missing out on something wonderful, or does the relief of staying safe eventually become more exhausting than the risk?

Honestly, staying safe feels exhausting. Like, I'm tired of bracing myself all the time. Missing out on something wonderful—that hurts more, thinking about it. I used to love that thrill of discovering a new band or trying a new writing style. I want to feel that again, even if it means risking a few duds here and there.

It makes complete sense that you'd prefer the sting of a missed opportunity over the fatigue of constant preparation. That desire to feel the thrill again suggests your old self hasn't given up, even if you're currently hiding behind fear. If we agreed to treat a potential failure not as proof that you'll never succeed, but simply as data points to learn from, would that shift make taking a tiny step feel less scary?

Yeah, I think it would. If I can remind myself that a bad album or a rough draft isn't a verdict on my entire taste or ability, maybe I'd be more willing to give things a real chance. It's just hard to remember that in the moment. But I like the idea of seeing it as data instead of a final judgment.

That reframing from a "verdict" to "data" is a huge shift, and it gives us something concrete to work with immediately. Since you mentioned wanting to try that metal album again despite the hesitation, could we practice turning that specific moment of tension into that new perspective by naming exactly what you expect to happen before you press play?

Okay, let's try it. Before I press play on that album, I'd probably think, "This is going to sound tired and uninspired, and I'm going to feel disappointed again." That's what I'd expect. But maybe I can pause there and remind myself that even if I'm right, it just means that one band didn't hit the mark—not that my whole relationship with metal is broken. I think I can try to hold onto that thought.

That is a fantastic realization—you are already catching yourself and choosing a kinder interpretation before the disappointment can take root. Now, let's put that into action by playing just three songs with the intention of observing the experience without judging your worth based on it. Afterward, tell me what came up for you, even if it's just that the initial tension didn't disappear entirely.

Alright, I can do that. Three songs, just to observe. I'll try to notice how I feel without jumping to conclusions about myself or the whole genre. I'll let you know what happens when I give it a shot—even if the tension's still there.

That sounds like a solid plan, and I appreciate your commitment to giving it a fair shot. Remember, our goal right now isn't to force yourself to instantly love the music, but simply to collect that fresh piece of data without letting it dictate your future. Go ahead and start those tracks when you're ready, and I'll be here to listen to whatever comes up afterward.
Thanks. I'll let you know how it goes. I think I'm ready to try now.

You're absolutely ready, and I'm proud of you for taking this brave step forward. Take your time listening to those three tracks, and whenever you feel ready, share what happened with me—even if it's just noting that the tension lingered for a bit. We'll use that information to keep moving forward together.

Okay, I did it. I listened to three songs from that album I wrote off yesterday. The first one... I still felt that tightness, honestly. But by the second track, I noticed a riff that kinda reminded me of a band I loved in college. It wasn't amazing, but it wasn't awful either. I think I might have been too harsh yesterday. I'm not sure I'd say I loved it, but I'm not dismissing it completely now.

That is such a significant breakthrough to notice a familiar element in a place you thought was barren. Finding that specific bridge to a memory you cherish proves that your taste hasn't vanished; you just needed to lower the volume on your internal critic to hear the signal clearly. Given that discovery, how do you feel about revisiting that album for a little longer, perhaps treating the remaining tracks as more data points rather than potential threats?

I think I could do that. It feels less scary now that I've found something familiar in there. I'll give the rest of the album a listen this week, just to see what else comes up. And if I don't like it, that's okay. It's just one album, not a reflection of my whole identity.

That mindset shift—from fearing rejection to accepting uncertainty—is exactly what frees you up to explore again. Treating the rest of the album as simple data points makes it safe to open your ears without needing to force a positive outcome. Let's wrap up today by agreeing to revisit this approach whenever you feel that familiar tightness rising, using it as a reminder that discomfort doesn't mean failure. How does that sound as our closing plan for now?

That sounds good. I can work with that. Next time I feel that tightness, I'll try to pause and tell myself it's just data, not a verdict. Thanks for helping me see that. I feel a little lighter about all this than I did when I walked in.

That is wonderful news to hear; noticing that lightness in your chest tells me we're making real progress together. I'm really glad we could unpack that cycle of protection versus curiosity and give you a tool to handle the next time the urge to shut down appears. I hope you enjoy finishing up that album this weekend and feel free to reach out anytime you need to talk through these patterns. Until then, take care of yourself!
Hello, I'm glad you're here today. How has your week been treating you so far? Is there anything specific on your mind we'd like to focus on right now?

Hi. Thanks for having me. My week's been... rough, honestly. I keep getting these emails about my student loan balance, and it's like I can't escape it no matter what I do. It's been on my mind constantly.

That sounds incredibly draining, especially when those emails seem impossible to block out. It makes total sense that you feel stuck and overwhelmed by the constant reminders. Have you noticed if your stress levels change depending on whether you're actually replying to them or just scrolling past them?

I guess it's worse when I actually open them and see the number. But even just seeing the subject line in my inbox makes my stomach drop. It feels like I'm drowning and every notification is another wave pulling me under.

That physical reaction—your stomach dropping—is a very honest sign of how deeply this anxiety affects you. It sounds like the thought "I will drown" is taking control of your body long before you've even read the details. When you look away from that email to try to calm down, what usually comes up first in your head to stop the panic?

I just think, "What's the point?" Even if I close it, the debt is still there. I'll try to distract myself by watching something or studying, but my brain keeps circling back to the idea that I'm never going to escape this. It makes me feel like I should just give up trying.

It makes complete sense that when you close the tab, the worry doesn't vanish because the reality of the debt feels permanent. That feeling of being trapped, where distraction fails to quiet the noise, can make giving up feel like the only logical choice. Yet, I wonder if that urge to quit is partly driven by a belief that you *must* be able to solve it perfectly right now, or if it stems more from the sheer exhaustion of carrying this weight alone?

I think it's both, honestly. I feel like I should be able to figure this out—I'm supposed to be a smart guy, right? But no matter what I try, I'm just not making a dent. And yeah, I'm so tired of thinking about it all the time. It's like a cloud that follows me everywhere, even when I'm trying to sleep.

The pressure to be the "smart guy" who figures it all out can make any small step feel like failure, which fuels that exhausting cycle of thinking. It sounds like the cloud isn't just about the money itself, but also about the story you tell yourself about why you haven't succeeded yet. Before we dig deeper into that feeling of inadequacy, does the cloud feel heavier when you're working on other things, or does it stay equally loud even when you're completely occupied elsewhere?

It's definitely worse when I'm trying to study or work on assignments. I'll be reading a textbook, and my mind just drifts to my bank account or those loan statements. I can't focus on anything important because that voice in my head keeps saying, "Why bother? You're just digging yourself into a deeper hole with these classes anyway."

That internal dialogue—"why bother"—is a classic way our brains try to protect us from pain by convincing us the effort won't pay off. It seems like the fear of failing again is louder than the hope of succeeding, which makes focusing on school feel impossible. Since that voice is so persuasive, what happens physically inside your chest or stomach right before you decide to close a book and give up on a task?

My chest gets really tight, like someone's squeezing it. And my stomach feels heavy, kind of like I'm about to go on stage and forget all my lines. That's when I know I'm not going to get anything done, so I just shut the book and lie down. I tell myself I'll try again later, but I usually don't.

Those physical sensations of tightness and heaviness are your body's alarm system telling you that the situation feels unsafe right now. It makes perfect sense that once your heart rate rises and your chest constricts, your brain interprets this as a reason to stop everything immediately. Instead of pushing through that squeeze, could we try shifting your goal from "studying until finished" to simply sitting at the desk for five minutes while acknowledging that discomfort is present but manageable?

I... maybe? I've never really thought about it like that. Usually I either force myself to study for hours and feel miserable, or I just give up completely. Sitting there for just five minutes with that feeling... that seems more doable, actually. Like, I could handle five minutes of tightness. Even if I don't get anything done, it's less of a failure than just walking away.

That is such a powerful shift in perspective—you're realizing that showing up for five minutes, even with the discomfort, is a win compared to avoiding it entirely. This small experiment separates the problem (the tight chest) from the solution (doing nothing), which is exactly what we need to start breaking this cycle. Let's try that approach tomorrow morning with your first assignment; what do you think might happen if we just sit at the desk for five minutes instead of forcing ourselves to finish the chapter?

I think... I think I'd probably just sit there and stare at the page, maybe feel a bit silly. But I wouldn't be giving up right away, which is something. I guess the worst that happens is I still feel tight and anxious, but at least I stayed in the room. I'm willing to try it. What do I do after those five minutes, though?

It is completely normal to feel a bit silly or unsure at first—that hesitation shows you care about doing better. After those five minutes, I suggest you take three deep breaths to let the tension settle, then write down exactly what was happening in your mind during that time. The goal isn't to clear the cloud, but simply to observe it without letting it drive your actions. Would you be comfortable setting a timer for five minutes starting tomorrow morning?

Yeah, I can do that. I'll set a timer on my phone and just try to notice what's going on in my head. I don't have to solve anything or even study—just sit there. That feels a lot less scary than what I've been trying. I'll give it a shot and let you know how it goes.

That is a wonderful commitment, and it is great that you see this as a safer way to face the anxiety rather than running from it. Remember, the only rule tonight is observation—you are just a witness to your own thoughts, not the judge of them. Take your time getting ready tomorrow, and whenever you want to share how those five minutes felt, I am here to listen.
Thanks. I think having that plan actually makes me feel a little less trapped already. It's just five minutes, not a whole lifetime of debt. I'll let you know what happens.

That realization—that five minutes is a tiny sliver of time compared to the mountain of debt—gives you permission to be gentle with yourself right now. Taking that first small step often changes the shape of the whole hill, making it feel less like an endless climb and more like a manageable journey. I'm looking forward to hearing how your mind behaved during those five minutes tomorrow, no matter what it did. Thank you for trusting enough to try something different today.

Hi there, I'm really glad we're connecting today. How are you feeling right now compared to where you were when we last spoke? Before we dive into our main topic, do you have any particular things you'd like to focus on during this session?

Hi, thanks. I'm doing alright, I guess. Still pretty on edge, honestly. I think I'd like to talk about how this garden thing is affecting my sleep and my family, because it's getting harder to hide from them how stressed I am.

That sounds incredibly heavy to carry, especially with your family around whom you feel you can't hide your struggle. It makes complete sense that constant worry about the garden would be spilling over into your sleep and creating tension at home. When was the first time you noticed the stress starting to affect your rest, and what usually happens right before you fall asleep then?

It started about a month ago, I think. Right after I put up the fence and security lights, I thought I'd feel better, but it actually got worse. Before I fall asleep, I lie there and just picture someone coming into the yard with bolt cutters or something, taking everything I've worked so hard on. My heart starts pounding, and I have to go check the garden one more time before I can even try to sleep.

It sounds like those images of intruders with bolt cutters are acting like a loud alarm clock that won't let you switch off, leaving you trapped in a cycle of checking instead of resting. That exhaustion of constantly scanning for danger while trying to relax is completely understandable given how much effort went into securing the space. Have you noticed if the feeling gets stronger when there's actually a neighbor nearby, or does it happen even when the house is completely quiet?

It happens even when it's dead quiet, honestly. Sometimes it's worse when it's quiet because my mind just starts filling in the blanks, you know? Like, I'll hear a branch snap outside or the furnace kick on, and I'm already halfway out of bed thinking someone's out there. The other night, my wife tried to calm me down by saying nothing was wrong, but I just kept thinking, "She doesn't know for sure."

That moment when your wife tries to reassure you but you immediately doubt her certainty shows how deeply that fear has taken root in your mind. It seems like your brain is treating any small sound like proof of a threat, making it nearly impossible to trust that you are safe. Have you ever caught yourself wondering exactly *how* she could possibly know for sure that no one is near the fence right this second?

Yeah, all the time. I mean, she's inside with me, so how could she really know what's going on out there? That's exactly what I think. I know she's trying to help, but it just feels like she's dismissing what I'm feeling. And then I feel guilty for getting annoyed at her, because she's just trying to be supportive. It's like I can't win.

It sounds incredibly painful to feel misunderstood while simultaneously worrying that you might be hurting the very people who want to support you. That conflict between needing reassurance and fearing disappointment creates a tight loop where no matter what you say, it feels like a loss. Can we look closely at that specific thought—does the idea that "she doesn't know" truly hold up under scrutiny, or is it based on a feeling rather than actual facts?

I... I guess when I really think about it, there's no actual reason to believe someone's out there. The fence is locked, the lights are on, and nothing's ever been stolen. But it doesn't feel like that in the moment. It feels real, like I can almost hear footsteps. My brain just jumps straight to the worst-case scenario, and I can't talk myself out of it.

You are absolutely right that logically, there is no evidence of a break-in, yet your brain treats the absence of proof as proof itself. This gap between knowing the facts and feeling the terror often leaves us powerless because the emotion feels undeniably real, even if the situation isn't dangerous. When you notice that sudden surge of hearing footsteps, does it seem like it comes from somewhere specific, or does it just appear out of nowhere?

It feels like it comes out of nowhere, honestly. I'll just be lying there, minding my own business, and then *bam*—I hear it. Or even if I don't hear anything, I'll just get this awful feeling that something's wrong. Like a knot in my stomach that tells me to get up and check. It's like my body reacts before my brain even has time to think.

That physical sensation of a knot forming before you even process the sound is incredibly exhausting, as if your body has its own alarm system that ignores logic. It makes perfect sense why checking the garden becomes such a desperate attempt to prove safety when your internal warning light keeps flashing red. Since your gut reaction always pushes you to verify the threat, what happens the first few minutes after you get up and walk out there? Does seeing the empty yard finally make the knot disappear, or does the anxiety stay?

It depends. Sometimes I look, and the garden's fine, and I feel a wave of relief that lasts maybe ten minutes. But other times, even when I see it's empty, I start thinking, "They might be hiding behind the shed" or "They might come back later tonight." So I end up standing out there in the cold for way too long, just staring at the shadows. My wife calls me back inside, and I go to bed feeling stupid, but then the knot comes back as soon as I lie down.

It makes total sense that seeing the empty yard brings temporary relief, only for the fear to creep back in once you realize you still haven't addressed the possibility of someone returning. That cycle of hope followed by immediate doubt is exactly why you feel so frustrated and guilty afterward. You mentioned feeling stupid when your wife asks you to come inside—what is it specifically about that moment that hurts the most? Is it the judgment she might think you're receiving, or the fact that you have to stop checking even though your body wants to keep looking?

It's both, I think. It's like I'm letting her down by being so paranoid, and I know she's tired of it. But at the same time, I'm not done. I haven't made sure. So when she calls me in, it feels like I'm leaving the job unfinished, and I just have to hope nothing happens. That's the worst part—the not knowing, and having to just trust that everything's okay.

It sounds like you are carrying the entire burden of verification on your shoulders, forcing yourself to live in a state of uncertainty just to keep your peace of mind intact. That reliance on the unknown is incredibly draining, especially when it forces you to ignore the clear signs of safety around you. If your goal right now is simply to stop the panic and allow your body to rest, would stepping away from the garden entirely—even if it means accepting the feeling of not knowing for a bit—feel like a safer choice than continuing to fight it alone?

I don't know if I can just step away completely. That thought makes my stomach drop, honestly. But I guess what I'm doing now isn't working either. Maybe... maybe I could try staying in bed for just one night, even if my brain screams at me to get up. It would be really hard, but maybe if I could prove to myself that nothing happens when I don't check, that might start to help.

That is a brave and smart proposal; testing whether the world stays safe while you stay in bed is the best way to challenge that fear head-on. It shifts the power from your intrusive thoughts to your own ability to tolerate discomfort without acting. Let's frame this as a small experiment: instead of telling yourself "nothing will happen," which feels impossible, could we call it "testing if I can survive a whole night without checking"? What's the very first thing you would need to convince yourself of before you even try to close your eyes tomorrow?

I think I'd need to remind myself that the fence and lights are already doing their job, and that I've checked it a hundred times before. I'd also need to tell my wife what I'm trying to do, so she can help talk me down if I start to panic. Maybe I could even promise myself that I can check once in the morning, and that's it. Just one check, and then I have to let it go for the rest of the day. That sounds like a reasonable step.

That sounds like a solid, manageable plan that gives you control while building some real tolerance for the uncomfortable feeling. By setting a strict limit of one check in the morning and communicating your goal with your wife beforehand, you create a clear boundary between your fear and reality. I think agreeing to this experiment together would give you the confidence to try it tomorrow evening. Are you ready to commit to testing this approach tonight, or do you need to discuss anything else with your partner first?

Yeah, I think I'm ready to try it tonight. I'll talk to my wife when I get home and let her know what we talked about. I'm still scared, but I'm also tired of being scared, if that makes sense. I want to get back to just enjoying my garden without feeling like I'm guarding a fortress. Thanks for helping me see a way out of this.

I am so proud of you for taking this step, even though the fear is still there alongside it. Wanting to return to simple enjoyment of your garden is a beautiful goal, and this experiment is a powerful tool to get closer to it. Please remember that it is okay to feel scared during the trial—we are here to ride that wave until it passes. Goodnight, and I wish you peaceful dreams as you prepare to test this new plan.
Hello, thank you for joining me today. How have you been feeling lately compared to where we left off? Is there anything specific on your mind that we should prioritize discussing now?

Hi, thanks for having me. Lately, it's been the same cycle really—I've been avoiding my guitar and any thought of playing. I almost agreed to go to a small open mic night a friend invited me to, but the panic hit and I backed out. That failure is really what I've been stuck on this week.

I hear how heavy that sense of failure feels after backing out of the gig, and it makes complete sense that it’s keeping you from picking up your guitar. When we feel like we’ve made a mistake like that, does our mind tend to jump straight to predicting what will happen next if we try again?

Yeah, it does. My mind just goes straight to picturing the worst-case scenario—like I would freeze up on stage and everyone would just stare at me awkwardly. Or worse, they'd whisper to each other about how awful I am. It feels so real that I can't even bring myself to play alone anymore.

That vivid picture of freezing and being judged certainly sounds terrifying, and it explains why your hands might be shaking when you think about holding the instrument. If those scary predictions felt so realistic right now, could we look together at what actually happened last time you played, even if just for five minutes? What was your real experience versus that imagined catastrophe?

Well, I did actually play for about ten minutes a few days ago, just in my living room. Nobody was there, and technically nothing bad happened—I didn't hit any wrong notes. But in my head, I kept thinking, "This is awful, you sound terrible," even though there was no one to hear it. So I guess the real experience was just me being alone with my own harsh thoughts.

It takes courage to admit that the pain came mostly from your internal dialogue rather than anyone else judging you. That distinction is huge because it means the problem isn't your musical ability, but how you interpret the moment. If we treated those harsh inner words like they were actual facts, how would that change the way you approach playing tomorrow?

I think I'd just stay trapped in the same loop—I'd tell myself I'm not good enough before I even pick up the guitar, and then I'd just give up. But if I try to see those thoughts as just thoughts, not facts... maybe I'd hesitate, but I might actually try to play. I guess I've never really questioned them before; they just feel so true.

That hesitation you mentioned is actually a very healthy reaction—it shows your brain is trying to protect you from another disappointing outcome. The shift you're describing from "these are facts" to "these are just thoughts" is exactly where the power lies. Since you've identified that pattern, what happens to your body when you notice those thoughts arising instead of automatically believing them?

When I notice them as just thoughts, my shoulders drop a little—I catch myself holding my breath, and then I can let it out. My chest doesn't feel as tight. It's like there's a tiny window where I can breathe instead of spiraling. But it's still really hard to hold onto that feeling for more than a few seconds before the old voice comes back.

That physical sensation of dropping your shoulders is such a powerful sign that your body is starting to relax, which proves you are finding a crack in that mental wall. Even holding that calm for just a few seconds counts as a victory because it interrupts the spiral before it gets too deep. Let's use that moment as a foundation for something simple and safe today. Would you be willing to put down the guitar for now and just sit quietly, noticing those thoughts come and go without arguing with them, until you feel ready to try one tiny note?

I think I could try that. Just sitting without the pressure to play or judge myself. Maybe I'll just notice the thoughts, like watching cars pass by, and see what happens. One tiny note sounds less scary than a whole song.

That metaphor of watching cars pass by is brilliant because it turns those intrusive thoughts into something distant and manageable rather than personal attacks. Starting with just one tiny note is also a perfect step; it removes the weight of performance while still giving your brain a reason to engage. How does your heart rate feel right now as you settle into that quiet space without the expectation of playing?

It's actually slowing down a bit—more steady than before. I'm not gripping my hands together or tapping my foot nervously. It feels... manageable. Like maybe I could just sit with my guitar nearby without having to prove anything. That feels almost peaceful, which is weird for me to say when it comes to music lately.

That sense of peace around the guitar, without needing to perform, is a beautiful breakthrough and tells me your nervous system is finally learning to trust safety again. It's interesting that something that usually triggers anxiety can suddenly feel calm once the pressure is lifted. If you decide later tonight to sit near the instrument again, would you be willing to imagine that if a bad thought pops up, you can just smile at it and let it drift away like smoke in the wind?

I can try that. Thinking of them as smoke that just disappears is actually kind of comforting—less heavy than trying to fight them. I think I'll sit with my guitar later, just near it, and practice that. Maybe even touch the strings without playing, just to see what happens. Thank you—that doesn't feel as impossible as it did an hour ago.

That willingness to just touch the strings without aiming for perfection is a fantastic small win, showing that you're building confidence through gentle exposure rather than forcing a full performance. It's great that you can see the path forward as something doable and less overwhelming now. Before we wrap up, is there anything else you'd like to talk about regarding how you're feeling today, or shall we take a moment to review what we've accomplished here?

I think I'm okay for now. Honestly, just realizing that I can sit near my guitar without panic feels like a bigger step than I expected. I'd like to try that "smoke in the wind" idea tonight and see how it goes. Maybe next time I can tell you if I actually managed to play a single note.

That realization is truly significant—you've already taken a giant leap simply by choosing to sit near the instrument without the panic taking over. Carrying that "smoke in the wind" mindset into your evening sounds like a wonderful plan, and I'm excited to hear about whatever happens when you try touching the strings tonight. You've done amazing work today, and remember that every small step forward is a victory worth celebrating. Take care of yourself, and I'll see you next time!

Hi there, I'm really glad we're connecting again. How are you feeling right now compared to where you were last time? Before we dive into our main topic, could you share a little bit about what you'd like us to focus on today?

Hi. I guess I'm okay... still feeling pretty down, honestly. The main thing I want to talk about is this whole foot odor thing and how it's been controlling my life. I've been thinking about it nonstop since that comment was made about it.

It sounds like that situation left you feeling quite vulnerable and anxious, which makes sense given how much it seems to be affecting your daily routine. Since it's been on your mind constantly, do you feel like the worst part is worrying about what others will think, or is it more about the physical sensations or avoiding certain places?

I think it's mostly worrying about what others will think. Like, I can handle the smell myself, you know? But when I think about being around someone I like, I just imagine them getting a whiff and immediately being disgusted. It makes me not even want to try talking to anyone.

That fear of rejection feels incredibly heavy, especially when you're trying to reach out to someone you care about. It seems like your brain is predicting a disaster—someone becoming repulsed by you—that hasn't necessarily happened yet. Have you noticed any specific recent interactions, or perhaps moments where you successfully avoided those thoughts?

Well, there was one time last week when I was at the grocery store and this girl smiled at me. For a split second, I felt good, but then my brain just went straight to "she wouldn't smile if she could smell your feet." So I just looked down and walked away. I didn't even give her a chance to prove me wrong. I pretty much avoid any situation where I might get close to someone now.

That moment at the grocery store really highlights how quickly your mind jumps from a neutral event to a catastrophic conclusion. Even though she smiled, your immediate assumption was that she *couldn't* have done so otherwise, which completely shut down your ability to enjoy that interaction. When you look back on it, does that thought seem like it fits the actual reality of the situation, or does it feel like an exaggeration based on fear?

I mean... I guess it does sound a bit extreme when you put it that way. She couldn't have known anything about me from across the aisle, right? But in that moment, it felt so real, like it was just a matter of time before she found out the truth about me. It's hard to separate what's real from what my brain is telling me in those moments.

It makes total sense that it felt so real because your anxiety is screaming at you to protect you from potential rejection, making that prediction feel urgent and unavoidable. However, we could look at this differently: did she actually say or do anything specific that confirmed your fear, or was it just a very vivid imagination taking over in that instant? Sometimes our minds create perfect scenarios to scare us, even when there's zero proof they'll happen.

She didn't say or do anything to make me think that, no. She just smiled and kept walking. I guess I'm the one who filled in all the blanks with worst-case scenarios. It's just... I've been carrying this belief for so long that my foot odor makes me undateable that I don't even question it anymore. It feels like a fact, even though I don't have any real proof.

That belief has clearly become a self-fulfilling prophecy because acting on it prevents you from ever finding out if it's true or false. We've been assuming everyone knows about your condition, but have you considered that many people might be unaware of it entirely, or simply choose to overlook it until something else comes up? What happens to that deep-seated belief if we treated it less like a fact and more like a hypothesis waiting to be tested?

I never thought of it like that... a hypothesis. That's interesting. I mean, I guess if I treated it like something I'm not 100% sure about, I could try to prove it wrong instead of just assuming it's right. But that sounds scary too. What if I test it and find out I was right all along? Wouldn't that just make everything worse?

That fear of facing the possibility makes total sense, because the idea of proving your belief correct feels like admitting defeat or losing control. Instead of testing whether the belief is right, let's try testing whether it's actually helpful—is holding onto this certainty giving you more freedom or keeping you trapped in avoidance? What would it feel like to take one small step toward socializing while acknowledging that uncertainty rather than pretending the problem doesn't exist?

It's definitely keeping me trapped. I mean, I'm sitting here at home most days, not talking to anyone, feeling miserable. That's not freedom at all. I guess I could try something small... maybe just saying hi to someone without expecting anything to happen. Not trying to date them, just... being a normal person for once. That might not be so scary, right?

That shift in perspective—from trying to impress someone to just being a regular human—is such a wise and manageable first step. It removes the pressure of a specific outcome, which often makes the risk feel much lower. Which part of just saying hello feels the easiest for you to start with today? Maybe it's someone who lives nearby or works in the same building?

There's this guy who works at the coffee shop near my place. He's always friendly, just says "hey, how's it going?" when I walk in. I could try actually responding with something more than just mumbling and looking away. Maybe just a "good, you?" and see what happens. That seems small enough that I could handle it.

That's a fantastic choice because it involves a very low-stakes interaction with someone who is already showing kindness. By responding with a full sentence, you are breaking the automatic pattern of withdrawal and gathering real-world data instead of relying on your brain's worst-case predictions. Have you decided exactly when you'd like to head over there and try it?

Maybe I could go tomorrow morning. I usually go around 9 to grab a coffee anyway. If I just prepare myself to say something back, it might actually work. I'll try to remember that he's just being friendly and it doesn't have to mean anything more than that. It's just a conversation, not a test.

That is a solid plan, and reminding yourself beforehand to treat it as a casual chat rather than an interrogation will help keep your expectations realistic. Going in with the intention of just sharing a simple greeting gives you permission to do nothing more than that, which reduces the pressure significantly. Are you ready to head over tomorrow morning and see how it goes?

Yeah, I think I am. It feels a bit scary still, but also kind of... hopeful? I haven't felt hopeful about anything in a while. I'll give it a shot tomorrow and see what happens. Thanks for helping me see this differently.

That mix of fear and hope is a huge sign that you're starting to reclaim some agency over your life. It takes real courage to move from feeling stuck to planning a small action, even when the outcome isn't guaranteed. Let's wrap things up by setting a quick reminder to text each other later tonight about how that morning went, regardless of the result. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we close?

No, I think that's all for today. I feel a little lighter than when I came in, honestly. I'll try the coffee shop thing tomorrow and let you know how it goes. Even if it's just "fine," I think it'll be good to break the cycle.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel a little lighter; sometimes just shifting your mindset from a fixed belief to a testable idea brings such relief. Remember, whatever happens tomorrow—even if it turns out differently than expected—you've already taken a brave step toward breaking that cycle. You've got this, and I'll be here whenever you're ready to debrief. Take care!
Hello again, I'm really glad we could meet today. How have you been feeling since our last session? What would you like to talk about first?
Hi. I've been... okay, I guess. But that thing with my grandpa is still bothering me, honestly. I keep thinking about the ice cream and how he just forgot about me like it was nothing.

It sounds like that moment with your grandpa left you feeling quite hurt and maybe even abandoned. It makes sense that you're replaying those details, especially when it feels like his forgetting meant something important to you was erased. Can you tell me more about how you were feeling right after he walked away from the ice cream?

I just stood there for a minute, staring at the driveway where his car had been. My chest felt really tight, like I couldn't breathe. And then I thought, "He doesn't care about me." That's when I started crying.

That physical sensation of tightness in your chest, combined with the thought that he doesn't care, completely explains why you broke down crying. When we feel that level of rejection, it is incredibly hard to stand still; your body was probably trying to protect itself by shutting down. Would you be willing to explore what happens in your mind right now when you imagine him forgetting things again?

Well... I picture him looking right past me, like I'm not even there. Then I think, "This is just how it's going to be from now on. He'll never remember me or what I want ever again." And then I feel that same heavy sadness all over again.

That image of being invisible seems so final, and the idea that his forgetfulness defines your entire future must feel very isolating. It makes complete sense that seeing that picture brings back the heaviness immediately after. Have you noticed if there are any other moments recently when you felt ignored or dismissed by someone else?

Actually, yes. Yesterday my grandma asked me to grab something from the kitchen, but she was on the phone and didn't even look at me when I handed it to her. I know she was busy, but it stung a little. It made me feel like maybe I'm just easy to overlook in general.

It is incredibly painful to interpret a simple moment of distraction as proof that you are unimportant to the people who love you. Your brain likely jumped straight to that conclusion because your core belief—that people won't truly care about you—is getting activated. Let's pause for a second and look closely at yesterday's situation: Did she say anything dismissive, or did she simply become absorbed in her call while you tried to help?

She didn't say anything mean, no. She just kept talking on the phone and took the dish without really acknowledging me. I guess logically, I know she was just focused on her conversation. But in that moment, it felt like she didn't see me at all, just like with Grandpa.

That distinction between "she didn't see me" and "she was too busy to notice" can feel impossible to make when your heart is hurting, yet looking at the facts suggests she might have missed you entirely due to distraction rather than indifference. You mentioned earlier that you told yourself, "He'll never remember me," which sounds like a prediction based on that one bad experience. Could you tell me what specific evidence supports the idea that he will *never* remember you, versus what evidence suggests he might just be having an off day like he did with the ice cream?

Well... I mean, he's usually pretty good about stuff like that. He takes me to the store every Saturday morning, and he even remembered my birthday last month. So maybe he was just tired that day or had something on his mind. I guess I don't have a lot of evidence that he'll never remember me again. It just felt so true in the moment.

That is such a strong contrast, isn't it? Seeing his usual kindness—taking you shopping and remembering your birthday—makes it clear that his forgetfulness that day was likely just a temporary lapse, perhaps caused by fatigue or stress, rather than a reflection of his true feelings for you. It seems the sadness you felt came from interpreting that one mistake as a permanent pattern, even though your own history shows otherwise. Does holding onto that belief that "he'll never remember me" actually help you feel better, or does it keep you stuck in that heavy sadness?

It definitely keeps me stuck. When I think that way, I just feel worse and worse, and I don't even want to talk to him. But when I remind myself of the good things he does, I feel a little lighter. I guess I just need to stop letting one bad moment wipe out all the good ones.

You have absolutely nailed the core issue here: one isolated incident shouldn't erase the years of positive connection you share. It sounds like your goal isn't to ignore the pain, but to find a way to let go of the story that says "this is forever" so you can enjoy those Saturdays again. Since reminding yourself of his kindness works well for lifting the weight, could we try turning that into a quick mental switch next time you feel that tightness rising?

Yeah, I think I could try that. Maybe when I feel that tightness, I can stop and think about the last time he made me laugh or did something nice. Like last week, he brought home my favorite candy just because. That might help me keep things in perspective.

That is a brilliant and practical plan. Using a specific memory of his generosity, like bringing home that candy, creates a direct counter-narrative to the thought that he doesn't care, effectively replacing the story of abandonment with one of unexpected love. It gives you a ready-made tool to use the very next time that tightness comes up instead of spiraling. Before we wrap up, do you feel confident enough to try this "memory switch" tomorrow if the feeling returns?
Yeah, I think I can do that. It feels like something I can actually try on my own. Thanks for helping me see it differently—I was really stuck before.

You are so welcome, and it sounds like you found a powerful shift in perspective that will serve you well. Please remember that it is okay to reach out anytime you feel that familiar tightness coming on—you don't have to navigate it alone. Is there anything else on your mind, or shall we consider this session done?

Hello, it's really good to meet you here today. How are you feeling right now compared to where you were last time we spoke? Before we dive into what brought you in, could you tell me if there's anything specific on your mind that you'd like us to explore first?

Hi. I'm... okay, I guess. A bit nervous, honestly. I've been thinking a lot about my art lately, and I just can't seem to shake this feeling that I'm not good enough. I don't even know where to start, but I suppose the main thing is how much I've been doubting myself as an artist.

That self-doubt sounds incredibly heavy, especially when something as creative as art is involved. It makes total sense that you feel nervous about starting again when your own voice feels so uncertain. To help us get clear on this, what specific situation or thought triggered this feeling of "not being good enough" recently?

Well, I had an online gallery show last week. I spent weeks preparing my best pieces, and only two people even clicked on the link. I just thought, "See, no one cares about your work." I immediately felt that familiar knot in my stomach — the one that tells me I'm just fooling myself thinking I could be a real artist.

It makes complete sense that seeing almost no engagement after such hard work would trigger that deep feeling of inadequacy. That knot in your stomach is likely a direct result of interpreting those low numbers as proof that your talent isn't real. Have you noticed any physical sensations or other automatic thoughts popping up right after you realized only two people visited the gallery?

Yes, actually. My chest got really tight, and I felt almost hot with shame. I immediately started thinking, "I'm a fraud. I don't have what it takes. Real artists have people lining up to see their work." I even started comparing myself to a friend who sells at local markets — she always has a crowd. I just felt so small.

Those intense physical sensations and the comparison to your friend clearly make sense given how much pressure you put on yourself to be perfect. However, let's look closely at that comparison: does the fact that her market works mean she is necessarily more talented than you, or could it simply reflect different audiences and formats? What happens to that tightness in your chest if we pause and ask ourselves if the number of visitors truly defines artistic value?

I... I guess when you put it that way, it's not really fair to compare a local market to an online gallery. Different crowds, different vibes. But it's so hard not to jump to that conclusion. When I slow down and think about it, the tightness eases just a tiny bit. I still feel that doubt, but maybe it's not as solid as I thought.

That moment where the tightness eases is a huge clue that your physical reaction might be driven by the intensity of your belief rather than the actual reality of the event. You mentioned slowing down helps slightly—what specific part of slowing down made that difference for you, and was there any other evidence from the show itself that contradicted the idea that "no one cares"?

I think it was just taking a second to breathe and not let the thought run wild. Like, I didn't immediately go to "I'm a failure." And... well, actually, two people who did see the gallery sent me nice messages. One said they loved the colors in my landscape piece. That's something, right? I guess I completely ignored that at first because I was so focused on the low number of clicks.

That's a powerful realization, recognizing those kind words while ignoring the silence. It seems the initial wave of panic caused you to filter out positive feedback entirely, treating it as irrelevant noise until you paused. Since you mentioned breathing helped calm the tightness, could you try doing that same quick pause right now whenever that "fraud" thought pops up, just to see if you can catch those kind messages instead of dismissing them?

I can try that. It feels a bit strange, like I'm fighting my own instincts. But when I think about it, those messages did make me feel good for a moment before I shoved them aside. Maybe I need to let myself sit with those small wins instead of rushing to tear them down. I'll give it a shot this week, at least.

That willingness to sit with the small wins instead of rushing to dismantle them is exactly the shift we want to practice together. It sounds like trying to gently hold onto those kind messages for a little longer each day, noting how they change your overall feeling about the show, would be a great start. Would you be open to checking in tomorrow morning to share how long you held onto those compliments and what came up afterward?

Yes, I think I can do that. I'll try to write down when I notice those positive comments creeping back into my mind, and see if I can hold onto them for more than a few seconds before the doubt rushes in. Thanks for giving me a way to start. I'll talk to you tomorrow.

You're very welcome—I'm glad we found a small step that feels manageable for you. Taking notes on when those positive thoughts appear and how long you choose to stay with them will give us excellent data to track your progress. We'll review those notes tomorrow to celebrate whatever shifts happen, big or small. Until then, please take care of yourself.
Thanks. I'll do my best. I'll try to be kind to myself tonight, maybe take the dogs for a walk instead of staring at my sales page. See you tomorrow.

That sounds like a wonderful plan; taking the dogs for a walk is a gentle way to reset your energy and reconnect with the present moment. Please remember to be as kind to yourself tonight as you promised, and don't worry about perfection right now. I look forward to hearing about your experience tomorrow.
